title: Notice of Proposed Amendment to Fifth Circuit Rule 32.3 and Form 6
body: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
bodyShort: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
summary: The Fifth Circuit proposed amending Rule 32.3 and Form 6 to add a generative-AI certification for appellate filings. The proposal would have required counsel and unrepresented filers to certify either no GenAI drafting or human review and approval of all generated text, including citations and legal analysis.
keyProvisions: Would have required Form 6 certification whether generative AI was used in drafting.; If used, all generated text, citations, and legal analysis had to be human-reviewed.; The Fifth Circuit later decided not to adopt this proposed rule.

title: Court Decision on Proposed Rule Regarding Artificial Intelligence
body: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
bodyShort: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
summary: After public comment, the Fifth Circuit decided not to adopt its proposed AI certification rule. The notice leaves no special AI disclosure or certification requirement in effect, but expressly warns parties and counsel that existing appellate duties require careful checking for truthfulness and accuracy.
keyProvisions: The court declined to adopt a special AI rule for drafting briefs.; Parties and counsel remain responsible for truthfulness and accuracy under existing appellate rules.

title: Risks Associated with the Use of AI Tools to Generate Documents for Filing with the Court
body: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Central District of California
summary: The Central District of California Bankruptcy Court’s AI tools notice warns filers that AI-generated court documents may contain fabricated citations, misstatements, or unsupported facts. It advises line-by-line review and verification before filing, and warns that inaccurate or fabricated content may produce sanctions or denial of relief.
keyProvisions: The notice warns that AI tools may generate inaccurate, outdated, inapplicable, or fabricated legal content.; It says filers should conduct careful line-by-line review before filing AI-assisted documents.; Filers should confirm every cited case, statute, rule, and quotation exists and is accurately quoted.; Inaccurate citations or unsupported factual assertions may lead to sanctions or denial of relief.

title: Standing Order Regarding Newly Assigned Cases
body: U.S. District Court for the Central District of California — Judge Michelle Williams Court
summary: Judge Michelle Williams Court’s Central District of California civil standing order requires every motion, pleading, or paper to include a declaration about AI use or non-use. If AI drafted any portion, the filer must verify the content, identify AI-generated portions, and faces sanctions or striking for noncompliance.
keyProvisions: Every motion, pleading, or other paper must attach a declaration disclosing AI use or non-use.; The filer must certify either no AI drafting or that AI-drafted portions were reviewed and verified.; The declaration must identify which portions of the filing incorporate generative AI outputs.; Inaccurate or undeclared AI outputs may lead to sanctions, including State Bar referral.; Failure to submit the declaration may result in striking the filing.

body: U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado — Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell
summary: Magistrate Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell’s District of Colorado guidance discusses responsible AI use and hallucinations in court submissions. title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
body: United States District Court for the Southern District of Iowa
summary: The Southern District of Iowa AI notice permits litigants to use AI to assist legal proceedings but strongly encourages caution. It states that litigants are personally responsible for verifying AI-generated quotations, citations, paraphrased assertions, and legal analysis before submission, and says the court does not currently require disclosure of AI use in filings.
keyProvisions: The page strongly encourages caution when using AI in litigation because of risks of fabricated cases, holdings, or representations.; Litigants are personally responsible for verifying AI-generated material before submitting it to the court.; The verification responsibility expressly includes quotations, citations, paraphrased assertions, and legal analysis.; The court does not currently require disclosure of AI use in filings, but may require disclosure by order in a specific case.; Failure to review and verify accuracy may result in Rule 11 sanctions, monetary penalties, or dismissal.

title: Nebraska Civil Rule 7.1(d) Generative Artificial Intelligence and Certificate of Compliance
body: United States District Court for the District of Nebraska
summary: The District of Nebraska Civil Rule 7.1(d), effective December 1, 2024, requires civil briefs to include a certificate stating either that no generative AI program was used in drafting or that a human signatory verified the accuracy of all generated text, including all citations and legal authority.

summary: A Supreme Court of Indonesia letter of 2 September 2026 circulating draft judgment-writing guidance and templates for consultation. title: Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya v Union of India, 2026 INSC 947
body: Supreme Court of India
summary: Supreme Court judgment of 2 September 2026 setting aside a customs penalty of Rs 425.27 crore because the Additional Commissioner's order relied on AI-generated citations that were non-existent or misrepresented. AI may serve as training wheels but entrusting it with the pilot's seat would be imprudent and dangerous; the matter was remanded to a different officer.

title: Recommendation Guide on the Use of Artificial Intelligence for Lawyers [Avukatlar İçin Yapay Zekâ Kullanımı Tavsiye Rehberi]
body: Union of Turkish Bar Associations [Türkiye Barolar Birliği], Information and Technology Law Commission
requirements: verification; confidentiality; consent; competence; supervision; record-keeping; prohibition; disclosure
versions: [{"version":"First edition, 2026","date":"2026-08-28","url":"https://d.barobirlik.org.tr/2026/yapayzekatavsiyerehberi.pdf","changes":"First national Turkish bar instrument on AI. Product of the TBB 'AI and Advocacy Workshop', Ankara, 14-15 February 2026. Foreword by TBB President R. Erinç Sağkan; presented by Commission spokesperson Dr Resul Göksoy."}]
summary: A 44-page principle-based, technology-neutral guide covering lawyers, trainee lawyers and law-office staff. It classifies AI use into risk tiers, sets duties of human oversight, verification, professional secrecy, data minimisation and client information, and adds practical annexes: vendor criteria, model office-policy clauses and client-engagement wording. Advisory, reviewed periodically by TBB.
keyProvisions: Final responsibility rests with the lawyer: AI output is never a final legal opinion and must not be given to a client, court, authority or third party unchecked.; Risk-based classification by data type, impact on the client, proximity to the legal outcome, whether the tool is open or closed, cross-border transfer risk and contractual safeguards: free assistive use, use subject to safeguards and where needed consent, and prohibited uses.; No legislation, precedent, citation or fact from an AI tool may be filed with a court, arbitrator, mediator or administrative body without confirmation against official sources; hallucinated citations may be a grave breach of professional care, and errors discovered later must be corrected promptly.; Non-anonymised client data, case and enforcement file content, evidence, special-category data, trade secrets and negotiation strategy must not be entered into public or contractually unprotected AI systems.; Clients must be informed, and where needed give consent, whenever AI use touches their data, strategy or the outcome of the service; a client may ask that AI not be used on their file.; Time saved by AI must not be billed as lawyer time, and AI or general software costs must not be passed on without prior agreement; AI use is not itself a ground to reduce the fee.; Profiling, scoring or predicting individual judges' decisions is incompatible with professional practice, as are social scoring, manipulative techniques and emotion recognition.; Marketing claims such as guaranteed results, predicting court outcomes or lawyer-free legal advice are barred, as is facilitating non-lawyers or systems that appear to give independent legal advice.; Vendor criteria table covering data provenance, data location and cross-border transfer, a contractual undertaking that prompts and documents are not used for model training, security controls, transparency on error rates and a written data-processor agreement.; AI literacy modules to be built into trainee education and in-service training, with a TBB-coordinated trainer pool and materials standard.

summary: The SRA's first warning notice devoted to AI, issued 17 August 2026 after 42 reports of potential misuse in a year. body: Connecticut Judicial Branch, Committee on Artificial Intelligence in the Connecticut Legal System
summary: The committee established by the Connecticut Judicial Branch to examine AI in the legal system closed with a final report on 10 August 2026. title: Practice Direction HC 142: Responsible Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Court Documents
body: High Court of Ireland
summary: Ireland's first court rule on AI, signed by the President of the High Court on 29 July 2026 and in operation from 1 September 2026. It covers all civil documents and requires independent human verification of every AI-assisted citation, a declaration in affidavits and witness statements that generative AI was not used for substantive content, and disclosure for expert reports.
keyProvisions: Applies to pleadings, submissions, affidavits, witness statements and expert reports prepared after 1 September 2026.; Every AI-assisted citation or proposition must be independently verified by a human; checking with another AI tool is insufficient.; Affidavits and witness statements must carry a declaration that generative AI was not used to generate substantive content.; Expert reports require a no-substantive-use declaration or disclosure of AI use.; Sanctions include rejection of documents, adverse or personal costs, strike-out and referral to the regulator.

body: United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina
summary: The Western District of North Carolina superseded its 2024 AI order on July 29, 2026. Attorneys and pro se parties may use AI, but every filing is deemed to certify factual support, legal validity, existing and accurate authorities, accurate quotations, and required human verification.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union

summary: The EU AI Act sets risk-based obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems, including law firms and legal tech vendors operating in the European Union. Prohibited practices and AI literacy duties applied from 2 February 2025, GPAI rules from 2 August 2025 and Article 50 transparency from 2 August 2026, with high-risk obligations now deferred to 2027 and 2028.
keyProvisions: Article 4 requires providers and deployers to ensure sufficient AI literacy among staff, applicable from 2 February 2025.; Article 5 prohibited practices applied from 2 February 2025.; General-purpose AI model obligations applied from 2 August 2025; Commission enforcement powers from 2 August 2026.; Article 50 transparency obligations, including marking of synthetic content, applied from 2 August 2026.; Annex III stand-alone high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027; Annex I product-embedded systems from 2 August 2028.

body: Iowa Supreme Court and Iowa Judicial Branch
bodyShort: Iowa Supreme Court and Iowa Judicial Branch
summary: The Iowa Supreme Court order filed July 21, 2026, adopts Chapter 27 governing judicial use of AI tools effective January 1, 2027. keyProvisions: The chapter governs use of AI tools by judicial officers and adjudicative assistants in adjudicative duties.; A judicial officer must maintain independent decision-making responsibility and must not delegate or defer to AI work product.; Judicial officers and adjudicative assistants must independently verify the accuracy of all factual or legal sources in AI-prepared work product.; An adjudicative assistant must obtain judicial-officer approval before using an AI tool for adjudicative duties.; AI tools may not be used with judicial case information for adjudicative duties unless approved by the AI innovation and governance committee.

summary: European Commission guidelines, approved 20 July 2026 as C(2026) 5054 final, on the EU AI Act Article 50 transparency duties that applied from 2 August 2026. Providers mark synthetic output in a machine-readable, detectable way; deployers disclose deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest, unless the text has had substantive human review.
keyProvisions: Providers must mark AI-generated output so it is machine-readable and detectable.; Deployers must disclose deepfakes and AI-generated text published on matters of public interest.; Obligations apply from 2 August 2026; under new Article 111(4) of the AI Act, generative systems placed on the market before that date must meet Article 50(2) marking by 2 December 2026.; Paragraphs 134 to 136 define the human-review exception for public-interest text: substantive examination by a person with relevant knowledge, fact-checking as a minimum, and no AI edits after sign-off.; Guidelines are interpretive and accompany the Code of Practice on AI-generated content.

body: South African Judiciary (2026 Judiciary Conference, Umhlanga, Durban)
versions: [{"version":"Final adopted","date":"2026-07-16","url":"https://www.judiciary.org.za/images/news/2026/FINAL%20ADOPTED%202026%20Judiciary%20Conference%20Resolutions.pdf","changes":"Adopted at the 2026 Judiciary Conference held in Umhlanga, Durban, 13–16 July 2026."}]
summary: Resolutions adopted by the South African Judiciary on 16 July 2026. Section 5 directs the Judiciary Administration and Information Technology Steering Committee to finalise the draft judiciary AI policy, requires the Judiciary to retain governance over AI procurement and deployment, restricts initial AI use to efficiency tools, and mandates ongoing judicial education on responsible AI use.
keyProvisions: 5.2 — the Steering Committee is to finalise the Draft Policy on Artificial Intelligence for adoption, defining with greater specificity the permissible and prohibited uses of AI and the distinction between administrative and adjudicative functions, to safeguard confidentiality and the integrity of the administration of justice.; 5.3 — the Judiciary is to retain ownership and governance over the development, procurement and use of AI systems, keeping human oversight, judicial reasoning and judicial determination central, with training data reflecting South Africa's constitutional values.; 5.4 — AI should be leveraged through customised and secure platforms, initially for court recording and transcription, translation, case management and document summarisation.; 5.5 — the Judiciary should provide ongoing education on responsible AI use, including prompt design and verification, while maintaining legal research, analytical, reasoning and judgment-writing skills.; 5.1 — modernisation of court infrastructure, integrated case management and electronic filing, supported by cybersecurity and ICT capacity.

title: Guidance on using AI to prepare for court
body: Provincial Court of British Columbia
summary: Plain-language guidance published by the Provincial Court of British Columbia on 8 July 2026 for lawyers and self-represented litigants. title: Pooja Ramesh Singh v Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd, 2026 INSC 668
body: Supreme Court of India
summary: Supreme Court judgment of 2 July 2026 setting aside NCLT and NCLAT orders that relied on six non-existent, AI-hallucinated precedents. A decision resting on fake or hallucinated material is no decision in law; Bar and Bench owe a zero-tolerance duty to verify AI-generated authority, and the Bar Council of India was directed to frame guidelines and disciplinary measures.
keyProvisions: Orders founded even partly on fake or hallucinated precedents must be set aside.; Advocates commit professional misconduct by citing AI-generated judgments without verification.; Courts and tribunals must retain absolute control over AI in adjudication and must not trust authorities they cannot verify.; Bar Council of India to constitute a committee on AI use by advocates and prescribe disciplinary consequences.

body: Texas Business Court

It imposes no separate disclosure or certificate, but it states that the filing attorney or party remains independently responsible for accuracy and existing legal and ethical duties.

title: Revised Ethics Guidelines for Legal Practitioners in South Africa on the Use of Generative AI
body: Law Society of South Africa AI Committee (drafters, published via De Rebus)
summary: Revised draft ethics guidelines on generative AI for South African legal practitioners, published 1 July 2026 in De Rebus by drafters working with the LSSA AI Committee after a 2026 consultation. Practitioners are fully responsible for AI-assisted work, must assess local relevance and bias, and must address cybersecurity risks. Not formally adopted by the LSSA or Legal Practice Council.
keyProvisions: Legal practitioners are fully responsible for AI-assisted work product.; Output must be evaluated for accuracy, local legal relevance and bias.; Practitioners must address cybersecurity risks such as prompt injection and data corruption.; Offered as a collaborative contribution; not formally adopted by the LSSA or LPC.

keyProvisions: Fine of 2 per cent of case value for bad-faith litigation (CPC arts 80-81).; Referral to OAB/PR for disciplinary investigation.; Use of AI does not remove the lawyer's verification duty.; Consistent with TJSC (Feb 2025), the Londrina federal court (Jul 2025) and TST (Mar 2026) decisions.

title: The Use of AI for the Preparation of Court Documents: Update on Consultation Findings
body: Civil Justice Council
summary: Interim report from the Civil Justice Council for England and Wales, published 30 June 2026, summarising responses to its AI and court documents consultation. It records a strong consensus that no AI-specific formal requirements are needed for professional drafting, considers proportionate transparency for expert evidence, and flags concerns about AI-shaped witness statements and litigants in person.
keyProvisions: No new AI-specific rules recommended for pleadings and skeleton arguments prepared by lawyers.; Proportionate transparency for AI use in expert evidence remains under consideration.; Concern recorded about witness statements shaped by AI rather than in the witness's own words.; A distinct approach for litigants in person is anticipated in the final report, expected later in 2026.

keyProvisions: Applies to all motion submissions in Part 34.; The certification must state whether GenAI was used to draft affidavits, affirmations, or memoranda.; If GenAI was used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed for accuracy and approved.; The program, documents, and drafted parts must be specified.

summary: Nepal's judiciary-wide ICT policy approved by the Supreme Court full bench in mid-2026. Strategy 5.2 adopts AI as an innovation tool: AI-based systems will support drafting, research and case management, but AI shall not be used in a way that directly intrudes on judicial decisions, and third-party AI must be assessed for reliability and bias before use.
keyProvisions: 5.2.1: AI-based systems for drafting and research support; no AI use that directly affects judicial decisions.; 5.2.2: internal or third-party AI systems assessed for reliability, transparency, non-bias and algorithmic processes.; 5.2.3: AI-assisted data entry in the case-management system.; Awareness and training for judges, officials, Bar members and court users.

title: Connecticut Practice Book Section 4-9: Generative Artificial Intelligence Compliance
body: Connecticut Judicial Branch (Rules Committee of the Superior Court)
summary: A statewide Connecticut court rule effective 23 June 2026 on publication in the Connecticut Law Journal. Anyone who uses generative AI to create or edit a filed document must independently verify every citation, authority and item of evidence, and the filer's signature certifies diligent compliance. Sanctions include nonsuit or default. It is among the first statewide binding verification rules.
keyProvisions: Applies to any filed document created or edited with generative AI, by lawyers or self-represented parties.; Every citation, legal authority and item of evidence must be independently verified before filing.; Filing constitutes a certification of good-faith, diligent compliance with the rule.; Non-compliance may be sanctioned, including by nonsuit or default judgment.
sources: [{"label":"Connecticut Judicial Branch — news post on Practice Book Section 4-9","url":"https://www.jud.ct.gov/legalresources/NewsLog/Post?id=6805"}]

title: Practice Book Amendments: Generative Artificial Intelligence Compliance
body: Connecticut Superior Court
summary: The Connecticut Superior Court’s June 23, 2026 Practice Book amendments add Section 4-9 on generative AI compliance and revise Section 4-2. Anyone using generative AI to create or edit a court-filed document must independently verify all AI-produced citations, legal authorities, or evidence, and filing represents diligent compliance.
keyProvisions: Section 4-9 defines generative AI and covers court-filed documents.; A person using generative AI to create or edit a filing must independently verify AI-produced citations, legal authorities, or evidence.; By filing, a person represents good-faith diligent efforts to comply with the rule.; The Section 4-2 signature certification incorporates Section 4-9 compliance.

title: In re Amendments to Article V, Rule 1.1 of the Supreme Court Rules (Professional Conduct) and Adoption of Interim Generative AI Guidelines
body: Supreme Court of Rhode Island
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2026-06-17","url":"https://www.courts.ri.gov/Miscellaneous%20Orders/Supreme-2026-06_In_reAmendments_Article_V_Rule_1_1_Professional_Conduct.pdf","changes":"Amends Rule 1.1 Comment [6] and adopts interim generative AI guidelines for lawyers and for judicial officers"}]
summary: By order of 17 June 2026 the Rhode Island Supreme Court amended Article V, Rule 1.1 Comment [6] so that competence expressly includes keeping abreast of the benefits and risks of developing technology, and adopted advisory interim generative-AI guidelines for Rhode Island lawyers and for judicial officers. The guidelines do not carry the force of law.
keyProvisions: Rule 1.1 Comment [6] now requires lawyers to keep abreast of the benefits and risks associated with existing and developing technology; Lawyers must review all GAI output for accuracy, verify citations and facts, and correct false or misleading arguments before filing; A lawyer may charge only for actual time spent; everyday GAI tool costs are non-billable overhead, and GAI training costs generally may not be billed; A lawyer must disclose GAI use when the client asks, or when entering client information into a GAI system; Judicial officers may consult but should never rely on GAI-produced content when drafting orders and decisions, and GAI must never influence or appear to influence a conclusion; Rule 2.9(C) risk: GAI output may import outside information amounting to prohibited independent factual investigation; Even a single incorrect citation may trigger a Rule 8.3 reporting obligation, including as to opposing counsel's output

title: Protocol for the use of artificial intelligence in the Judicial Function (Ethics Committee)
body: Ethics Committee of the Judicial Function (Comite de Etica de la Funcion Judicial)

It awaits formal adoption.

title: Standing Order in re Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools to Review Criminal Discovery
body: United States District Court for the Northern District of West Virginia — Judge Thomas S. Kleeh
bodyShort: Northern District of West Virginia (Judge Kleeh)
summary: The Northern District of West Virginia issued a June 16, 2026 standing order for AI tools used to review criminal discovery. Defense counsel must obtain government consent before exposing sensitive materials to AI tools, identify and describe the tool, and certify confidentiality, non-retention, and deletion protections.
keyProvisions: All criminal actions in the district are subject to restrictions on AI tools and sensitive discovery materials.; The legal defense team may not expose sensitive materials to any AI tool without prior written consent from the government.; Defense counsel must identify and describe the AI tool in a written authorization request.; Defense counsel must certify that the tool does not retain or use sensitive materials for model training or expose them to unauthorized third parties.; Defense counsel must certify confidentiality measures and deletion of sensitive materials from the tool at the end of the case.

title: Amendments to the Collection of Rules of Advocates' Ethics and Dignity of the Profession introducing § 23e on technology and AI
body: Polish Bar Council [Naczelna Rada Adwokacka]
versions: [{"version":"Adopted at the NRA plenary session in Rzeszów","date":"2026-06-13","url":"https://www.adwokatura.pl/z-zycia-nra/zmiany-w-zbiorze-zasad-etyki-adwokackiej-naczelna-rada-adwokacka-przyjela-nowe-regulacje-dotyczace-korzystania-ze-sztucznej-inteligencji-w-wykonywaniu-zawodu-adwokata/","changes":"New § 23e added and § 19(6) amended at the plenary session held 12–13 June 2026; resolution number not stated in the published announcement."}]
summary: A resolution of the Polish Bar Council adopted at its 12–13 June 2026 plenary in Rzeszów amending the advocates' ethics code. It adds § 23e regulating the use of technological tools, including AI, and amends § 19(6). The rules bind Polish advocates and are enforceable through the disciplinary system.
keyProvisions: An advocate may use technological tools, including AI, only in an auxiliary capacity.; Technology may not process information covered by professional secrecy unless the tool's mechanisms guarantee proper protection of that data.; The advocate must personally assess and verify the results produced by the tool so as not to harm the client.; Use of technological tools does not release the advocate from personal responsibility for the form and content of professional activities.; Clients need not generally be told which tools are used, but may request disclosure of the technologies used and their purpose.; The advocate must have the competence to assess the tool's limitations and associated risks.

title: Council of State, Third Section: parameters for AI use in proceedings and disciplinary referral
body: Council of State (Consejo de Estado, Seccion Tercera)
versions: [{"version":"Decision reported 9 June 2026","date":"2026-06-09","url":"https://www.infobae.com/colombia/2026/06/09/consejo-de-estado-fijo-reglas-para-usar-la-inteligencia-artificial-en-la-justicia-tras-caso-de-abogado-que-habria-inventado-sentencias-con-chatgpt/","changes":"Initial decision; reported by Infobae and El Tiempo, official text not obtained."}]

title: Proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707: Machine-Generated Evidence
body: Judicial Conference of the United States, Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure
summary: A proposed United States federal evidence rule that would subject machine-generated evidence, including AI output offered without an expert, to the reliability standards of Rule 702. Public comment closed 16 February 2026. In June 2026 the Standing Committee declined to recommend adoption and returned the rule for further study alongside deepfakes; the earliest effective date is after 1 December 2027.
keyProvisions: Would apply Rule 702 reliability requirements to evidence produced by a machine or process without a testifying expert.; Public comment period ran to 16 February 2026.; Standing Committee did not recommend action on 3 to 4 June 2026; rule revised and returned for study with deepfake issues.; Reported in the September 2026 reports to the Judicial Conference.

body: District Courts of Calhoun, DeWitt, Goliad, Jackson, Refugio and Victoria Counties — Judge Stephen Williams; Judge Lisa Harvey Moore; Judge Eli Garza
bodyShort: District Courts of Calhoun, DeWitt, Goliad, Jackson, Refugio and Victoria Counties (Judge Garza)

Attorneys and self-represented litigants using AI for legal research, drafting, or analysis must submit a certification that AI-created legal content was verified by a human using traditional legal sources.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2026-06-02","url":"https://kybar.org/Portals/0/Documents/Ohio%20AI%20Guide%20for%20Attorneys.pdf","changes":"Issued and distributed to Ohio lawyers and judicial officers"}]
summary: Nonbinding Board staff guidance applying the Ohio Rules of Professional Conduct and the Code of Judicial Conduct to AI. It covers competence, confidentiality, client communication, independent professional judgment, fees, candor to the tribunal and hallucinated citations, supervision of staff and vendors, and a substantial judicial section on competence, independent decision-making, ex parte risk and confidentiality.
keyProvisions: The Ohio Rules of Professional Conduct do not prohibit lawyers from using AI, but AI is now a 'relevant technology' for the duty of competence; Lawyers may bill only for time actually spent, not the time a task would have taken without AI; standard AI tool costs are usually non-billable overhead; Filing documents with fictitious citations, quotes or propositions of law implicates Prof.Cond.R. 3.3(a), 8.4(c), 8.4(d) and 3.1; A lawyer who learns a filing contains a hallucination must immediately notify the court and opposing counsel; A lawyer must comply with local rules and standing orders on the use and disclosure of AI tools (Prof.Cond.R. 3.4); A judge should never use AI to decide the ultimate conclusion in a case and should avoid AI-produced first drafts of decisions or orders; Judges and staff must not enter confidential case information, or anything revealing judicial mental processes, into general or free public AI tools

body: Law Society of England and Wales

summary: The Law Society of England and Wales' practical guide to generative AI for solicitors and firms, updated in June 2026. It is permissive with cautions: solicitors may use generative AI but must keep a human in the loop, verify output, protect client confidentiality, understand the tool's limits and ensure staff are competent and supervised.
keyProvisions: Generative AI output must be reviewed by a competent human before it is relied on.; Client and confidential information should not be entered into tools without appropriate contractual and technical safeguards.; Firms should set an AI use policy and train staff on approved tools.; Solicitors should understand how the tool works, including whether prompts are retained or used for training.

title: Effective supervision guidance (AI sections)
body: Solicitors Regulation Authority
summary: The SRA's Effective Supervision guidance for solicitors and firms in England and Wales gained dedicated AI sections in June 2026. Supervisors are treated as accountable for AI-assisted work by staff and must have systems for supervising matters where AI is used. The 17 August 2026 warning notice on AI misuse cross-refers to it.
keyProvisions: Supervisors remain accountable for work product produced with AI assistance by the people they supervise.; Firms need systems that let supervisors see how AI is being used on matters.; Junior staff and support staff using AI tools must be supervised in the same way as any other delegated work.; Referenced as a companion document in the SRA warning notice on misuse of AI.

title: 22 NYCRR Part 161 — Use of Artificial Intelligence Technology
body: New York State Unified Court System (Rules of the Chief Administrator of the Courts)
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2026-06-01","url":"https://www.nycourts.gov/rules/part-161-use-artificial-intelligence-technology","archiveUrl":"https://web.archive.org/web/20260802114549/https://www.nycourts.gov/rules/part-161-use-artificial-intelligence-technology","changes":"Added to the Rules of the Chief Administrator by Administrative Order AO/75/26 dated 25 March 2026; effective 1 June 2026"}]
summary: Part 161 applies to all New York Unified Court System courts in civil and criminal cases. Using an AI tool to prepare a paper is permitted and need not be disclosed, but the attorney or party must independently ensure it contains no fabricated cases, statutes or other material; signing certifies that review, and failure may draw sanctions.
keyProvisions: Section 161.3 states as statewide policy that attorneys and parties should not be required, on submitting papers, to disclose that they used AI; Section 161.4: a court may in its discretion adopt a part rule and is encouraged to adopt the Appendix A model rule, under which the attorney or party independently ensures the paper contains no fabricated cases, statutes or other material and the signature certifies that review; Applies to all UCS courts in both civil and criminal cases; Defines AI as any machine-based system capable of making predictions, recommendations and/or decisions based on human-defined objectives and inputs; Use of an AI tool to prepare a paper is permitted and need not be disclosed; Any attorney or party who uses an AI tool must carefully review the paper and independently ensure it contains no fabricated or fictitious cases, statutes or other material; Signing the paper certifies that such a review was conducted; Failure to satisfy the requirement may result in sanction or other remedial action

body: Supreme Court of Florida

title: General Pretrial and Trial Procedures: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey — Judge Evelyn Padin
summary: Judge Evelyn Padin’s revised May 28, 2026 general pretrial and trial procedures require mandatory certification for any generative AI use in court filings. The certification must state that the GAI work product was diligently reviewed by a human being for accuracy and applicability, including correcting errors and eliminating hallucinations.
keyProvisions: All matters pending before Judge Padin, including pro se matters, are covered unless stated otherwise.; Any GAI use in court filings requires mandatory human-review certification.; The review should include correcting errors and eliminating hallucinations.; Noncompliance may lead to sanctions, striking, or bar referral.

body: United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida — Judge Anne-Leigh Gaylord Moe
summary: Judge Moe of the Middle District of Florida requires every filing in the civil case to include a verbatim certification about AI use. The May 27, 2026 order requires disclosure and a description if AI was used, and requires the signer to personally read cited cases.
keyProvisions: Every filing must contain one of two verbatim certifications stating whether artificial intelligence was used.; Traditional Westlaw or LexisNexis research and traditional search engines are excluded from disclosure.; If AI was used, the certification must describe how it was used and state that the filer personally read every case.; Filings made before the order must receive a Rule 11 compliance certification or be withdrawn within ten days.

title: Draft Commission Guidelines on the classification of high-risk AI systems (Article 6)
body: European Commission
summary: Draft guidelines published by the European Commission on 19 May 2026 on classifying AI systems as high-risk under Article 6 of the EU AI Act, including administration-of-justice uses listed in Annex III. A targeted consultation closed in summer 2026 and final guidelines are expected by the end of 2026, ahead of the deferred 2 December 2027 application date.
keyProvisions: Explains the Annex III use cases, including AI intended to assist judicial authorities in researching and interpreting law.; Sets out the Article 6(3) derogation for systems that do not pose a significant risk.; Draft only; final guidelines expected end of 2026.

title: Administrative Order No. 26-15: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Filings by Attorneys and Self-Represented Litigants
body: Eleventh Judicial Circuit of Florida — Judge Ariana Fajardo Orshan
bodyShort: Eleventh Judicial Circuit of Florida (Judge Orshan)
summary: The Eleventh Judicial Circuit of Florida requires attorneys and self-represented litigants to disclose generative AI use when it drafts or generates content used in court filings or records. Effective May 19, 2026, the required certification covers citations, record citations, drafted language, facts, and legal analysis.
keyProvisions: AI may assist preparation, research, drafting, document review, filing review, discovery review, and discovery requests.; Use of generative AI to draft or generate content used in a filing or record must be disclosed.; The certification states the filer has read and verified citations, record citations, drafted language, quotations, facts, and legal analysis.; Disclosure is not required for routine research, cite-checking, or grammar, spelling, and clarity edits.; The order vacates and supersedes Administrative Order No. 26-04.

body: Bar Standards Board
summary: Regulatory guidance from the Bar Standards Board, valid from 18 May 2026, on how the Core Duties apply when barristers in England and Wales use AI. It requires verification of output before use, transparency with clients under rC19 where AI materially affects the service, and treats free public tools as generally unsuitable for legal work.
keyProvisions: Reads AI use into Core Duties CD1, CD2, CD3, CD6, CD7 and CD10.; Barristers must verify AI output before relying on it or presenting it to a court.; Where AI materially impacts the service provided, clients must be informed under rC19.; Free consumer tools are generally unsuitable for confidential legal work.

title: Proposed Rule 707: Evidence Produced by Artificial Intelligence and Presented at Trial Without an Expert
body: Federal Rules of Evidence / Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules
bodyShort: Federal Rules of Evidence / Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules
summary: The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules reported a revised proposed Rule 707 that would regulate AI-produced evidence offered at trial without an expert witness, require the proponent to establish Rule 702-style reliability, ordinarily require expert explanation, and require reasonable notice to adverse parties.
keyProvisions: Applies when evidence is a product of artificial intelligence and is offered without an expert witness but would be subject to Rule 702 if testified to by a witness.; Requires the proponent to establish helpfulness, sufficient facts or data, reliable principles and methods, and reliable application.; Ordinarily requires an expert to explain how the AI system reliably produced the evidence, with exceptional circumstances for other proof.; Makes the evidence admissible only if the proponent gives adverse parties reasonable notice of the intent to offer it.; The committee decided not to release the revised draft for a new public comment period at that time and planned further AI expert vetting.

Treaty Office chart of 3 September 2026 shows 20 signatures without ratification; not yet in force."},{"version":"Opened for signature","date":"2024-09-05","url":"https://www.coe.int/en/web/conventions/full-list?module=treaty-detail&treatynum=225","changes":"Signed in Vilnius by 10 states plus the EU; corrected certified copy per Committee of Ministers decision of 30 April 2025."},{"version":"Adopted by the Committee of Ministers","date":"2024-05-17","url":"https://rm.coe.int/1680afae3c"}]
summary: The first international treaty on AI, adopted 17 May 2024 and opened for signature in Vilnius on 5 September 2024. Parties must ensure AI lifecycle activities respect human rights, democracy and the rule of law, with transparency, accountability, remedies and risk assessment. As of 3 September 2026 only the EU has ratified; five ratifications are needed.

title: Practice Note SC GEN 25: The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users
body: Supreme Court of Victoria
summary: Practice Note SC GEN 25 of the Supreme Court of Victoria, issued 14 May 2026, replaces the court's May 2024 guidelines for litigants. Court users must keep meaningful human control over AI-assisted work, may not verify one AI tool's output with another, must ensure sworn documents are in the deponent's own words, and may be directed to identify AI-produced portions.
keyProvisions: Meaningful human control is required over any AI-assisted material filed with the court.; Checking one AI tool's output with another AI tool does not satisfy the verification duty.; Affidavits and witness statements must be in the deponent's own words.; The court may direct a party to identify which parts of a document were AI-produced.

title: Judicial Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: Supreme Court of Victoria
summary: Guidelines issued by the Supreme Court of Victoria on 14 May 2026, alongside Practice Note SC GEN 25, governing judicial officers' and chambers staff use of AI. Judges may not use generative AI for decision-making or the substantive content of judgments, must protect confidential case material, and must verify any AI-assisted administrative output.
keyProvisions: Judicial officers may not use generative AI for decision-making or drafting the reasoning of judgments.; Confidential and suppressed case material must not be entered into external AI tools.; Any administrative use of AI by chambers must be verified by the judicial officer.

body: Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
summary: A practice direction issued by the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia in May 2026 as a companion to the Federal Court's GPN-AI. It sets expectations for lawyers and self-represented litigants using generative AI in family law and general federal law matters, including verification of AI-assisted content and readiness to explain AI use to the court on request.
keyProvisions: Practitioners and parties are responsible for verifying AI-assisted documents before filing.; The court may ask how generative AI was used in preparing a document.; Companion to Federal Court of Australia practice note GPN-AI.

title: Alabama State Bar Formal Opinion 2026-01: Artificial Intelligence Use — Best Practices Under Existing Professional Conduct Rules
body: Alabama State Bar, Office of General Counsel
versions: [{"version":"FO 2026-01","date":"2026-05-01","url":"https://www.alabar.org/assets/2026/05/FO-2026-01.pdf","changes":"Initial publication; the source gives a month only (published May 2026), so the day is recorded as the 1st"}]
summary: The Alabama State Bar's first formal opinion on AI. It applies ARPC 1.1, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 3.1, 3.3, 5.1 and 5.3 to generative and agentic AI, requires independent verification of AI citations before filing, prefers enterprise or closed AI systems, bars billing for AI time savings, and supplies a compliance checklist.
keyProvisions: Independently verify every legal citation generated by AI against an authoritative database before filing (ARPC 1.1, 3.1, 3.3); Input into most generative AI platforms is disclosure; prefer enterprise or closed systems, anonymise prompts, and obtain informed consent where risk cannot be eliminated (ARPC 1.6); No Alabama rule mandates disclosure of AI use to clients in all circumstances, but proactive communication is prudent (ARPC 1.4); A lawyer may bill only for time actually spent; review and judgment time is billable, time saved by AI is not (ARPC 1.5); AI is to be supervised like a nonlawyer assistant; the supervising lawyer remains fully responsible for the work product (ARPC 5.1, 5.3); Check each court's local rules and standing orders for AI disclosure or certification requirements before filing

AI is to assist, not replace, judicial decision-making; permitted uses are case management, legal research, predictive analytics and document processing, with bias, privacy and training safeguards.
keyProvisions: Human-centric: judges remain the ultimate arbiters and AI assists only.; Permitted: case management, legal research, predictive analytics and document processing.; Ethical and transparent use with safeguards against bias, plus explainability and accountability.; Strict privacy and data-security standards.; Structured training programmes for judges and court staff; High Courts retain implementation autonomy.

It targets education, healthcare, agriculture, finance and public service delivery, and proposes an independent Responsible AI Authority within the first year. Justice, courts and legal services are not named as target sectors.
keyProvisions: Framework built on multiple pillars with policy recommendations across eight target sectors; the administration of justice is not among them.; Proposes an independent Responsible AI Authority modelled on comparable national AI offices.; Implementation coordinated with the National Information Technology Agency, the Data Protection Commission and the Cyber Security Authority.; Non-binding policy; Ghana has no AI statute and no AI risk-classification law.

title: Supreme Court Rol 23.322-2025: suspension and fine for AI-fabricated doctrinal citations
body: Supreme Court of Chile, Third Chamber (Corte Suprema, Tercera Sala)

summary: The Supreme Court suspended a lawyer for one month and fined her 5 UTM under articles 531 and 542 of the Organic Code of Courts for a cassation brief citing a non-existent 2023 treatise and a non-existent 2021 work, produced with AI; the unintentional-error defence was rejected as a breach of procedural good faith.
keyProvisions: One-month suspension from practice plus a 5 UTM fine.; Disciplinary basis: Codigo Organico de Tribunales arts 531 and 542.; Lawyers must verify the accuracy of AI-generated sources; the good-faith excuse was rejected.; Lower courts apply art. 531 similarly (2nd Civil Court of Concepcion, 1 UTM, February 2026).

Chapter 2 governs user conduct: users must understand that generative AI may hallucinate and must cross-check outputs against official documents, case files and legal databases before use; AI may only assist adjudication and deployments must incorporate risk management.
keyProvisions: Art. 8: verify AI-generated data, factual summaries and legal citations against reliable sources before use.; AI assists adjudication only; users retain decision autonomy.; Risk management required for system deployment.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Practice Note (GPN-AI)
body: Federal Court of Australia
summary: Practice note GPN-AI, issued by the Federal Court of Australia on 16 April 2026, sets the court's expectations of all participants who use generative AI in proceedings. Practitioners and parties remain responsible for verifying AI-assisted content, must be able to explain how AI was used if asked, and the court may make orders regulating AI use in a particular proceeding.
keyProvisions: Paragraph 4.10: use of generative AI must be disclosed, without any direction, where it was used to summarise or analyse information a witness relies on, to create images or video, or in any other manner that might reasonably affect admissibility; Parties and practitioners are responsible for the accuracy of any AI-assisted material filed.; The court may direct a party to disclose whether and how generative AI was used.; The court may make case-specific orders limiting or conditioning AI use.; Affidavit and expert evidence must reflect the deponent's own knowledge and opinion.

title: OAB/SP Ethics and Discipline Tribunal ruling on partners' duty to supervise AI use (proc. 25.0886.2025.014989-0)
body: Sao Paulo Bar Ethics and Discipline Tribunal (Tribunal de Etica e Disciplina da OAB/SP, 1a Turma)

summary: The Sao Paulo Bar's ethics tribunal held that partners and managers must ensure AI use by associates, contractors, trainees and non-lawyer staff is supervised, and must fully review all AI-generated output before it is filed, with special care for case-law research, citing article 77 of the Code of Civil Procedure and OAB Recommendation 001/2024.
keyProvisions: Partners are responsible for supervising AI use across the firm, including by non-lawyers.; Full review of every AI output before filing.; Heightened care where AI is used for legal research and case-law.; Applies CPC art. 77 duty of truthfulness and Recomendacao 001/2024.

title: Williamson County Local Rules: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Filings
body: Williamson County District Courts and County Courts at Law
bodyShort: Williamson County District Courts and County Courts at Law
summary: Williamson County local rules contain a dedicated AI-in-filings section. Attorneys and self-represented litigants using AI for legal research or drafting must ensure AI-generated information is accurate and must attach a certificate to any filing where AI-generated information is used. It was on the court's website when read on 6 September 2026; the court's text is the record.
keyProvisions: AI users must ensure AI-generated information is accurate and correctly portrayed.; A Certificate Regarding Use of Artificial Intelligence must be attached to any filing where AI-generated information is used.; The certificate requires traditional-source verification of AI-created legal content.

title: CGAE Interpretive Circular 3/2026: use of generative AI systems and the duty of verification
body: General Council of Spanish Lawyers (Consejo General de la Abogacia Espanola)
versions: [{"version":"Dated Madrid 20 March 2026; approved by the Pleno 10 April 2026, amended 13 April 2026","date":"2026-04-13","url":"https://www.icaib.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Circular-interpretativa-3-2026_Deontologia-aprobada-Pleno-modificaciones-13-4-2026.pdf","changes":"Original text, from the ICAIB mirror of the CGAE circular."}]
summary: Interpretive circular under Article 23 of the Right of Defence Act construing the Spanish code of conduct. Generative-AI drafting is lawful, but filing AI-assisted documents with unverified errors breaches diligence and responsible technology use and is a serious infraction under Article 125.u EGAE; the signer is solely responsible and tool failure proves a breach of supervision.
keyProvisions: AI is an auxiliary function subject to human supervision, never a substitute for the lawyer.; Uncritical or substitutive delegation of essential professional tasks breaches diligence and independence, with or without errors.; Serious infraction under Art. 125.u EGAE; very serious under Art. 124.g in extreme or repeated cases causing defencelessness.; Recommendations: know the tools, read every AI output critically, cross-check against reliable legal sources, use AI only in fields mastered, keep internal traceability of AI use.; Confidentiality and professional secrecy are reserved to a separate circular.

title: Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy (published GN 3880 of 2026; withdrawn by Notice 3978 of 2026)
body: Department of Communications and Digital Technologies
versions: [{"version":"Draft for public comment","date":"2026-04-10","url":"https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202604/54477gen3880.pdf","changes":"Approved by Cabinet 25 March 2026 (and a special sitting on 1 April 2026); published as General Notice 3880 in Government Gazette 54477 for comment to 10 June 2026."},{"version":"Withdrawal","date":"2026-06-12","url":"https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202606/54840gen3978.pdf","changes":"Withdrawn in its entirety by Notice 3978 of 2026, Government Gazette 54840 (signed by Minister Solly Malatsi on 4 June 2026), after the draft was found to contain fabricated academic citations generated by AI."}]
summary: South Africa's draft national AI policy, gazetted for comment on 10 April 2026, proposed new oversight bodies including a National AI Commission. It was withdrawn in its entirety on 12 June 2026 after reporting established that several of its 67 academic citations — journals and authors alike — did not exist, apparently AI hallucinations in the policy's own drafting.
keyProvisions: Published as General Notice 3880 in Government Gazette 54477 on 10 April 2026 for public comment until 10 June 2026.; Withdrawn in its entirety by Notice 3978 of 2026 in Government Gazette 54840, dated 12 June 2026 and signed 4 June 2026 by the Minister of Communications and Digital Technologies.; Cabinet approved the withdrawal to allow a rework establishing national standards on the ethical use of AI.; The withdrawal is the clearest South African precedent that AI-fabricated citations invalidate an official document.

title: CSM Recommendations on the use of artificial intelligence in judicial activity (Recomendacoes no uso de IA)
body: High Council of the Judiciary (Conselho Superior da Magistratura)
versions: [{"version":"Approved by the Plenario 8 April 2026; PDF published May 2026","date":"2026-04-08","url":"https://csm.org.pt/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Recomendacoes_Uso_IA.pdf"}]
summary: Recommendations proposed by the CSM's AI Monitoring Group for judges' use of AI, citing AI Act Annex III point 8(a). Ten principles include effective human control, non-substitution, exclusive judicial responsibility and transparency; only systems supplied by the case-management platform or the CSM may be used; every AI-assisted decision must carry an express reference to AI use.
keyProvisions: Principle 2 and Rec. 7: AI may never replace judges in deciding, assessing facts or evidence, or interpreting the law.; Rec. 6: complete, critical personal review and validation of any AI draft before it becomes a decision.; Rec. 8: no judicial data in non-validated systems; open tools only for study on open sources.; Rec. 10: express reference in the decision that it was produced with the aid of an AI system and fully reviewed by the signatory.; Rec. 9: GDPR principles, security, traceability and no reuse; CSM-validated systems presumed compliant.

title: TSJ Navarra, Social Chamber (Apr 2026): Art. 247 LEC proceedings archived after apology for AI-invented citations
body: High Court of Justice of Navarre (Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Navarra)
versions: [{"version":"April 2026 (rapporteur Maria Jose Ramo)","date":"2026-04-04","url":"https://www.elespanol.com/espana/tribunales/20260404/abogada-cito-recurso-sentencias-inventadas-ia-libra-sancion-pedir-perdon-tribunal/1003744194050_0.html","changes":"Reported by El Espanol on 4 April 2026; official text not obtained."}]
summary: Counsel's October 2025 appeal quoted passages attributed to the Constitutional Court, Supreme Court and two regional high courts that did not match any real ruling. The chamber opened Article 247 LEC bad-faith proceedings in February 2026 but archived them without fine after the lawyer apologised and withdrew the citations, while warning about AI hallucination and the non-delegable verification duty.
keyProvisions: Careless use of AI in judicial filings has deontological implications and can amount to procedural bad faith.; Prompt acknowledgement and withdrawal weighed against sanction.; Follows TSJ Navarra Auto 2/2024, the first Spanish decision on ChatGPT-generated filings.

title: Advisory on the Use of Publicly Available AI Tools
body: Law Society of Singapore
summary: An advisory issued by the Law Society of Singapore on 2 April 2026 on lawyers' use of publicly available AI tools such as consumer chatbots. Client information must not be entered into tools that may retain or train on it, output must be verified against primary sources, and lawyers remain responsible under the Legal Profession rules.
keyProvisions: Client confidential information must not be entered into public AI tools without safeguards.; Output from public tools must be verified against primary legal sources before use.; Lawyers remain professionally responsible for AI-assisted work.

title: Standing Order on Artificial Intelligence (Judge Wendy W. Berger)
body: United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida, Judge Wendy W. Berger
summary: A standing order issued 2 April 2026 by Judge Wendy Berger of the Middle District of Florida governing AI-assisted filings. Counsel and self-represented parties are responsible for the accuracy of any AI-generated content; misrepresenting its accuracy can lead to sanctions up to dismissal or default judgment and referral to the state bar or the court's grievance committee.
keyProvisions: Filers remain fully responsible for verifying AI-generated citations, quotations and facts.; Misrepresentation of the accuracy of AI content may result in dismissal, default or monetary sanctions.; Attorneys may be referred to the Florida Bar or the court's grievance committee.

title: Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial and Court Administration
body: High Court of Gujarat
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2026-04-01","url":"https://gujarathighcourt.nic.in/hccms/sites/default/files/miscnotifications/Policy%20on%20the%20use%20of%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20in%20the%20Judicial%20and%20Court%20Administration.pdf","changes":"Original policy; PDF metadata date, published April 2026."}]
summary: Gujarat High Court policy of April 2026 for the district judiciary, issued under Articles 227 and 235. AI is permitted solely as a neutral administrative and research instrument through High Court-defined tools; it may not be used for decision-making, reasoning, drafting substantive orders, bail or sentencing; AI citations and summaries must be independently verified.
keyProvisions: AI shall not be used for decision-making, reasoning, drafting of substantive orders, judgment preparation, bail, sentencing or any substantive judicial process (cl. 3.1, 8).; Permitted: research and precedent identification, translation, administrative support and language refinement of drafts (cl. 7).; Independent verification of AI-generated citations, statutory references and summaries (cl. 10).; Public AI tools restricted; sensitive case material must not be uploaded (cl. 9.2-9.3); only High Court-approved tools.; To be read with the IT Act, the DPDP Act 2023 when in force, the Contempt of Courts Act 1971 and the Gujarat High Court Rules 1993.

Part E governs AI and generative AI in profiling and automated decision-making, requiring human oversight, barring decisions made on a sole automated factor, and requiring staff training and appointed reviewers.

title: Part 61 Rules: Generative Artificial Intelligence Certification and Remote-Appearance Ban
body: New York Supreme Court, New York County, Civil Term — Judge Nancy M. Bannon
bodyShort: New York Supreme Court, New York County, Civil Term (Judge Bannon)
summary: Justice Nancy M. Bannon’s Part 61 rules, last updated April 2026, require certifications for all motion, hearing, trial, and permitted letter submissions stating whether generative AI was used. If used, the certification must identify the program, documents, and portions drafted, and remote appearances may not use any AI program.
keyProvisions: Motion, hearing, trial, and permitted letter submissions must include a GenAI certification.; If GenAI was used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed and approved.; The program, documents, and portions drafted by GenAI must be identified.; Use of any AI program during a remote oral argument, conference, or appearance is strictly prohibited.

Pleadings using generative AI must include a bold verification listing the AI program and use, certifying accuracy and confidentiality, and confirming no AI-created, edited, enhanced, or altered evidence is attached.
keyProvisions: GenAI users must include a bold verification in pleadings.; The verification discloses programs used and the role of AI in work product, research, or drafting.; The order prohibits sensitive information, AI-created evidence, AI voice-translation interpreters, and AI-reliant expert methodology.

body: 457th District Court of Montgomery County — Judge Vincenzo J. Santini
bodyShort: 457th District Court of Montgomery County (Judge Santini)
summary: Judge Santini’s 457th District Court order requires any attorney or self-represented litigant using generative AI in work product, research, or drafting to include a bold verification in pleadings. summary: A draft policy circulated for comment by the Office of the Chief Justice in April 2026 setting binding standards for responsible, ethical, secure and transparent AI use in the South African Judiciary. It distinguishes adjudicative from administrative functions, prohibits AI from adjudicative work, and imposes an explainability requirement. Not adopted as of 4 September 2026.
keyProvisions: AI systems are assistive tools only and may not substitute for judicial reasoning, discretion or decision-making.; AI is expressly prohibited from any adjudicative function, including evaluating evidence, assessing witness credibility, interpreting or applying law, generating substantive legal reasoning, and determining bail, sentence or risk.; Any AI system deployed in the Judiciary must produce outputs that are intelligible and open to scrutiny (explainability requirement).; Draws a clear distinction between adjudicative and administrative functions.

summary: Egypt's umbrella AI governance guide, published March 2026 by the Egyptian Center for Responsible AI. It defines a four-tier risk classification with a mandatory dual-check conformity model for high-risk systems, drawing on UNESCO, OECD, ISO/IEC and the G7 Hiroshima Process. It does not name justice or the courts.

body: High Court of Kenya at Milimani

The Kenya Law page for the April 2026 ruling returned 404 on 4 September 2026 and the account rests partly on press reports, so this record is unverified."},{"version":"Ruling setting aside the 23 December 2025 judgment (Chigiti J)","date":"2026-04-16","url":"https://new.kenyalaw.org/akn/ke/judgment/kehc/2026/5485/eng@2026-04-16","changes":"Judgment of 23 December 2025 set aside; the AI-founded application struck out with costs against the applicant."}]
summary: Two 2026 High Court rulings in the same litigation set Kenya's de facto position: AI-generated pleadings are procedurally deficient. Mwamuye J held that computer-generated documents or AI outputs cannot substitute for human-drawn documents; Chigiti J then set aside the resulting judgment, reasoning that the Civil Procedure Rules do not authorise AI-drafted pleadings and that their use confers an unfair advantage.

summary: Kenya's horizontal AI bill, published 19 February 2026. It creates an Office of the Artificial Intelligence Commissioner, a four-tier risk classification set by regulations, obligations for high-risk systems including human oversight and human rights impact assessments, a public register of high-risk systems, and regulatory sandboxes. Justice and court uses are not named.
keyProvisions: Classification: unacceptable risk (prohibited), high risk for critical sectors including healthcare, education, agriculture, finance, security, employment or public administration, limited risk and minimal risk; categories to be prescribed by the Cabinet Secretary on the Commissioner's recommendation.; Clause 26: high-risk providers and deployers must conduct a pre-deployment risk assessment with human oversight, a human rights impact assessment, ensure transparency, traceability and explainability, and keep records of inputs, training datasets and outputs for at least five years.; Clause 26(1)(g): systems generating or manipulating images, voice or likeness require explicit consent and clear AI-generated labelling.; Clause 28: automated decisions with significant legal effects must carry Data Protection Act safeguards including rights to human intervention, to express views and to contest; annual compliance reports go to the Commissioner.; Clause 27: a public register of high-risk AI systems, including those used by county governments.
sources: [{"label":"The Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Kenya Law official)","url":"https://new.kenyalaw.org/akn/ke/bill/senate/2026-02-19/the-artificial-intelligence-bill-2026/eng@2026-02-19"}]

title: 2026 Standing Case Management Order for Civil Cases in Judge Edwards’ Division: Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Courtroom
body: Superior Court of Fulton County, Georgia — Judge Belinda E. Edwards
bodyShort: Superior Court of Fulton County, Georgia (Judge Edwards)
summary: Judge Edwards of Fulton County Superior Court includes an AI-use section in her 2026 civil standing case management order. The February 19, 2026 order tells parties to note AI use at the end of filings and warns of sanctions or referrals for hallucinated or fictitious citations.
keyProvisions: All parties should note whether AI was used to prepare or draft a filing at the end of each filing.; Attorneys and pro se litigants using AI must be aware the court may act if hallucinated or fictitious citations appear.; The order lists striking pleadings, sanctions, and disciplinary referrals as possible actions.; Mistake, lack of technical expertise, and time constraints are not accepted as good-faith excuses for hallucinated citations.

title: AEPD Guidance on agentic AI from a data-protection perspective (Orientaciones sobre IA agentica)
body: Spanish Data Protection Agency (Agencia Espanola de Proteccion de Datos)
summary: Guidance for controllers and processors deploying AI agents that plan and execute multi-step tasks with personal data. It identifies agent-specific risks such as autonomy, tool access and chained actions, and directs risk assessment and DPIAs, human oversight, data minimisation and clear processor arrangements. Not legal-sector specific but relied on by Spanish bars for AI use in firms.
keyProvisions: Agentic systems require risk analysis beyond prompt-level supervision.; Human oversight and limits on autonomous actions.; Data minimisation and purpose limitation across tool calls.; Contractual allocation of controller and processor roles with providers.

title: A.M. No. 25-11-28-SC: Governance Framework on the Use of Human-Centered Augmented Intelligence in the Judiciary
body: Supreme Court of the Philippines (En Banc)
appliesTo: judges; court-staff; lawyers; litigants; providers; all
requirements: disclosure; verification; prohibition; confidentiality; supervision; record-keeping; competence
summary: The Supreme Court of the Philippines' judiciary-wide AI framework, adopted 18 February 2026 and announced on 19 March 2026. It binds justices and judges, court personnel, court users including members of the Bar and the public, and AI vendors, and creates a permanent Committee on Human-Centered Augmented Intelligence.
keyProvisions: AI tools or their output must under no circumstance serve as the sole, primary or determinative basis of any adjudicatory outcome.; Mandatory AI-use disclosure for court-issued adjudicatory documents: tool and version, purpose, extent of use, degree of human oversight, output preserved, and a responsibility statement.; No AI tool shall be used to process confidential, privileged, sensitive or secret information without express authority and under strict supervision of the Court.; No AI tool may be used in the judiciary unless authorised by the Supreme Court En Banc, following a phased pilot-then-rollout process.; A lawyer shall not evade responsibility by claiming that a breach was the fault of, or caused by, an AI tool.; Developers must disclose a tool's logic, limitations and safeguards; trade-secret claims limiting disclosure must be justified; the AI Committee may require ethical impact assessments, adversarial red-teaming and bug-bounty testing.; PHILJA is directed to run AI certificate training for the Bench; the IBP is directed to monitor the profession's AI use and report to the Court.

No. 25-11-28-SC full text","url":"https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/11/101138"},{"label":"Supreme Court — SC adopts framework for the judiciary's use of AI (19 Mar 2026)","url":"https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/sc-adopts-framework-for-judiciarys-use-of-artificial-intelligence/"}]

title: Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals Rule 1.17 — Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2026-02-18","url":"https://www.okcca.net/cases/2026/OK-CR-7/","archiveUrl":"https://web.archive.org/web/20260607172109/https://www.okcca.net/cases/2026/OK-CR-7/","changes":"Adopted by order In re: Addition of a New Rule to the Rules of the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals, 2026 OK CR 7"}]
summary: Rule 1.17 requires that where generative AI has been used in drafting any document filed in the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals, the party or counsel must ensure every AI-produced or AI-modified portion has been verified as accurate by a person responsible for the document. Non-compliance may lead to waiver, striking of the document, or contempt.
keyProvisions: Applies to any document filed in the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals; Where generative AI has been used, every portion produced or modified by it must be verified as accurate by a person responsible for the document; Generative AI is defined as any type of AI that generates content or data in response to a prompt or query by a user; Failure to comply may result in waiver of the affected issue(s) on appeal, striking of the non-compliant document from the record, and/or a finding of contempt

title: Consultation: The Use of AI for the Preparation of Court Documents
body: Civil Justice Council
summary: The Civil Justice Council consulted from 17 February to 14 April 2026 on whether the Civil Procedure Rules for England and Wales should impose AI-specific requirements on court documents, including transparency or disclosure duties for pleadings, skeleton arguments, witness statements and expert reports. Interim findings were published on 30 June 2026; the final report is pending.
keyProvisions: Asked whether the CPR should require parties to disclose AI use in preparing court documents.; Covered professional drafting, witness statements, expert evidence and litigants in person separately.; Consultation closed 14 April 2026.; Followed by an interim update on findings dated 30 June 2026.

body: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California — Judge Lisa J. Cisneros

Attorneys and unrepresented parties remain responsible for submissions, and failure to verify briefs and citations may lead to sanctions or striking.
keyProvisions: Parties are not categorically prohibited from using lawful technological assistance, including AI.; Attorneys and unrepresented parties must understand limitations of tools they use.; The court imputes computer-based tool errors to the signer.; Failure to verify briefs and citations may support sanctions or striking a filing.

title: Administrative Order No. 26-10: Disclosure of Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Attorneys and Self-Represented Litigants
body: Eighteenth Judicial Circuit of Florida — Judge Melanie Chase
bodyShort: Eighteenth Judicial Circuit of Florida (Judge Chase)
summary: The Eighteenth Judicial Circuit of Florida required attorneys and self-represented litigants to disclose generative AI use on filings and certify independent accuracy review. Administrative Order 26-10 took effect February 13, 2026, but was rescinded by Administrative Order 26-24 on June 1, 2026.
keyProvisions: Generative AI use in preparing a pleading, motion, memorandum, response, proposed order, or court record must be disclosed on the face of the filing.; The filing must certify that factual assertions, legal authority, and citations were independently reviewed and verified for accuracy.; The order prohibits fabricated or hallucinated authority, reliance on AI-generated citations without verification, and failure to disclose.; Administrative Order 26-24 rescinded this order on June 1, 2026 after the Florida Supreme Court amended Rule 2.515(d)(2).

title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Court Proceedings (consolidated civil, family and criminal practice directions)
body: Ontario Superior Court of Justice
versions: [{"version":"Consolidated practice directions, AI section added","date":"2026-02-12","url":"https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/news/new-practice-directions-on-the-responsible-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-court-proceedings/","changes":"AI section added to the consolidated civil, family and criminal provincial practice directions; civil direction last updated 17 March 2026."}]
summary: Announced 12 February 2026 and added to the Ontario Superior Court's consolidated civil, family and criminal practice directions. The directions require all legal information obtained with AI assistance to be verified against trusted and authoritative sources, require authorities to be hyperlinked to publicly accessible sites such as CanLII, and set out the consequences of misuse.
keyProvisions: AI-generated references may include incorrect or fictitious authorities; all AI-assisted legal information must be verified against trusted and authoritative sources.; Authorities must be hyperlinked to publicly accessible sites such as CanLII, with paragraph-level references.; Counsel must comply with the factum authenticity certification in r. 4.06.1(2.1) of the Rules of Civil Procedure.; Misuse may result in cost orders, dismissal of a hearing, contempt proceedings, public reprimand or referral to the Law Society of Ontario.

title: Tribunal da Relacao de Guimaraes, 10 Feb 2026: six non-existent appellate rulings generated by AI
body: Guimaraes Court of Appeal (Tribunal da Relacao de Guimaraes)
versions: [{"version":"Acordao 10 February 2026","date":"2026-02-10","url":"https://cnnportugal.iol.pt/inteligencia-artificial/tribunal/relacao-de-guimaraes-acusa-advogado-de-citar-acordaos-que-so-existem-na-imaginacao-da-ia/20260303/69a6c222d34e28842c814a7c","changes":"Reported by CNN Portugal on 3 March 2026; official text not obtained."}]
summary: In a criminal appeal concerning illegal weapons possession the defence cited excerpts from six Relacao and Supreme Court rulings that do not exist. The court called this absolutely inadmissible, explained AI hallucination, held legal professionals to a higher standard, ordered 5 UC in costs and suggested reporting the lawyer to the Ordem dos Advogados.
keyProvisions: Citing non-existent case law generated by AI is inadmissible and breaches professional duties.; Costs of 5 UC, about EUR 500, imposed on the appellant.; Referral to the Portuguese Bar Association suggested.

title: 90th Judicial District Standing Order Regarding Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: 90th Judicial District Court of Texas — Judge Phillip Gregory
bodyShort: 90th Judicial District Court of Texas (Judge Gregory)
summary: The 90th Judicial District standing order applies to all pending and future cases in Young and Stephens Counties. It requires a certificate in each pleading generated with AI, certifying traditional-source verification of AI-created content, and separately prohibits AI recording, listening, or transcription in courtrooms and court offices.
keyProvisions: Attorneys and self-represented litigants using AI for legal research or drafting must include a certificate in each AI-generated pleading.; The certificate requires traditional-source accuracy verification of AI-created language, citations, arguments, and legal analysis.; AI recording, listening, or transcription in courtrooms and court offices is prohibited.

title: CGPJ Instruction 2/2026 on the use of AI systems in judicial activity (Instruccion 2/2026)
body: General Council of the Judiciary (Consejo General del Poder Judicial)
versions: [{"version":"Pleno agreement 28 January 2026, BOE no. 27 of 30 January 2026 (BOE-A-2026-2205)","date":"2026-01-30","url":"https://www.boe.es/diario_boe/txt.php?id=BOE-A-2026-2205","changes":"Original; in force on publication."}]
summary: Binding instruction to Spanish judges and magistrates on AI in jurisdictional work: effective human control, no autonomous decision-making or substitution of judicial reasoning, no AI content without personal critical validation, no unapproved tools except study with open sources and no judicial data, full judicial responsibility, CGPJ supervision of personal-data processing and CGPJ-provided training.
keyProvisions: Art. 4 principles: effective human control, non-substitution, judicial responsibility, independence, fundamental rights, confidentiality and security, bias prevention, proportionality, training.; Art. 8 prohibited uses: autonomous decision-making, replacing assessment of facts, evidence or law, incorporating AI content without personal validation, processing specially protected data or profiling beyond legal authorisation.; Art. 9: only systems supplied by the competent administrations; open tools only for study with open-source information.; Arts 12-13: CGPJ supervision of personal-data processing and provision of judicial AI training.

title: Artificial Intelligence Ethics Charter
body: Court of Justice of the European Union
requirements: prohibition; verification; disclosure; confidentiality; supervision; record-keeping
versions: [{"version":"Charter adopted by the CJEU","date":"2026-01-26","url":"https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2026-03/ethics_charter_ai_-_en.pdf","changes":"Builds on the CJEU Artificial Intelligence Strategy adopted 19 June 2023 and the work of the AI Management Board."},{"version":"Artificial Intelligence Strategy","date":"2023-06-19","url":"https://curia.europa.eu/jcms/upload/docs/application/pdf/2023-11/cjeu_ai_strategy.pdf","changes":"Set the principles and created the AI Management Board composed of Members of both courts and administration representatives."}]
summary: A charter adopted by the Court of Justice of the European Union on 26 January 2026 governing AI tools developed or deployed inside the institution, including tools that assist the Court of Justice and the General Court in their judicial functions. It names automation bias as a specific risk to case-law development and judicial quality.
keyProvisions: 'AI systems shall not be entrusted with decision-making responsibilities'; Judges and Advocates General remain in full control of judicial procedures.; Content generated by AI without verification must be labelled as such if shared beyond the user who requested it.; Users must take a critical approach to machine-generated output, check accuracy and completeness in each case, and report errors.; All AI use must comply with the institution's confidentiality protocols, internal security rules and data-protection standards.; Training, validation and testing datasets must be relevant, representative and, so far as possible, free of error and bias.
