summary: Korea's horizontal AI statute, promulgated 21 January 2025 and in force from 22 January 2026 with its Enforcement Decree. It defines high-impact AI by sector, imposes transparency duties including notice that generative outputs are AI-generated, and imposes risk-management, explanation and human-oversight duties on high-impact operators. Justice uses are not separately enumerated.

body: Eleventh Judicial Circuit of Florida — Judge Ariana Fajardo Orshan
bodyShort: Eleventh Judicial Circuit of Florida (Judge Orshan)
summary: The Eleventh Judicial Circuit of Florida prohibits court personnel from using non-approved generative AI platforms for court business, effective January 15, 2026. title: Practice Note: Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Local Court of New South Wales
summary: A practice note of the Local Court of New South Wales, commencing 12 January 2026, extending the Supreme Court's SC Gen 23 regime to the state's busiest court. keyProvisions: Mirrors Supreme Court Practice Note SC Gen 23 for Local Court proceedings.; Prohibits generative AI in the content of affidavits, witness statements and character references.; Requires disclosure in evidence documents that generative AI was not used.; Practitioners remain responsible for verifying citations in AI-assisted submissions.

title: Procedural Direction PIC13: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Personal Injury Commission of New South Wales
summary: The Personal Injury Commission's direction, in force from 1 January 2026, applies the New South Wales model to workers compensation and motor accidents disputes and goes further in two respects: expert witnesses must disclose AI use, program and version and keep prompt records, and parties may not use AI technology during a hearing.
keyProvisions: Gen AI must not generate the content of written statements; statements must disclose that Gen AI was not used to create their content.; Confidential, de-identified or legally privileged material must not be entered into a Gen AI program unless the platform is contractually closed and does not train on the data.; Where Gen AI assisted written submissions, the author must personally verify that all citations, authorities and legislative references exist and are accurate; verification may not be done with an AI tool.; Experts must disclose any Gen AI use, the program and version, how it was applied, and keep records of prompts or settings.; Parties must not use AI technology, including speech-to-text and transcription applications, during Commission hearings whether in person or virtual.

title: General Application Practice Directive #12: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Submissions
body: Court of King's Bench for Saskatchewan
summary: Signed by Chief Justice M.D. Popescul and effective 1 January 2026. The directive does not prohibit appropriate AI use; it places the onus on whoever files or presents materials to ensure accuracy, authenticity and reliability, and requires independent verification of every AI-derived authority against official, commercial or CanLII sources.
keyProvisions: Nothing in the directive prohibits appropriate use of AI; the onus is on the filer for accuracy, authenticity and reliability.; Counsel and self-represented litigants are responsible for all information, authorities and analysis in written and oral submissions; reliance on AI does not diminish that duty.; AI-generated, summarised or cited legal material must be independently verified against official court or legislative sites, recognised commercial publishers, or CanLII.; Verification must confirm that citations correspond to real authorities, quotations are accurate and AI summaries reflect the source.; Unverified or fabricated authorities may attract cost consequences or other sanctions; blind reliance on AI is inconsistent with professional competence.

title: New York City Bar Formal Opinion 2025-6: Ethical Issues Affecting Use of AI to Record, Transcribe, and Summarize Conversations with Clients
body: New York City Bar Association Committee on Professional Ethics
summary: Formal Opinion 2025-6 addresses AI note-takers and transcription tools used in client communications. Clients must be notified and consent obtained whenever an AI-empowered system records their calls; lawyers must independently review AI transcripts and summaries, understand the tools' technical limits under Rule 1.1, and manage privilege and discovery risks in stored records.
keyProvisions: Clients must be notified and their consent obtained whenever calls are recorded by an AI-empowered system; Lawyers must independently verify the accuracy of AI-generated transcripts and summaries rather than relying on them unreviewed; Attorneys must safeguard AI-generated records and consider privilege, storage and discovery implications; Rule 1.1 competence requires understanding the technical features and limits of the AI tools used by the lawyer and by clients; Where clients use their own AI tools, retainers should disclaim reliance on unreviewed summaries and warn of confidentiality risks; Firms must train subordinates on ethical duties for AI in client communications

title: Guidelines on the use of generative AI by courts and tribunals (CEPEJ(2025)18Final)
body: European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice, Council of Europe
summary: Guidelines adopted 19 December 2025 by the Council of Europe's CEPEJ for courts and tribunals in its 46 member states on using generative AI. Judicial use must be transparent, AI output can never bind a judge, the right to a human judge is guaranteed, and confidential case data must be protected. They replace the February 2024 information note.
keyProvisions: A human judge must always take the decision; generative AI output is never binding.; Judicial use of generative AI should be transparent to parties where it affects proceedings.; Confidential and personal data in case files must not be entered into unsecured tools.; Outputs must be verified for accuracy before any reliance.

body: Advisory Committee on Civil Rules / Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure
bodyShort: Advisory Committee on Civil Rules / Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure
summary: Rules Suggestion 25-CV-S asks the federal Civil Rules committee to consider amending Rule 11(a) so documents with citations and generative-AI-created content include a certification that supervised human review confirmed authorities exist, citations are accurate, and the authorities support the propositions cited.
keyProvisions: The suggestion proposes a Rule 11(a) certification for any document containing citations filed with a court.; The proposed certification covers content created with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence.; The signer would certify that they or a supervised individual reviewed AI-created content for existing and accurately cited authorities.; The signer would certify that cited authorities support the propositions for which they are cited.; The proposed text acknowledges corrective action, including sanctions, for hallucinated content submitted to the court.

title: Hawaii Supreme Court Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts: Final Report (SCMF-24-0000305)
body: Supreme Court of Hawaii, Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts
summary: Hawaii's judiciary studied AI for eighteen months and concluded HRCP Rule 11 already covers AI abuse, while recommending the Supreme Court consider a federal-style AI disclosure declaration for state-court filings. The committee separately adopted internal guardrails for judiciary use of AI tools.
keyProvisions: Existing rules including HRCP Rule 11 are broad enough to provide adequate safeguards against AI abuse in state-court filings; The Court should consider adopting a disclosure rule mirroring D. Haw. General Order 23-1; Under the proposed rule an AI-assisted filing would be accompanied by a declaration confirming AI use and that all cited authorities have been verified; The committee adopted Hawaii State Judiciary Guardrails for the Acceptable Use of AI Tools and Platforms for judges and staff; Advisory only; no implementing Supreme Court order as of September 2026

title: Charte d'utilisation de l'intelligence artificielle au sein de la juridiction administrative
body: Conseil d'État (Council of State), France
versions: [{"version":"First version","date":"2025-12-11","url":"https://www.conseil-etat.fr/Media/actualites/documents/2025/decembre-2025/charte-d-utilisation-de-l-intelligence-artificielle-au-sein-de-la-juridiction-administrative","changes":"Initial charter, adopted after consultation with staff, unions and elected representatives and reviewed by the collège de déontologie."}]
summary: A deontological charter published on 11 December 2025 binding every member, magistrate and staff member of the French administrative jurisdiction — Conseil d'État, cours administratives d'appel, tribunaux administratifs, Cour nationale du droit d'asile and Tribunal du stationnement payant. It sets seven principles for generative AI, excludes high-risk AI systems, and covers external chatbots, which are not blocked but tightly conditioned.
keyProvisions: 'L'IA est un outil qui jamais ne décide': AI may not interpret a rule of law or case law, establish or assess facts, apply law to a case, reason legally or propose an outcome.; Human verification is systematic — AI output, especially legal and case-law references, must never be assumed true or complete and must be checkable by another means.; Users adopt AI-generated content as their own and cannot 'se défausser sur l'IA' for errors or omissions.; Give up using external AI where data security and confidentiality cannot be assured: entering information into a public chatbot 'équivaut à la publier sur internet'.; Users must guard against anchoring, confirmation, training and discriminatory bias, and weigh the environmental cost of each prompt.; The charter covers only limited-risk AI under the AI Act; high-risk judicial AI (Annex III point 8(a)) is excluded.
sources: [{"label":"Conseil d'État — charter page (official)","url":"https://www.conseil-etat.fr/qui-sommes-nous/deontologie/charte-d-utilisation-de-l-intelligence-artificielle-au-sein-de-la-juridiction-administrative"},{"label":"Conseil d'État — charter (official PDF)","url":"https://www.conseil-etat.fr/Media/actualites/documents/2025/decembre-2025/charte-d-utilisation-de-l-intelligence-artificielle-au-sein-de-la-juridiction-administrative"}]

title: Revised Administrative Order Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence and Its Use in the Superior Court of Cabarrus County
body: Superior Court of Cabarrus County, North Carolina — Judge Senior Resident Superior Court Judge Martin B. McGee
bodyShort: Superior Court of Cabarrus County, North Carolina (Judge McGee)
summary: The Cabarrus County Superior Court revised its generative AI administrative order on December 8, 2025. The order permits AI-assisted advocacy without disclosure when reviewed and adopted, but requires disclosure when AI generates, alters, enhances, or analyzes evidence and addresses deepfakes, confidentiality, validation, and sanctions.
keyProvisions: The revised order distinguishes AI that affects evidence from AI that affects advocacy only.; AI used solely to draft legal argument need not be disclosed when the lawyer reviews and adopts it as advocacy.; A party that generates, offers, materially alters, enhances, or analyzes evidence using AI must promptly disclose the nature and scope of use.; Users must protect confidentiality and privilege when employing AI tools.; Parties must use best efforts to verify authenticity, validity, and reliability where synthetic or AI-enhanced media may be involved.

title: UNESCO Guidelines for the use of AI systems in courts and tribunals
body: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
versions: [{"version":"Final","date":"2025-12-03","url":"https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000396582","changes":"Published 3 December 2025; launched at the Athens Roundtable on AI and the Rule of Law, London, 4 December 2025."},{"version":"Draft for consultation","date":"2024-09-01","url":"https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000390781"}]
summary: Published 3 December 2025 after a global consultation, the Guidelines are UNESCO's ethical and operational framework for AI in judicial systems. Fifteen principles in five groups - human rights and equality; safety, security and accuracy; explainability, transparency and auditability; awareness and accountability; human-centred decision-making - are paired with recommendations for judicial organisations and individual judges.
keyProvisions: AI is an assistive, not substitutive, tool; it shall not replace judicial decision-making (principles 1.13-1.15).; Judges should verify AI-generated information independently, avoid over-reliance and disclose when AI tools influenced a decision.; Judicial organisations should set procurement standards with risk and rights-impact review, run training and monitor systems across their lifecycle, including the ability to disable them.; Explainability: a decision that cannot be understood cannot be used to affect someone's rights.

title: Beijing Tongzhou District People's Court: counsel criticised for filing AI-fabricated precedents
body: Beijing Tongzhou District People's Court, selected for the People's Court Case Database
versions: [{"version":"Case Database entry","date":"2025-12-01","url":"https://www.chinanews.com.cn/fz/2026/01-15/10552373.shtml","changes":"Selected for the People's Court Case Database in December 2025; reported nationally 15-16 January 2026."}]
summary: A plaintiff's lawyer filed supplementary submissions citing two reference cases generated by an AI model and never verified. The judge found the cited case numbers belonged to unrelated real cases and wrote a criticism into the judgment without a fine. Entered in the People's Court Case Database in December 2025, it sets graduated consequences for unverified AI citations.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must verify the authenticity of AI-sourced materials before submission.; Consequences graduated by severity: criticism and education for minor cases; fines or detention under Civil Procedure Law art. 114 for serious cases.; Applies to all litigation participants, including self-represented parties.

title: Ústavní soud, usnesení sp. zn. I. ÚS 3004/25 — procedural fine for a constitutional complaint citing non-existent decisions
body: Constitutional Court of the Czech Republic [Ústavní soud]
versions: [{"version":"1.0","date":"2025-12-01","url":"https://nalus.usoud.cz/Search/GetText.aspx?sz=1-3004-25_1","changes":"Decision imposing a CZK 25,000 procedural fine on counsel."}]
summary: The Czech Constitutional Court fined counsel Mgr. Pavel Kehl CZK 25,000 over a constitutional complaint citing decisions that did not exist or whose holdings were grossly misdescribed. The court identified anglicisms, sentence fragments and inconsistent citation formatting as indicators of AI drafting, and held counsel fully responsible for hallucinated arguments.
keyProvisions: Cited authorities including III. ÚS 2987/18, III. ÚS 3881/18 and II. ÚS 2264/14 either did not exist or were grossly misinterpreted.; Indicators of AI generation: anglicisms, incomplete sentence fragments, inconsistent citation formatting and confusion between decision types.; A lawyer bears full responsibility for every argument in a filing, including any hallucinating arguments produced by artificial intelligence.; The CZK 25,000 fine was a quarter of the CZK 100,000 statutory maximum, reflecting a first offence and the remediable nature of the defects.
sources: [{"label":"Ústavní soud — I. ÚS 3004/25 full text (NALUS)","url":"https://nalus.usoud.cz/Search/GetText.aspx?sz=1-3004-25_1"}]

title: B 05.2 Data Security Manual [Tietoturvaopas], Annex 5 'AI guide for the advocate' [Tekoälyopas asianajajalle]
body: Finnish Bar Association [Suomen Asianajajaliitto / Suomen Asianajajat], board
requirements: verification; confidentiality; competence; supervision; record-keeping; risk-classification
versions: [{"version":"13.11.2025 update","date":"2025-12-01","url":"https://asianajajat.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/B-05.2-Tietoturvaopas-hallitus-23.11.2018-paiv.-12.12.2019-24.9.2021-14.12.2023-19.4.2024-ja-13.11.2025-voimassa-1.12.2025-lukien.pdf","changes":"Board updated Annex 5, the AI guide, on 13 November 2025; the manual is in force from 1 December 2025. Annex 5 now runs to twelve numbered requirements plus a Microsoft 365 Copilot deployment guide."},{"version":"19.4.2024 update","date":"2024-04-19","url":"https://asianajajat.fi/asianajajalle/saantely/saadoksia-ja-ohjeita/","changes":"Board added Annex 5 (the AI guide) and amended the 'Background' section to note that AI use increases the risks of handling confidential data."},{"version":"Original","date":"2018-11-23","url":"https://asianajajat.fi/asianajajalle/saantely/saadoksia-ja-ohjeita/","changes":"Manual adopted by the Bar's board on 23 November 2018; earlier updates 12 Dec 2019, 24 Sept 2021 and 14 Dec 2023."}]
summary: The Finnish Bar's information-security manual, recommendatory in character but functioning as commentary on the binding B 05.1 guideline. Its Annex 5, first added in April 2024 and substantially updated in November 2025, is Finland's principal profession-facing generative-AI guidance for advocates, in force from 1 December 2025.
keyProvisions: Annex 5 point 2: whether advice rests wholly or partly on AI output, the advocate is personally liable to the client; tools err in ways that are hard to detect and outputs can look credible while containing factual errors or fabricated references, so the advocate must always verify correctness before use.; Annex 5 point 1: a business-grade licence of the AI application must be acquired, applying binding guideline B 05.1 point 6; a free consumer version is not a business subscription.; Annex 5 point 4: AI tools may be used only if it can be assured that privileged material is not used, stored or shared contrary to confidentiality; terms and settings, including those of extensions and agents, must be checked so inputs are not used for model training or to answer other users.; Annex 5 point 6: firms must ensure staff AI literacy under AI Act Art. 4, covering how AI works, its limits, prohibited uses, human oversight (outputs assessed critically before use) and transparency about when AI was used and how it shaped the result; literacy must be refreshed as systems change.; Annex 5 points 3, 7, 8 and 9: periodic risk assessment of each tool; access rights scoped so AI cannot surface material beyond its intended audience; blocking use of firm data or user content for third-party model training; and logging and monitoring of AI use assigned to competent staff because models drift and fabricate.; Main text: where a cloud service such as an AI solution offers a version with wider security features that separate the customer's data from other users' data, that version must be adopted.

title: Hong Kong Generative AI Technical and Application Guideline
body: Digital Policy Office, Government of Hong Kong
summary: A cross-sector governance guideline published by Hong Kong's Digital Policy Office in April 2025 and updated in December 2025. It sets out a technical and application framework for developers and deployers of generative AI, covering governance, risk assessment, data protection and safety. It is not legal-sector specific but applies to law firms deploying AI in Hong Kong.
keyProvisions: Provides a governance and risk framework for generative AI developers and users.; Addresses data protection, security and content accuracy across sectors.; Voluntary guideline forming part of the Ethical AI Framework.

title: Circular 25-824: Generative AI in Legal Practice: Risks and Tips
body: Law Society of Hong Kong
summary: A circular issued by the Law Society of Hong Kong in December 2025 setting out the risks of generative AI in legal practice and practical tips for solicitors. It cautions that output may be inaccurate or fabricated and must be verified, that client confidentiality must be protected when using tools, and that solicitors remain responsible for all work product.
keyProvisions: Solicitors must verify AI-generated content, including citations, before use.; Client confidential information must not be entered into tools without safeguards.; Solicitors should understand the tool and its data handling before adoption.
sources: [{"label":"Law Society of Hong Kong — Circular 25-824 (PDF)","url":"https://www.hklawsoc.org.hk/-/media/HKLS/pub_e/circular/2025/25-824a1.pdf"}]

title: Aanbevelingen AI in de advocatuur
body: Nederlandse orde van advocaten (Netherlands Bar)

Month-only date: the source gives the month, so the 1st is recorded as the date."}]
summary: The Dutch Bar's recommendations on responsible AI use, published at the end of 2025 and organised around the five statutory core values of the profession. They are notable in Europe for recommending that lawyers ask the client's permission before using AI on a file, and for requiring manual verification of every citation and fact.
keyProvisions: Deskundigheid: basic knowledge of generative AI is essential for every lawyer — LLM principles, prompting, bias mitigation, hallucinations, error detection, regulation and cybersecurity.; 'Verifieer altijd de output': check citations, case law and facts manually before use, and use only tools that cite sources.; 'Vraag toestemming aan de cliënt voor AI-gebruik in het dossier' — seek client permission for AI use on the matter.; No confidential or client data in free or public AI models; apply privacy by design, run a DPIA, and keep input and output inside the firm environment.; Know the data flows — storage country, sub-processors, security — and select suppliers by reading the actual contract and privacy terms, not marketing claims.; Onafhankelijkheid: supervise staff and suppliers, adopt a firm-wide AI policy and implement a control cycle; be alert to tools that simply confirm the prompt.

title: Ethical Considerations and Recommendations for the Use of AI by Judges and Judicial Staff (2025 Annual Report)
body: New York State Unified Court System Advisory Committee on AI and the Courts
summary: The December 2025 annual report of the New York court system's Advisory Committee on AI and the Courts, containing principles-based ethical considerations and recommendations for judges and judicial staff using AI. It supplements the October 2025 interim policy, addressing impartiality, confidentiality, competence and the need for human judgment in every judicial decision.
keyProvisions: Judges must ensure AI use is consistent with the Rules Governing Judicial Conduct.; AI may assist with research and drafting but must not replace judicial reasoning.; Recommends ongoing training and periodic review of approved tools.; Reinforces the interim policy's ban on confidential data in public tools.

title: Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court: Interim Guidelines for Use of Generative AI
body: Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court
versions: [{"version":"Interim","date":"2025-12-01","url":"https://www.mass.gov/guidance/interim-guidelines-for-use-of-generative-ai","changes":"Announced in the December 2025 State of the Judiciary address; the source gives a month only (announced December 2025), so the day is recorded as the 1st"}]
summary: Massachusetts' first judicial AI instrument. The SJC's interim guidelines let court personnel use generative AI for administrative work using only public information, bar tools that retain or train on entered information, and deliberately leave attorney conduct untouched pending possible later rules.
keyProvisions: Apply to court personnel only: judges, clerks, registers, recorders, employees, law clerks, interns and contractors; Permit generative AI for administrative tasks using only public information; Prohibit tools that retain or train on entered information; Do not govern attorney conduct and do not require attorney AI disclosure in filings; Described by Chief Justice Budd as a modest first step; subject to revision

title: Denton County Probate Courts Standing Order Regarding Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: Denton County Probate Courts — Judge Denton County Probate Judges
summary: The Denton County Probate Courts standing order requires attorneys and self-represented litigants to sign and submit an AI certification form in probate cases. The form includes an attestation that any information created or contributed by generative AI was independently verified through traditional legal sources by a human being.
keyProvisions: All attorneys and self-represented litigants must sign and submit the attached AI certification form.; The certification requires human verification of any GenAI-created legal content.; The order applies to all pending and future Denton County probate cases.

title: Eastern District of Texas Local Rules CV-11(g) and AT-3(m) on Generative AI
body: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas
summary: The Eastern District of Texas amended its local rules to address generative AI. Current CV-11(g) tells pro se litigants and represented parties that they remain bound by Rule 11 and must review and verify all content generated with AI, while AT-3(m) similarly reminds attorneys that AI cannot replace independent legal judgment.
keyProvisions: Local Rule CV-11(g) warns that GenAI can produce factually or legally inaccurate content.; Litigants using GenAI must review and verify all content to satisfy Rule 11.; Attorney Rule AT-3(m) applies the same responsibility to lawyers.

summary: The Bar Council's ethics guidance for barristers in England and Wales on generative AI, first issued January 2024 and updated November 2025. Barristers may use these tools but must verify all output, avoid disclosing confidential or privileged material to public systems, and remain responsible for their work under the Core Duties.
keyProvisions: Barristers must independently verify any legal proposition or authority produced by generative AI.; Client and privileged information should not be entered into public tools without safeguards.; Barristers should understand the tool's limitations, including hallucination and bias.; Use of AI does not alter the barrister's personal responsibility under the BSB Handbook.

title: Legal Ethics Opinion 1901: Reasonable Fees and the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Virginia State Bar (approved by the Supreme Court of Virginia)
versions: [{"version":"Approved","date":"2025-11-24","url":"https://vsb.org/common/Uploaded%20files/LEOs/1901.pdf","changes":"Approved by the Supreme Court of Virginia and effective immediately; VSB Council approved the proposed opinion on 12 June 2025"}]
summary: LEO 1901 addresses how Virginia lawyers may bill for work assisted by generative AI. It concludes that value-based and flat fees may reflect efficiency gains, the skill of effectively incorporating the technology, and the value of the output, and remain reasonable under Rule 1.5(a); a lawyer need not reduce a flat or value-based fee solely because AI accelerated the work.
keyProvisions: Value-based fees may reflect efficiency gains and the specialised skill of effectively incorporating AI, and remain reasonable under Rule 1.5(a); A lawyer is not ethically required to reduce a flat or value-based fee solely because generative AI accelerated the work; The 'skill requisite to perform the legal service properly' may increase when using AI; Rule 1.5(b) may require additional explanation of why the lawyer's experience or technical skill contributes value even where time spent has fallen

summary: Slovenia's AI Act implementing statute designating five market-surveillance authorities: the Information Commissioner for prohibited practices and high-risk systems in biometrics, criminal justice, migration and democratic processes; AKOS as single contact point and sandbox operator; the Bank of Slovenia; the Insurance Supervision Agency; and the Market Inspectorate. It also sets procedures, offences and fines.

title: Guidelines for the use of generative AI
body: Supreme Court of Western Australia

The document carries no date on its face; 2025-11-20 is taken from the PDF's creation metadata and should be re-confirmed against the court before it is treated as authoritative."}]
summary: Principles-based guidelines of the Supreme Court of Western Australia for lawyers, self-represented litigants and expert witnesses. AI-generated content relied on in proceedings must be verified by a human who takes legal responsibility; confidential, suppressed or privileged material must not be entered into public tools; and AI use must be disclosed when the court directs.
keyProvisions: AI-generated content must be verified by a human who takes legal responsibility for the document; that a document was AI-assisted is no answer to errors or omissions.; Confidential, suppressed or legally privileged information must not be entered into public or unsecured generative AI tools.; Affidavits and witness statements must be drafted in the witness's own words; AI content must not substitute the witness's voice.; Expert reports must comply with the Harmonised Expert Witness Code of Conduct (Practice Direction 4.5.2.1); experts should consider what disclosure of AI use is needed.; Generative AI must not be used to mislead the court or other parties about the work undertaken; use should be disclosed when directed or otherwise appropriate.

title: Acta 244-2025: Judicial Ethics Code (article 17 on responsible use of technology and AI)
body: Supreme Court of Chile (Corte Suprema)
versions: [{"version":"Approved at the XXVIII Jornadas de Reflexion (23-24 October 2025); published in the Diario Oficial","date":"2025-11-19","url":"https://www.bcn.cl/leychile/Navegar?idNorma=1218674","changes":"First Judicial Ethics Code and first AI rule for Chilean judges."}]
summary: Chile's first Judicial Ethics Code, adopted by auto acordado and published on 19 November 2025. Article 17 permits AI as a support tool but declares judicial decisions always human and non-delegable, requires judges to verify any AI result independently, forbids automatic incorporation of AI text into rulings, and requires control over data shared with external platforms.
keyProvisions: Judicial decisions are human and non-delegable; no delegation of evidence assessment or dispute resolution to AI.; Judges must independently verify AI-generated references.; No automatic or unreflective incorporation of AI text into filings or judgments.; Automated transcription and translation only as preliminary support, reviewed and certified by a person.; Control of data shared with external platforms; confidentiality in virtual hearings.

title: Mezu v. Mezu, No. 361, Sept. Term 2025 (Appellate Court of Maryland, reported, 29 Oct 2025)
body: Appellate Court of Maryland
summary: Maryland's leading AI-hallucination decision. The Appellate Court of Maryland published Mezu as a warning to the bar, holding that failing to read AI-generated citations before filing can produce briefs citing multiple fictitious cases, and referred the signing attorney to the Attorney Grievance Commission. Delegation to a law clerk was no defence.
keyProvisions: The court reported the case to address the recurring problem of AI-drafted briefs containing incorrect, inaccurate or fictitious citations; The brief contained citations to multiple fictitious cases, misquoted passages, and citations that did not support the propositions cited; Failure to read AI-generated citations before filing is the operative breach; Based on the nature and severity of the conduct the court referred the attorney to the Attorney Grievance Commission; Delegation of research to a law clerk did not excuse the signing attorney

title: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: New York State Unified Court System
summary: An interim policy adopted by the New York State Unified Court System on 10 October 2025 for judges and non-judicial employees. It permits only approved generative AI tools, requires training, forbids entering confidential or non-public information into public tools, and requires that all output be reviewed and verified by the human user, who remains accountable for the result.
keyProvisions: Only court-approved AI tools may be used for official work.; Judges and staff must complete training before using approved tools.; Confidential, sealed and personal information must not be entered into public AI tools.; All AI output must be reviewed for accuracy; responsibility stays with the user.

title: CCBE Guide on the use of generative AI by lawyers
body: Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe
summary: Guide published 2 October 2025 by the CCBE, which represents European bars and law societies, on how lawyers should use generative AI. It is permissive with cautions: lawyers must understand tool limitations, verify all output, protect professional secrecy and client confidentiality, and consider the EU AI Act's literacy and transparency duties.
keyProvisions: Lawyers remain fully responsible for advice and documents produced with generative AI.; Output must be checked for accuracy, including invented citations and misstatements of law.; Professional secrecy requires care over what is entered into tools and where data is processed.; Recommends firm-level policies, training and awareness of the AI Act's Article 4 literacy duty.

title: GenAI FAQ
body: United States District Court for the District of Minnesota
summary: The District of Minnesota GenAI FAQ, dated October 1, 2025, describes common generative AI litigation uses and limitations. It states that the court does not currently require disclosure of AI use in filings, gives practice pointers on confidentiality and checking research, and reminds litigants that legal, procedural, ethical, and protective-order obligations still apply.
keyProvisions: The FAQ defines generative AI and describes common litigation uses such as legal research, drafting, revision, summarization, translation, and presentations.; The FAQ states that generative AI cannot check the accuracy of its own responses.; The District of Minnesota does not currently require disclosure of AI use in court filings.; The FAQ advises users to avoid entering privileged, confidential, or sensitive information when data may be retained or accessed.; Users must always use generative AI consistently with ethical obligations, Federal Rules of Civil and Criminal Procedure, and protective orders.

title: Interim Principles and Guidelines on the Court's Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: Federal Court of Canada
summary: Interim principles published by the Federal Court of Canada on 29 September 2025 governing the court's own use of AI. The court commits not to use AI or automated decision-making in determining the outcome of cases without prior public consultation, and sets accountability, transparency and confidentiality requirements for administrative uses by judges and staff.
keyProvisions: The court will not use AI or automated decision-making to decide cases without public consultation.; Administrative uses of AI by judges and staff must be accountable and transparent.; Confidential and personal information in court records must be protected in any AI use.

title: Law 23 September 2025 no. 132 on artificial intelligence (Legge 132/2025)
body: Italian Parliament (Parlamento italiano)

Article 13 confines AI in the intellectual professions to support tasks and requires clients to be told in clear language which AI systems a professional uses. Article 15 reserves every judicial decision to the magistrate.

title: Practice Direction Number 5 of 2025: Accuracy of References in Submissions
body: Supreme Court of Queensland
summary: Issued by Chief Justice Bowskill on 24 September 2025, this practice direction responds to generative AI by requiring every written submission to name the individual person responsible for its contents. Naming oneself certifies that all references have been verified and that the document reflects the practitioner's own professional judgment.
keyProvisions: Written submissions must name the responsible person or persons at the end of the document; naming a firm is not sufficient.; The person making oral submissions is the responsible person for those submissions and also for the written submissions.; The responsible person must verify the accuracy and relevance of all references to legislation, authorities and other sources.; Practitioners responsible for submissions containing non-existent material may be referred to the Legal Services Commissioner or required to show cause against a personal costs order.; Self-represented litigants must check references against AustLII, Queensland Judgments and the official legislation sites; reliance on fake material may cause an adjournment and adverse costs.; Expressly cites Ayinde v Haringey [2025] EWHC 1383 at [5] and the Queensland Law Society's AI guidance statement.

title: Idaho Office of Administrative Hearings: Guidelines for Administrative Law Judges Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: Idaho Office of Administrative Hearings
summary: Idaho's administrative judiciary adopted a near-total ban on adjudicative AI use. ALJs may not use AI to draft orders or decisions, to research law, or to summarise evidence and party submissions; limited transcript use is allowed; and ALJs may require parties to certify that AI-drafted content was checked by a human.
keyProvisions: ALJs are not permitted to use AI or generative AI to write orders or decisions, at any stage of drafting including outlines; ALJs are not permitted to use AI or generative AI for legal research in case proceedings; ALJs are not permitted to use AI or generative AI to analyse or summarise evidence or party submissions, partly because uploaded data including PII may be retained for training; AI-generated voice-to-text transcripts from licensed non-retaining software are permitted but may not be cited; citations must be to the recording and verified; ALJs may request AI disclosure statements from represented and self-represented parties at their discretion, with recommended certification language; Governing canons: Idaho Code of Conduct for ALJs 1.2, 2.2 and 2.5
sources: [{"label":"OAH AI Guidelines (PDF)","url":"https://oah.idaho.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/OAH-AI-Guidelines.pdf"}]

title: Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) in Anwaltskanzleien — Leitfaden und Checkliste für KI-Dienstleister
body: Österreichischer Rechtsanwaltskammertag (Austrian Bar), Ausschuss IT und Digitalisierung
versions: [{"version":"Stand September 2025","date":"2025-09-23","url":"https://www.anwaltsblatt.at/fileadmin/user_upload/Anwaltsblatt/PDF/oerak_25_leitfaden-KI-folder_a4_250923.pdf","changes":"Issued by the ÖRAK's IT and digitalisation committee and distributed with the Anwaltsblatt."}]
summary: The Austrian Bar's four-page guide of September 2025 on using AI in law firms, with an annexed checklist that an AI provider must sign before a firm may instruct it. It applies § 9(2) RAO confidentiality and the binding § 40(3) RL-BA service-provider requirements to AI suppliers and makes staff AI competence a precondition of use.
keyProvisions: Entering mandate-related or confidential information into public or unsecured AI systems breaks confidentiality (§ 9(2) RAO) and is professionally impermissible.; Lawyers may instruct only AI providers that meet § 40(3) RL-BA; otherwise only abstract, anonymous questions without any client link may be asked.; The provider must confirm in writing: no use of firm input for model training, secure deletion, an Art. 28 GDPR processor agreement, EU or adequacy-country hosting (e.g. Switzerland, UK), equivalent compliance by sub-processors, and immediate notification if searched by police.; The police-notification duty falls away for sub-processors that store data only briefly and process it fully automatically without human access (§ 40(3)(4) RL-BA).; 'Die anwaltliche Sorgfaltspflicht erfordert eine ausnahmslose Überprüfung und Verifizierung aller KI-generierten Ergebnisse'; final responsibility stays with the lawyer.; AI use is permitted only where staff have AI competence, maintained by regular training, under a binding internal directive naming permitted tools, prohibited data and a responsible person.

body: Unified Judicial System of Pennsylvania

title: California Rule of Court 10.430 and Standard 10.80: Generative AI use by courts
body: Judicial Council of California
summary: Rule 10.430 of the California Rules of Court, effective 1 September 2025, requires every California court that permits generative AI use by judicial officers or staff to adopt a use policy by 15 December 2025. Policies must address confidentiality, bias, human review of output, and disclosure when public-facing content is fully AI-generated. Standard 10.80 offers a model policy.
keyProvisions: Courts permitting generative AI must adopt a written use policy by 15 December 2025.; Policies must prohibit entering confidential, personal or sealed information into public tools.; Staff must review AI output for accuracy and bias before use.; Public-facing written or visual content generated entirely by AI must be disclosed as such.

title: Points of Attention on the Use of Generative AI in Attorney Practice: Five Points for Appropriate Use
body: Japan Federation of Bar Associations (Nichibenren), AI Strategy Working Group

summary: Members-only guidance issued in September 2025 by the JFBA's AI Strategy Working Group setting five points for appropriate use of generative AI in legal practice: keep confidential and client-identifiable information out of external AI services; treat outputs including cited cases as unverified until checked against primary sources; the attorney bears final responsibility.
keyProvisions: Confidentiality: avoid inputting client-identifiable or confidential information into external generative-AI services.; Hallucination: verify AI-cited statutes and case law against primary sources before use.; Responsibility remains with the attorney; AI output is not exculpatory.; Client explanation and record-keeping of verification steps.

title: California Standard of Judicial Administration 10.80: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Judicial Officers
body: California Judicial Branch
summary: California Standard 10.80 gives statewide guidance for judicial officers using generative AI within their adjudicative role. It addresses confidentiality, discriminatory use, accuracy verification, hallucination correction, biased or harmful content, and whether to disclose AI use when creating content provided to the public.
keyProvisions: Judicial officers using generative AI in adjudicative tasks should not enter confidential, identifying, or nonpublic information into public systems.; Judicial officers should not use generative AI to unlawfully discriminate or disparately impact protected groups.; Judicial officers should take reasonable steps to verify accuracy and correct hallucinated output.; Judicial officers should remove biased, offensive, or harmful content from AI material used.; Judicial officers should consider disclosure if AI is used to create public content.

title: Standing Order Governing Civil Cases
body: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio — Judge Michael J. Newman
summary: Judge Newman’s Southern District of Ohio civil standing order adds an AI provision effective August 27, 2025. It bars attorneys and pro se parties from using AI to prepare any court filing, excludes legal search engines, internet search engines, and Microsoft Suite-type products, and requires immediate notice if AI use is discovered.
keyProvisions: The standing civil order states that a new AI provision is effective August 27, 2025.; No attorney for a party or pro se party may use AI in preparing any filing submitted to the court.; The ban does not apply to information gathered from legal search engines, internet search engines, or Microsoft Suite-type products.; Parties and counsel must immediately inform the court if they discover AI use in a document filed in their case or an opponent’s case.; The purpose is to prevent citation of false, misleading, or hallucinated cases and law.

summary: Criteria published in Mexico's Semanario Judicial de la Federacion on 22 August 2025 holding that AI may assist a judge only as an auxiliary tool, under an exercise of self-restraint and with respect for human rights, and that deliberation and the final decision remain strictly within the jurisdictional sphere.
keyProvisions: Technology operates as an auxiliary and not as a substitute; deliberation and decision remain in the strictly jurisdictional sphere.; The final decision in a judicial process must rest exclusively with judges and magistrates.; Reported guiding principles: proportionality and non-harm, protection of personal data, transparency and explainability, and human judicial supervision.

title: Standing Order Governing the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio — Judge Jeffery P. Hopkins
summary: Judge Hopkins’s Southern District of Ohio standing order, issued August 20, 2025, requires any party or self-represented litigant using generative AI to generate any portion of a motion, brief, pleading, or other filing to attach a separate declaration disclosing the use and certifying source review, accuracy, and Rule 11 compliance.
keyProvisions: The order identifies text-generation software powered by AI, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Harvey.ai.; Any party, including a self-represented litigant, who uses generative AI to generate any portion of a filing must attach a separate declaration.; The declaration must disclose generative AI use and be captioned “Disclosure and Verification of Use of Generative AI.”; The declarant must certify review of relevant source material, accuracy of submissions, and Rule 11 compliance.; Signers remain responsible under Rule 11 whether or not generative AI was used.

summary: Kenya's Judiciary is developing an AI Adoption Policy Framework, announced officially in August 2025, and circulated a draft AI Policy with draft Practice Directions for public participation in May 2026. Reporting describes a three-tier risk model, a certificate of human verification for AI-assisted filings, and a bar on AI displacing judicial decision-making. Not in force.
keyProvisions: Announced aim: guide integration of AI tools while safeguarding judicial independence, data privacy and due process (Judiciary of Kenya, 11 Aug 2025).; Reported draft: any AI-assisted filing must be accompanied by a certificate of human verification, placing responsibility on the advocate rather than the tool.; Reported draft: three risk tiers — bail assessment and predictive sentencing require mandatory human oversight and audits; legal research requires verification and disclosure; scheduling and transcription face general monitoring.; Reported draft: a clear boundary between administrative automation and adjudicative discretion, with AI as decision support only.

title: Policy Memorandum 25-40: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in EOIR Proceedings
body: United States Department of Justice, Executive Office for Immigration Review
summary: Signed by Acting Director Sirce E. Owen and effective 8 August 2025, this is the first Department of Justice component policy on generative AI binding practitioners. EOIR imposes neither a blanket prohibition nor mandatory disclosure, but treats hallucinated or erroneous AI content as a likely professional-conduct violation and directs adjudicators to refer suspected misuse for discipline.
keyProvisions: EOIR has no blanket prohibition on generative AI and no mandatory disclosure requirement in its proceedings.; Individual immigration judges, courts and the Board of Immigration Appeals may adopt standing orders or local operating procedures on AI use and disclosure.; Practitioners filing hallucinated or erroneous AI-generated content likely violate professional conduct obligations and may be disciplined under 8 C.F.R. 1003.102(c) for knowingly or recklessly offering false evidence.; Adjudicators who suspect improper AI use should refer the matter to EOIR's Attorney Discipline Program and, as appropriate, its Anti-Fraud Program.; Improper use of generative AI by an EOIR adjudicator may result in corrective or disciplinary action; unauthorised AI services on DOJ government-furnished equipment are prohibited.; Cites OCAHO's guidance established by adjudication in United States v. Wallcon, LLC, 21 OCAHO no. 1630 (2025), and OMB Memorandum M-25-21.

title: Camara de Apelacion en lo Civil y Comercial de Rosario, Sala II, Giacomino c/ Monserrat: AI-fabricated citations
body: Civil and Commercial Court of Appeals of Rosario (Camara de Apelacion en lo Civil y Comercial de Rosario)
versions: [{"version":"Judgment (CUIJ 21-11893083-2, August 2025)","date":"2025-08-01","url":"https://abogados.com.ar/la-primera-sentencia-argentina-contra-la-ia-el-riesgo-de-una-profesion-en-piloto-automatico/37412","changes":"Initial decision; reported by Abogados.com.ar, official text not obtained."}]

keyProvisions: No consent relieves a lawyer of the duty to verify sources.; Filing AI-fabricated jurisprudence breaches professional ethics regardless of good faith.; Referral to the Colegio de Abogados de Rosario.; Followed by General Roca (26 fabricated citations) and Neuquen referrals.

title: Louisiana Act No. 250 of 2025: verification and disclosure of AI-generated or falsified evidence (La. C.C.P. art. 371)
body: Louisiana Legislature
versions: [{"version":"Act No. 250 (2025 Regular Session, HB 178)","date":"2025-08-01","url":"https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1425558","archiveUrl":"https://web.archive.org/web/20260812134358/https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1425558","changes":"Signed 11 June 2025, effective 1 August 2025"}]
summary: Louisiana enacted a civil-procedure duty to police AI-falsified evidence. Counsel must exercise reasonable diligence to verify exhibit authenticity, disclose known falsification of their own exhibits including AI generation or alteration, and raise reasonable suspicion about an opponent's exhibits at the pretrial stage, on pain of contempt and discipline.
keyProvisions: Attorneys must exercise reasonable diligence to verify the authenticity of evidence before offering it to the court; A party that knows or has reason to know its own exhibits have been falsified, including by AI generation or alteration, must disclose that fact; A party with reasonable suspicion that opposing exhibits are AI-generated or falsified must raise it at the pretrial conference or a pretrial admissibility hearing; Counsel offering false or AI-manipulated evidence without disclosure face contempt and potential disciplinary action where they knew or should have known through reasonable diligence; Applies to civil proceedings only; does not address AI-drafted briefs containing hallucinated citations; Enrolled text not opened in this research run and must be confirmed before publication

title: Interim guidance on the use of artificial intelligence in the federal judiciary
body: Administrative Office of the United States Courts, Artificial Intelligence Task Force
versions: [{"version":"Interim guidance, distributed judiciary-wide","date":"2025-07-31","url":"https://www.uscourts.gov/data-news/reports/annual-reports/directors-annual-report/annual-report-2025/court-operations-annual-report-2025","changes":"First judiciary-wide AI guidance; temporary pending a permanent AI governance framework called for by the September 2025 Strategic Plan."}]
summary: Interim guidance developed by the Administrative Office's AI Task Force and distributed across the United States federal judiciary on 31 July 2025. It permits experimentation with AI while directing users to independently verify all AI-generated output, cautioning against delegating core judicial functions, and asking each court to define locally approved tools and tasks. The text itself is not published.
keyProvisions: Judiciary users must review and independently verify all AI-generated content and remain accountable for AI-assisted work.; Cautions against delegating core judicial functions to AI, including decision making and case adjudication.; Advises extreme caution when using AI on novel legal questions.; Courts should define the tasks for which locally approved AI tools may be used.; Users should consider whether AI use should be disclosed, to whom, and consistently with confidentiality and ethical duties.

body: High Court of Kerala
summary: A policy issued by the High Court of Kerala on 19 July 2025 for the state's district judiciary, the first by an Indian High Court. Judges and court staff may use AI only for assistance and must not use it to reach findings, orders or judgments; outputs must be verified and confidential case data kept out of public tools.
keyProvisions: AI tools may not be used to arrive at findings, reliefs, orders or judgments.; Approved AI may assist with administrative and clerical tasks only.; Any AI output used must be verified by the judicial officer.; Confidential case information must not be entered into public AI tools.

title: Guidelines on the scope of obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
body: European Commission
summary: European Commission guidelines published 18 July 2025 clarifying which organisations are providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act and what documentation, copyright and transparency duties attach from 2 August 2025. title: Orientacao Administrativa no 07/2025: Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Arbitrations
body: Brazil-Canada Arbitration and Mediation Centre (Centro de Arbitragem e Mediacao Brasil-Canada)
summary: Guidance for arbitrations administered by CAM-CCBC: all participants must understand AI tools and their limits; AI use must respect confidentiality; party representatives are responsible for the factual and legal accuracy of AI-assisted work; disclosure is not required as a general rule but should be discussed case by case; and arbitrators may not delegate decision-making to AI.
keyProvisions: Participants are responsible for understanding AI tools and their limitations.; Confidentiality and data-protection duties apply to AI use in arbitration.; Representatives must review AI output for accuracy; no use of AI to disrupt proceedings or falsify evidence.; Arbitrators retain their personal mandate; decision-making functions cannot be delegated.; Disclosure decided case by case; CAM-CCBC itself does not use AI in administration.

body: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California — Judge Peter H. Kang

title: Guide for the use of Artificial Intelligence for Lawyers (Guia para el uso de Inteligencia Artificial para Abogados)
body: Public Bar of the Federal Capital (Colegio Publico de la Abogacia de la Capital Federal)

summary: Buenos Aires bar guide built on four pillars: responsible use minimising hallucinations and bias; permanent human control with the lawyer as final decision-maker; protection of personal data and professional secrecy, including client authorisation before sharing confidential information; and continuous training. It states that AI does not exempt the lawyer from responsibility for anything signed or filed.
keyProvisions: Verify all AI outputs against referenced sources; beware hallucinations and false citations.; No client data on platforms without security guarantees; obtain client authorisation where appropriate.; Be transparent with clients about AI use and do not create false expectations.; Do not delegate decisions to AI; the lawyer bears sole responsibility for filings.; Continuous training, including prompt design.

body: Superior Court of Fulton County, Georgia — Judge Craig L. Schwall Sr.

summary: Judge Schwall of Fulton County Superior Court requires attorneys and pro se litigants to disclose AI use in criminal and civil filings. The July 11, 2025 standing order requires an AI-tool disclosure, independent-review certification, and verification that every legal, statutory, and record citation exists as cited.
keyProvisions: The order applies to briefs, proposed orders, and other written submissions in criminal and civil dockets.; AI use to prepare, draft, or review a filing must be disclosed in the document.; The required certification identifies the AI tool and certifies independent review for accuracy and good law.; Every citation to law, case, statute, or the record must be verified as accurate and as existing for the cited proposition.

title: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
body: European AI Office (independent chairs)
summary: A voluntary code drafted under the EU AI Office and published 10 July 2025 that gives providers of general-purpose AI models a route to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's GPAI obligations. Its chapters cover transparency, copyright and safety and security. Commission enforcement powers over GPAI providers became effective on 2 August 2026.
keyProvisions: Transparency chapter sets a model documentation form for downstream providers and regulators.; Copyright chapter commits signatories to respect rights reservations and lawful access to training data.; Safety and security chapter applies to models with systemic risk.; Signing is voluntary; signatories benefit from a presumption of good faith in enforcement.

title: Circular No. 242/2025: Updates on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Legal Practice
body: Malaysian Bar [Badan Peguam Malaysia]
versions: [{"version":"Original, with annexed advisory on the use of generative AI in legal practice","date":"2025-07-03","url":"https://www.malaysianbar.org.my/cms/upload_files/document/Circular%20No%20242-2025.pdf"}]
summary: The Malaysian Bar's principal AI instrument, issued 3 July 2025 by the Bar Council Cyber and Privacy Laws Committee and the Legal Tech, AI and Sandbox Committee. Its annexed advisory sets out recommended and prohibited uses, a nine-risk mitigation table and a four-R framework for practitioners adopting generative AI.
keyProvisions: All generative AI output must be independently verified against traditional legal databases; if verification is not possible the content must not be relied on.; Do not input personal data, NRIC or financial data or client-specific facts; redact before use and comply with the Personal Data Protection Act 2010.; All output must be subject to human oversight, legal judgment and ethical consideration.; Keep clear records of professional oversight and final review for audit purposes.; Read terms of use to establish whether inputs are retained or used for training; prefer legal-sector tools with privacy and regulatory controls.; Identifies unauthorised practice of law as a generative AI risk; AI must not substitute for trained legal minds.
sources: [{"label":"Malaysian Bar — Circular No. 242/2025 (official PDF)","url":"https://www.malaysianbar.org.my/cms/upload_files/document/Circular%20No%20242-2025.pdf"}]

title: Standing Order on the Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: United States Court of International Trade — Judge Jennifer Choe-Groves
bodyShort: United States Court of International Trade (Judge Choe-Groves)
summary: Judge Jennifer Choe-Groves of the Court of International Trade requires counsel and pro se litigants filing generative-AI-drafted text in her cases to disclose the program, manner of use, and portions drafted, certify human review for factual and legal accuracy, and certify no unauthorized disclosure of confidential information.
keyProvisions: Applies to submissions in cases assigned to Judge Choe-Groves containing text drafted with the assistance of generative AI.; Requires a disclosure notice identifying the program used, the manner in which it was used, and the specific text portions drafted.; Requires certification that counsel or the party reviewed the included text and legal research for factual and legal accuracy.; Requires certification that use of the AI program did not cause unauthorized disclosure of confidential or business proprietary information.; Allows any party to move for appropriate relief after such a notice is filed.

Pinson, with membership from state court classes and judicial partner agencies; Charge: assess risks and benefits of generative AI in the courts and recommend measures to maintain public trust and confidence; Principal focus on court rules and procedures; A parallel State Bar of Georgia committee reviews the Georgia Rules of Professional Conduct; Report submitted 3 July 2025; implementing order not verified

The certification covers review of all source material and verification of the accuracy of AI content under Rule 11.

title: Vägledning om användning av generativ AI i advokatverksamhet
body: Swedish Bar Association [Sveriges advokatsamfund]
requirements: verification; confidentiality; competence; supervision; consent; permissive
versions: [{"version":"Guidance to the board of the Swedish Bar Association","date":"2025-06-12","url":"https://www.advokatsamfundet.se/globalassets/advokatsamfundet_sv/advokatyrket/vagledning-om-anvandning-av-generativ-ai-i-advokatverksamhet.pdf","changes":"Fourteen-page guidance produced by the working group that drafted the 2024 general advice."},{"version":"Allmänna råd rörande användning av generativa AI-modeller i advokatverksamhet","date":"2024-06-13","url":"https://www.advokatsamfundet.se/globalassets/advokatsamfundet_sv/advokatyrket/allmanna-rad-rorande-anvandning-av-generativa-ai-modeller-i-advokatverksamhet.pdf","changes":"General advice adopted by the board on 13 June 2024."}]
summary: Guidance dated Stockholm, 12 June 2025, from a Swedish Bar Association working group on using generative AI in legal practice. It ties GenAI use to the Code of Conduct (VRGA) across four areas: regulatory compliance, advisory liability, professional secrecy, and principal liability and office organisation.
keyProvisions: GenAI can produce fluent text containing factual errors or references to cases and statutes that do not exist; output must be critically reviewed before it enters advice.; Advisory liability applies in full whether or not the advice rests on GenAI output (VRGA 5.3, 6.2).; Professional secrecy holds regardless of working method; client information must not be used to train the model or generate output for other users.; Client consent must be obtained where the tool's handling of information carries risks that contract terms and safeguards cannot address; standard terms are not sufficient.; Under VRGA 7.6.2 firms should adopt, publish and regularly update GenAI policies and provide staff training scaled to actual use.

It reaffirms MRPC 1.1 competence as the operative standard, examines AI and the unauthorised practice of law under MCL 600.916, and makes six institutional recommendations on member education, staff development and standing committee oversight. It is a living document, not an ethics opinion.

title: Assessment Tool for the operationalisation of the European Ethical Charter on the use of AI in judicial systems (CEPEJ(2023)16)
body: European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice, Council of Europe
summary: A self-assessment questionnaire adopted by CEPEJ in December 2023 and revised on 5 June 2025 that lets judicial institutions evaluate an AI tool or service against the 2018 Ethical Charter before and during deployment. It is aimed at public decision-makers procuring or building AI for courts and complements the Council of Europe's HUDERIA risk-assessment methodology.
keyProvisions: Structured questions for each Charter principle, applied to a specific AI system used in the judicial field.; Intended for decision-makers in judicial institutions procuring or building court AI.; May be supplemented by transparency, security and personal-data tools, and by the HUDERIA methodology.; Linked to the CEPEJ Resource Centre on Cyberjustice and AI, which catalogued 125 systems by end 2024.

title: Arkansas Supreme Court Administrative Order No. 25: Artificial Intelligence
body: Supreme Court of Arkansas
summary: Arkansas's court-side AI order. It warns that disclosing confidential or sealed client or case information to a generative AI model may breach Administrative Order No. 19, the Rules of Professional Conduct and the Code of Judicial Conduct, and bars court personnel from exposing CourtConnect data to external generative AI tools without Automation Committee approval.
keyProvisions: Intentional or inadvertent disclosure of confidential or sealed client or case information to a generative AI model may violate Administrative Order No. 19, the ARPC and the Code of Judicial Conduct; Court personnel with internal CourtConnect access may not intentionally expose court system data to any external generative AI tool; An exemption exists for court-approved research and analysis projects with prior approval of the Supreme Court Committee on Automation; The order does not require pre-filing disclosure or certification of AI use

summary: Japan's first framework AI statute, promulgated 4 June 2025 and fully in force from 1 September 2025. It establishes the AI Strategy Headquarters and a basic AI plan and sets duties of effort for the state, local governments, businesses and citizens. It contains no risk classification, no penalties, and no provisions specific to courts or legal services.

title: STJ SLS 3.596: refusal to suspend AI petition-drafting platform Resolve Juizado

body: United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama — Judge Annemarie Carney Axon
summary: Judge Axon of the Northern District of Alabama requires AI disclosure in civil submissions. The May 23, 2025 initial order requires attorneys and pro se parties who use AI to prepare filings to identify the AI tool and certify independent review for accuracy, legitimacy, and good law.

title: General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence, Version 1.0
body: Information and eGovernment Authority (iGA), Kingdom of Bahrain
summary: Bahrain's whole-of-government AI policy, issued by the Information and eGovernment Authority on 20 May 2025. It applies to all government entities and sets four pillars: legal compliance, adoption and use, awareness and education, and cooperation. It contains no judiciary-, court- or legal-services-specific provision.
keyProvisions: First principle — Human Decision-Making: AI is a tool to assist humans and the final decision in important matters must remain under human control, especially where individual and societal rights are concerned.; Pillar 1 requires government entities to comply with the Personal Data Protection Law No. 30 of 2018, the Law on Protection of State Documents and Information, Law No. 60 of 2014 on Cybercrime, the Open Data Policy and the GCC AI Ethics guideline.; Pillar 2 requires entities to consider AI in projects and procurements, to adopt AI only in coordination with the iGA, to follow iGA standards for launching AI initiatives, and to conduct regular audits and reviews.; Pillar 2 places responsibility for negative outcomes of AI use on responsible individuals rather than the technology.; Pillar 3 requires government entities to run AI awareness and training programmes for their employees.

title: General Order No. 25-01 Concerning the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Preparation of Filings
body: U.S. District Court for the District of Wyoming
summary: The District of Wyoming’s General Order 25-01 addresses artificial intelligence in the preparation of filings. It reminds represented and pro se litigants of Rule 11, recognizes potential benefits of AI, but strictly prohibits AI-generated arguments or citations not warranted by existing law, including hallucinated authorities.
keyProvisions: The general order applies to litigants appearing in the District of Wyoming, represented or pro se.; The court recognizes AI can be beneficial to attorneys, clients, and unrepresented litigants.; The order reminds filers that Rule 11 requires legal contentions to be warranted by existing law.; AI-generated arguments and citations not warranted by existing law are prohibited.; The order specifically identifies hallucinated citations to nonexistent cases as subject to sanction.

title: Supreme Court of Virginia Rules for Generative AI Use
body: Supreme Court of Virginia
summary: The Supreme Court of Virginia’s Rules for Generative AI Use govern judicial-system users, effective June 6, 2024 and amended May 7, 2025. The rules authorize only controlled generative AI use, require training certification, prohibit DeepSeek, restrict confidential and case-related inputs, and preserve human decision-making.
keyProvisions: The rules apply to individuals subject to the Chief Justice’s administrative authority over Virginia’s judicial system.; Generative AI use is authorized only to support and enhance judicial-system functions while protecting confidentiality and security.; Users must complete compliance training and certify that they have read and will comply with the AI Rules before using generative AI.; DeepSeek applications are prohibited on court-issued devices and personal devices used for official business or connected to judicial networks.; Users may not upload non-public, proprietary, confidential, personally identifying, or case-related information into non-vetted AI tools.

title: AI literacy (Article 4 AI Act): Questions and answers
body: European Commission
summary: European Commission questions and answers, published May 2025, on the Article 4 AI literacy duty of the EU AI Act that applied from 2 February 2025. Deployers, including law firms that use AI systems in the EU, must ensure staff have sufficient AI literacy proportionate to their role, the systems used and the people affected.
keyProvisions: Article 4 applies to providers and deployers of any AI system, not only high-risk systems.; Literacy measures should be proportionate to staff roles, technical knowledge and context of use.; No mandatory training format or certification; organisations choose the approach and should document it.; National market surveillance authorities may consider AI literacy when enforcing other obligations.

title: Draft Guidelines on the Application of the Privacy Protection Law to Artificial Intelligence Systems
body: Privacy Protection Authority of Israel

Comments closed 5 June 2025; still in draft as of 4 Sep 2026. Still a draft and not read in full, so this record is unverified."}]
summary: Draft guidance explaining how the Privacy Protection Law applies across the AI lifecycle, including training and operation. It requires a lawful basis and informed consent for personal data used in AI, transparency that data is collected via an automated AI system, DPO appointment and impact assessments, and internal policies restricting employee use of external generative AI tools.
keyProvisions: A lawful basis is required for personal data processing at every stage of an AI system's lifecycle, including model training.; Informed consent must disclose that data is being collected via an AI-based automated system.; Controllers must appoint DPOs, run data protection impact assessments and adopt written policies on generative AI use.; Unauthorised web scraping for AI training without consent is not permitted.; Data subject rights of access, correction and deletion apply and may require changes to the model.

summary: The Supreme Court of Guam’s administrative order adopts a judiciary-wide AI policy effective May 1, 2025. The policy covers attorneys, litigants, judges, and court personnel; says AI use should not be discouraged; does not mandate pleading disclosure; requires thorough review of AI-generated submissions; and protects sensitive information.
keyProvisions: The Supreme Court adopts the Judiciary of Guam Policy on Artificial Intelligence effective May 1, 2025.; The policy applies to judiciary employees, attorneys, judges, court personnel, and litigants.; Disclosure of AI usage should not be mandated in court pleadings.; All users must thoroughly review AI-generated content before submission in judicial proceedings.; AI applications must not compromise confidential communications, personal identifying information, health information, public safety data, or security-related information.; Judges remain ultimately responsible for their decisions.

title: Alaska Bar Association Ethics Opinion 2025-1: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law
body: Alaska Bar Association Ethics Committee

summary: Alaska's generative-AI ethics opinion. Lawyers may use generative AI but must understand it, review all output, protect client confidences through closed systems or anonymisation, disclose the basis of any AI charge within a reasonable time of engagement, avoid billing for time not worked, and supervise staff using AI.
keyProvisions: A lawyer may use generative AI but must first reasonably understand how it works, its limits and whether it safeguards client confidences; All AI output must be carefully reviewed before use or submission (ARPC 1.1, 3.3); Before inputting client confidences the lawyer must review data-retention, data-sharing and self-learning policies; if unprotected, inputs must be anonymised; AI costs may be billed only if the client's liability and the basis of computation are disclosed within a reasonable time after the representation begins (ARPC 1.5); Time saved by AI may not be billed as if worked manually; fees must remain reasonable and proportionate; Lawyers must comply where a court requires disclosure of generative AI use; Supervising lawyers must understand the technology well enough to oversee its use (ARPC 5.1, 5.3)

title: VIAC Note on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Arbitration Proceedings
body: Vienna International Arbitral Centre
summary: A short non-binding note published by VIAC in April 2025 for arbitrations under the Vienna Rules 2021. Six headings cover ethical rules, non-delegation of decision-making, confidentiality, responsible and competent use, management of AI use at the case-management conference, and evidence. Arbitrators may inform parties of the AI tools they plan to use and invite comment.
keyProvisions: Para 2: arbitrators retain full control over decisions and shall not delegate any decision to an AI tool.; Para 3: arbitrators and parties must ensure AI tools comply with confidentiality obligations and prevent unauthorised access to case data.; Para 4.2: arbitrators and parties are responsible for the outputs of the AI tools they use.; Para 5: AI use, disclosure and cost or time impact may be addressed at the case-management conference or in Procedural Order No. 1.; Para 6: admissibility, relevance and weight of AI-produced evidence are for the tribunal's discretion.

title: Ishfaq Ahmed v Mushtaq Ahmed, 2025 SCP 112 (PLD 2025 SC 582)

summary: Supreme Court of Pakistan judgment of April 2025 in a rent dispute in which Justice Syed Mansoor Ali Shah examined AI in the judiciary: AI can assist with research, drafting and case management but cannot replace judicial discretion, must respect the Article 10A fair-trial right, and hallucinated references require human verification.

title: Rules on the use of AI tools in advocacy practice (SAK Presidium Resolution 12/4/2025, as amended by 21/14/2025)
body: Slovak Bar Association, Presidium [Predsedníctvo Slovenskej advokátskej komory, SAK]
requirements: confidentiality; consent; verification; competence; supervision; record-keeping; prohibition
versions: [{"version":"12/4/2025","date":"2025-03-31","url":"https://sak.sk/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Uznesenie_12-4-2025_plne-znenie-k-25-11-2025-ff2a4b92.pdf","changes":"Original resolution adopted under § 75(1) of Act No. 586/2003 Coll. on Advocacy; effective 1 May 2025."},{"version":"21/14/2025 consolidated","date":"2025-11-25","url":"https://sak.sk/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Uznesenie_12-4-2025_plne-znenie-k-25-11-2025-ff2a4b92.pdf","changes":"Amending resolution of 6 Nov 2025 adding a ten-article methodological guidance and model client clauses; published in Vestník SAK issue 87 and effective 25 Nov 2025."}]
summary: Binding Slovak Bar rules on AI in legal practice. Confidential information and personal data may enter AI tools only in one of three modes: a local on-premise tool, a GDPR Art. 28 processor with a no-training guarantee, or express informed client consent waiving confidentiality. Verification of output is mandatory; billing self-training time is barred.
keyProvisions: Art. 3: AI use must not compromise independence, confidentiality, professional secrecy or conflict rules; the lawyer retains full responsibility for outputs used; AI does not replace professional judgement or legal argument.; Art. 4: confidential information and personal data must not be entered into AI tools except in mode (a) local tool under the lawyer's exclusive control, (b) express informed client consent, or (c) a GDPR Art. 28 processor with contractual confidentiality.; Guidance Art. 3(3): relying on AI output without human review is impermissible; the lawyer must actively verify facts, citations, legislation and legal conclusions to avoid hallucinations. Guidance Art. 3(4): the lawyer must demonstrably train trainees and staff.; Guidance Art. 6: mode (c) requires cumulative minimums — DPA, chain-wide contractual confidentiality, explicit no-training policy, sub-processor transparency, encryption in transit and at rest, MFA, EEA-preferred data location, retention and deletion policies. Enterprise versions strongly recommended; beta versions barred for protected data.; Guidance Art. 7: mode (b) consent operates as a waiver of confidentiality under § 23(2) of the Act on Advocacy, for a named provider and specific purpose, after disclosure of data-loss, training-use, third-country-transfer and hallucination risks.; Guidance Art. 8: clients must be informed of AI use where it may materially affect strategy, key decisions or the fee; a lawyer must not charge the client for time spent training themselves on the tool.; Guidance Art. 9: firms must adopt internal AI rules; recommended controls include an approved/prohibited tool list, regular team training, an AI-use register logging tool, mode and confirmation of human verification, and updated privacy notices naming AI providers.
