title: Nigeria Data Protection Act General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025 — Articles 43 and 44 (Emerging Technologies)
body: Nigeria Data Protection Commission
versions: [{"version":"NDPC/NDP ACT-GAID/01/2025","date":"2025-03-20","url":"https://ndpc.gov.ng/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/NDP-ACT-GAID-2025-MARCH-20TH.pdf","changes":"Issued 20 March 2025 (instrument dated 19 December 2024); effective 19 September 2025; replaces the NDPR 2019 as the operative implementing instrument."}]
summary: The binding directive implementing Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023. Article 43 imposes obligations on any controller or processor deploying artificial intelligence to process personal data — documented technical and organisational parameters, a DPIA filed with the Commission, anonymisation and low-risk testing, disparate-outcome review, and continuous monitoring after deployment.
keyProvisions: Article 43(1): controllers deploying emerging technologies such as AI must take account of the NDP Act, public policy and the GAID to safeguard data-subject privacy.; Article 43(2): design parameters must reflect the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions, the right to be forgotten, sensitive-data and child safeguards, cross-border rules, and privacy by design and default.; Article 43(3)-(4): parameters and the DPIA must be documented and filed with the Commission as part of Compliance Audit Returns; the DPIA must assess disparate outcomes and Data Subjects' Vulnerability Indexes.; Article 43(4)(b)-(e): assess anonymisation, test in low-risk environments, retool and retest, or discard tools posing unmitigable privacy risk; deploy continuous monitoring once judged safe.; Article 44(3): controllers must refrain from or cease using AI systems impossible to operate in compliance with international human rights law.

body: 21st and 335th Judicial District Courts of Texas — Judge Carson Campbell; Judge John D. Winkelmann
bodyShort: 21st and 335th Judicial District Courts of Texas (Judge Winkelmann)
summary: The 21st and 335th Judicial District standing order covers cases in Burleson, Lee, and Washington Counties. Attorneys and self-represented litigants using AI for legal research or drafting must submit a certification that AI-created language, citations, arguments, and legal analysis were verified through traditional sources by a lawyer.
keyProvisions: Applies to cases in Burleson, Lee, and Washington Counties.; Filers using AI for legal research or drafting must sign and submit a certification form before using AI-generated information.; The certification requires human/traditional-source verification of AI-created legal content.

title: Communiqué de presse — IA et protection des données à caractère personnel
body: National Commission for the Control of Personal Data Protection [Commission Nationale de Contrôle de la Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel, CNDP]

summary: Morocco's data protection authority's first public position on AI, issued in Rabat on 18 March 2025. It confirms that AI processing of personal data is governed by Law 09-08, flags automated decision-making as requiring particular safeguards, and announces that work on a dedicated deliberation on AI processing has begun.
keyProvisions: Lorsqu'ils utilisent les données à caractère personnel, les traitements d'intelligence artificielle (IA) sont encadrés par la loi 09-08.; Automated decisions require particular attention to integrity, transparency, fairness and legibility so that citizens always retain access to a route of recourse.; Work on a CNDP deliberation on AI processing has been initiated, following an international benchmark and consultation with foreign data protection authorities.; Opens hearings with national and international experts, scientific and professional organisations, institutions and civil society. No deliberation adopted as at 4 September 2026.

body: Nova Scotia Court of Appeal

summary: A notice of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal issued on 14 March 2025 governing the use of artificial intelligence in appeal proceedings. It requires parties and counsel to verify every authority and every piece of analysis derived from AI against authoritative sources before it is included in appeal materials.
keyProvisions: AI-derived authorities and analysis in appeal materials must be verified against authoritative sources.

title: Tribunale di Firenze, Sezione Imprese, order of 14 March 2025 (ChatGPT-invented Cassazione citations)
body: Court of Florence (Tribunale di Firenze)
versions: [{"version":"Order 14 March 2025, RG 11053/2024","date":"2025-03-14","url":"https://www.litis.it/2025/04/22/chatgpt-in-tribunale-le-allucinazioni-dellia-imbarazzano-un-avvocato-a-firenze/","changes":"Reported by Litis.it; official text not obtained."}]
summary: First reported Italian hallucination case. In an IP interim appeal the respondent's brief cited Cassazione rulings that did not exist; counsel said a trainee had used ChatGPT without his knowledge. The court rejected an Article 96 c.p.c. reckless-litigation claim because the citations did not affect the defence and no bad faith was shown, but censured the failure to verify.
keyProvisions: Failure to verify AI-generated citations is censured even where no sanction follows.; Art. 96 c.p.c. requires bad faith or gross negligence plus concrete effect on the proceedings.; The signing lawyer answers for a collaborator's undisclosed AI use.

title: Resolução CNJ nº 615/2025: Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Judiciary
body: Conselho Nacional de Justiça
summary: Resolution 615/2025 of Brazil's National Council of Justice, approved 11 March 2025 and effective 14 July 2025, replaces Resolution 332/2020 and governs AI across the Brazilian judiciary. It classifies AI uses by risk, requires mandatory human supervision of AI output, creates a National AI Committee, and permits judges and staff to use large language models within those controls.
keyProvisions: Establishes risk classification for AI systems used by courts, with high-risk uses subject to stricter controls.; Mandatory human supervision of all AI-assisted judicial work.; Creates a National AI Committee within the CNJ to oversee compliance.; Permits use of generative AI and LLMs by judges and staff subject to the resolution.; Replaces Resolution 332/2020.

title: NCAT Procedural Direction 7: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI)
body: New South Wales Civil and Administrative Tribunal
versions: [{"version":"Issued 7 March 2025, commenced 7 April 2025","date":"2025-03-07","url":"https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/dcj/ctsd/ncat/documents/procedural-directions/ncat-pd7-use-of-generative-ai.pdf","changes":"Based on Practice Note SC Gen 23, modified for the tribunal's jurisdictions."}]
summary: NCAT's procedural direction extends the New South Wales Supreme Court's generative-AI regime to Australia's busiest tribunal. It bars Gen AI from the content of statements, affidavits, statutory declarations and character references, requires verification that must not itself be done with an AI tool, and restricts what may be entered into any program.
keyProvisions: Gen AI must not generate the content of statements, affidavits, statutory declarations, character references or other evidentiary material, nor be used to alter, embellish, strengthen, dilute or rephrase a witness's written evidence.; Information subject to non-disclosure or non-publication orders, statutory publication restrictions, or produced under summons must not be entered into any Gen AI program unless the platform is contractually closed and does not train on the data.; Permitted uses include chronologies, indexes, witness lists, briefs, document and transcript summaries, and written submissions.; Where Gen AI assisted in written submissions, parties must verify in the body of the submissions that all citations, authorities and legislative references exist, are accurate and are relevant.; That verification must not be carried out solely by using a Gen AI tool.; Leave may be sought in exceptional cases to use Gen AI for an annexure or exhibit, identifying the program, version, whether it is open or closed source, and the benefit.
sources: [{"label":"NCAT — Procedural Direction 7 (official PDF)","url":"https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/dcj/ctsd/ncat/documents/procedural-directions/ncat-pd7-use-of-generative-ai.pdf"}]

title: Measures for Labelling AI-Generated and Synthesised Content
body: Cyberspace Administration of China with MIIT, MPS and NRTA
summary: Regulation in force from 1 September 2025 requiring providers to attach explicit labels and implicit metadata labels identifying provider and generation details to AI-generated text, audio, images and video, and requiring distribution platforms to verify metadata and add notices. Relevant to authentication of AI-generated material in litigation, although not itself an evidence rule.
keyProvisions: Explicit labels on AI-generated text, audio, images and video.; Implicit metadata labels carrying provider identification.; Platforms must check metadata and flag AI-generated content.

keyProvisions: Applies to AI use in citations of legal authority filed in cases assigned to Judge Scott.; The filer must disclose that generative AI assisted with citation of legal authority.; The filer must disclose the specific generative AI program used.; The filer must certify every citation of legal authority has been verified as accurate.

title: AAA-ICDR Guidance on Arbitrators' Use of AI Tools
body: American Arbitration Association - International Centre for Dispute Resolution

summary: A two-page March 2025 note encouraging AAA-ICDR arbitrators to use AI tools within their ethical codes: verify outputs against primary sources, retain complete control over decision-making under Canon V, disclose generative-AI use when it materially affects the process or reasoning, keep confidential information out of tools without data-protection guarantees under Canon VI, and stay competent.
keyProvisions: Arbitrators should critically evaluate and verify AI outputs and cross-reference them against primary sources.; Canon V: arbitrators retain complete control over decision-making; AI must support, not replace, judgment.; Arbitrators should disclose generative-AI use when it materially affects the process or the reasoning of decisions.; Do not enter party names or case specifics into tools that do not guarantee data protection.

summary: A practical resource from the Law Society of Alberta, first published January 2024 and updated March 2025, setting out rules of engagement for Canadian lawyers using generative AI. It is permissive with cautions: verify everything, protect confidentiality and privilege, understand the tool, comply with court disclosure directions, and keep the lawyer accountable for the work.

title: State Bar of Michigan: AI FAQs for Attorneys
body: State Bar of Michigan, Ethics and Practice Management Resource Center
summary: Michigan's operative AI guidance is a set of State Bar FAQs rather than a formal RI opinion. They impose verification, client-consent, vendor-security, billing and supervision duties under the MRPC, and adopt Ethics Opinion RI-381 as the vendor due-diligence standard for AI providers.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must understand AI capabilities and limitations including hallucination risk (MRPC 1.1) and must verify all AI-generated citations and text before filing (MRPC 1.3); Client consent is required before inputting protected client information into any AI tool, and the provider's security measures must be evaluated per Ethics Opinion RI-381 (MRPC 1.6(c)(1)); Where AI shortens a task, a lawyer may bill only the actual time worked; AI subscription costs are firm overhead and may not be passed to clients absent advance agreement; per-use transactional AI costs may be billed as out-of-pocket expenses if disclosed in the engagement agreement; A firm may not bill clients for time spent learning to use AI tools; Managing and supervising lawyers must ensure firm personnel comply with the MRPC when using AI (MRPC 5.1, 5.3); Submitting AI-hallucinated citations to a court violates MRPC 3.3; No blanket duty to disclose AI use to clients unless it implicates confidentiality, a court order, or materially affects the representation
sources: [{"label":"State Bar of Michigan AI FAQs","url":"https://www.michbar.org/opinions/ethics/AIFAQs"},{"label":"SBM Ethics Opinion RI-381","url":"https://www.michbar.org/opinions/ethics/numbered_opinions/RI-381"}]

title: Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices (Article 5 AI Act)
body: European Commission
summary: Interpretive guidelines from the European Commission, published 4 February 2025, explaining the prohibited AI practices in Article 5 of the EU AI Act, which applied from 2 February 2025. The guidelines are non-binding but set out how the Commission reads the bans on manipulative techniques, social scoring, untargeted facial scraping and emotion recognition in workplaces.
keyProvisions: Explains each Article 5 prohibition with examples and scope boundaries.; Non-binding; authoritative interpretation ultimately rests with the Court of Justice.; Applies to providers and deployers of AI systems placed on the EU market.

title: Richtlijnen voor advocaten voor het gebruik van Artificiële Intelligentie (OVB/Avocats.be guidelines on AI for lawyers)
body: Orde van Vlaamse Balies and Ordre des barreaux francophones et germanophone (Avocats.be)
versions: [{"version":"First version (bilingual NL/FR)","date":"2025-02-01","url":"https://www.ordevanvlaamsebalies.be/ovb_filesystem/ovb/OVB_OBFG_Richtlijnen-AI-Advocaten.pdf","changes":"Joint guidelines of the two Belgian bar federations, announced 31 January 2025 and dated 1 February 2025."}]
summary: Joint guidelines of Belgium's two bar federations, dated 1 February 2025, on lawyers' use of AI. They add no new deontological duties but apply existing ones: AI is neither forbidden nor mandatory, cited sources must be verified, professional secrecy must never enter a tool, and there is no duty to tell clients AI was used.
keyProvisions: 'Het gebruik van AI is niet verboden, noch verplicht' — use is a matter of the lawyer's own freedom and responsibility.; The lawyer must know the basics of AI and large language models.; The lawyer verifies the result including the sources cited — that the legislation, doctrine and case law relied on actually exist.; No documents or information covered by professional secrecy may be entered into an AI tool, unless the lawyer is absolutely certain it runs in a closed environment with adequate safeguards.; Personal data must be pseudonymised and kept out of prompts; where processing is essential the lawyer is transparent and seeks consent or another legal basis.; There is no duty to communicate AI use to the client, any more than for other IT applications; chatbot users must be told the system is automated.; Terms of use must be examined for training, transfer and storage, further processing, localisation, open/closed character, liability and IP/licence conditions.

title: Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Judiciary (Judicial AI Research Group)

summary: Non-binding guidelines finalised in February 2025 by the Judicial AI Research Group, a study society of judges founded in October 2023. They propose that courts may require parties to disclose AI use in submitted documents, including the tool, prompts and verification steps; warn about deepfake evidence; and state that existing procedural law governs admissibility.
keyProvisions: Courts may ask parties whether AI was used to prepare documents, images, audio or video and request tool, prompt and verification details.; Existing civil and criminal procedure rules govern admissibility of AI-generated evidence.; LLM outputs may contain fabricated citations and must be checked.

title: Oregon State Bar Formal Opinion 2025-205: Artificial Intelligence Tools
body: Oregon State Bar
summary: Formal Opinion 2025-205 from the Oregon State Bar, issued February 2025, applies the Oregon Rules of Professional Conduct to lawyers' use of AI tools. Lawyers must understand the tool they use, verify its output before relying on it, protect client confidentiality when entering information, and supervise nonlawyer and vendor use. A 2026 companion opinion addresses chatbots and AI agents.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must understand the capabilities and limits of the AI tools they use.; AI output must be verified; lawyers remain responsible for accuracy.; Client confidential information requires safeguards before entry into AI tools.; Supervisory duties extend to staff and vendors using AI on client matters.
sources: [{"label":"Oregon State Bar — Formal Opinion 2025-205 (PDF)","url":"https://www.osbar.org/_docs/ethics/2025-205.pdf"}]

title: Opinion 705: Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Professional Ethics Committee for the State Bar of Texas
summary: Opinion 705 from the Professional Ethics Committee for the State Bar of Texas, issued February 2025, addresses lawyers' use of generative AI under the Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct. Lawyers must understand the tools they use, protect client confidentiality, verify all output before reliance, supervise staff, and charge only for time actually spent.
keyProvisions: Competence requires a reasonable understanding of the generative AI tool and its risks.; Confidential client information must be protected; lawyers should review tool terms on data use.; AI-generated legal research and drafting must be verified for accuracy.; Lawyers may not bill clients for time not actually expended.
sources: [{"label":"Texas Center for Legal Ethics — Opinion 705","url":"https://www.legalethicstexas.com/resources/opinions/opinion-705/"}]

It sets approval, confidentiality, verification and accountability requirements for judges and court employees rather than for litigants.

title: Practice Note SC Gen 23: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Supreme Court of New South Wales

It prohibits using generative AI to draft affidavits, witness statements or expert reports without leave, requires affidavits to disclose that AI was not used, and holds practitioners responsible for verifying submissions.

title: Guidance on privacy and the use of commercially available AI products
body: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
summary: OAIC guidance applying the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles to organisations that deploy commercially available AI products. Privacy obligations attach to personal information input into an AI system and to output containing personal information, and the OAIC advises against putting personal information into publicly available generative AI tools.
keyProvisions: Due diligence is required on AI product selection, covering training data, security and third-party access.; APP 6 limits use of personal information input into AI systems to the primary purpose of collection absent consent or a reasonable-expectations exception.; AI-generated or inferred personal information is a collection under APP 3, requiring necessity, lawful and fair means, and consent for sensitive information.; APP 10 requires reasonable steps to ensure the accuracy of AI-generated personal information.; Privacy policies must disclose AI use and public-facing AI tools must be identified as such.; Best practice is not to enter personal information, especially sensitive information, into publicly available generative AI tools.
sources: [{"label":"OAIC — guidance on privacy and commercially available AI products","url":"https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-guidance-for-organisations-and-government-agencies/guidance-on-privacy-and-the-use-of-commercially-available-ai-products"}]

title: Rulebook on the anonymisation, publication and search of anonymised court decisions (NN 124/24)
body: Ministry of Justice, Public Administration and Digital Transformation (Ministarstvo pravosuda, uprave i digitalne transformacije)

summary: Implements the 2024 Courts Act duty to publish all court decisions. The ANON AI system performs automatic and semi-automatic anonymisation, metadata extraction and thematic classification; first-instance decisions are anonymised automatically, while higher-court and Supreme Court decisions are anonymised by authorised staff from ANON's proposals. The judge may order further anonymisation where persons could be identified.
keyProvisions: ANON AI system for anonymisation and indexing of published decisions.; Human authorised operators finalise anonymisation for higher courts and the Supreme Court.; Art. 3(3): the judge retains discretion to order further anonymisation.

title: Al-Hamim v. Star Hearthstone, LLC, 2024 COA 128 (Colo. Ct. App. 26 Dec 2024)
body: Colorado Court of Appeals
summary: The Colorado Court of Appeals published Al-Hamim to address AI hallucinations in appellate briefing. It held that fictitious AI-generated citations violate C.A.R. 28(a)(7)(B), exercised discretion not to sanction the self-represented appellant, and warned that future AI-hallucinated filings may result in sanctions.
keyProvisions: Submitting a brief containing AI-generated fictitious citations violates C.A.R. 28(a)(7)(B); The division declined to sanction the self-represented litigant but stated it will not look kindly on similar infractions in the future; First Colorado appellate treatment of the appropriate sanction for generative AI hallucinations

title: NPC Advisory No. 2024-04: Application of the Data Privacy Act to AI Systems Processing Personal Data
body: National Privacy Commission
summary: The National Privacy Commission's advisory applying Republic Act 10173, its implementing rules and NPC issuances to AI systems that process personal data across development, training, testing and deployment. It is the Philippines' baseline data-protection instrument for legal-sector AI use by firms and public bodies alike.

title: Illinois Supreme Court Policy on Artificial Intelligence
body: Supreme Court of Illinois
summary: A statewide policy from the Supreme Court of Illinois, effective 1 January 2025, authorising the use of AI by litigants, lawyers, judges and court staff. It deliberately does not require disclosure of AI use in pleadings, relying on existing rules of professional conduct and civil procedure to police accuracy, and warns that AI must not compromise due process or privacy.
keyProvisions: Use of AI by lawyers and self-represented litigants is permitted and expected to expand.; No requirement to disclose AI use in pleadings; existing rules on accuracy and candor apply.; Judges and court staff may use AI but retain full responsibility for decisions and work product.; AI use must not undermine due process, equal protection or access to justice.

title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
body: European Data Protection Board
versions: [{"version":"Adopted","date":"2024-12-17","url":"https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2024-12/edpb_opinion_202428_ai-models_en.pdf","changes":"Original opinion adopted under Article 64(2) GDPR at the request of the Irish supervisory authority."}]
summary: An EDPB opinion adopted on 17 December 2024 answering when an AI model can be treated as anonymous, how controllers justify legitimate interest at the development and deployment stages, and what follows if training data was processed unlawfully. It matters to law firms and legal-tech vendors deploying AI on personal data in the EU.
keyProvisions: Anonymity of an AI model must be assessed case by case; the mere absence of stored personal data is not enough.; Applies the three-step legitimate interest assessment from Guidelines 1/2024 to AI development and deployment.; Unlawful processing at the development stage may lead supervisory authorities to order fines, processing limitations, dataset erasure or model retraining.

title: Acuerdo PCSJA24-12243: Guidelines for the respectful, responsible, safe and ethical use of AI in the Judicial Branch
body: Superior Council of the Judiciary (Consejo Superior de la Judicatura)
requirements: verification; disclosure; prohibition; confidentiality; competence; supervision; record-keeping
versions: [{"version":"Original (in force on publication)","date":"2024-12-16","url":"https://www.ramajudicial.gov.co/documents/164295699/174277484/PCSJA24-12243.-USO-Y-APROVECHAMIENTO-DE-IA-EN-LA-RAMA-JUDICIAL.pdf","changes":"Initial guidelines, issued in compliance with Sentencia T-323/2024."}]
summary: Binding guidelines for all Colombian judges and judicial employees. Article 8 bars free commercial chatbots, use of AI to assess evidence, weigh facts or decide, and entry of personal or confidential data into tools that retain inputs; article 9 requires verification of every output; article 10 requires express disclosure in the file of tool, model, date, purpose and prompts.
keyProvisions: Art. 8(3)-(4): no AI for evidence assessment, fact-finding, value judgments or motivating decisions solely on AI output.; Art. 8(6): no personal, sensitive or confidential data in tools that retain or retrain on inputs.; Art. 9: verify the veracity, relevance and sufficiency of results and cited sources.; Art. 10: disclose in the decision the tool, model, provider, date, purpose, prompts and the passages reproduced.; Art. 13: Judicial School training plan; art. 14: report AI initiatives and malfunctions to the Digital Transformation Unit.

title: Statement on the use of artificial intelligence in Australian legal practice
body: Victorian Legal Services Board and Commissioner, Law Society of New South Wales and Legal Practice Board of Western Australia
summary: A joint statement issued 6 December 2024 by the regulators of Victoria, New South Wales and Western Australia on how the Legal Profession Uniform Law and conduct rules apply to AI. Solicitors must not enter confidential client information into public AI tools, must verify AI output, should disclose AI use to clients where appropriate, and remain responsible for their work.
keyProvisions: Confidential client information must not be entered into public generative AI tools.; Practitioners must verify AI output and remain responsible for advice and documents.; Clients should be told about AI use where it is relevant to the engagement or to costs.; Firms should have policies and training for responsible AI use.

It is addressed to advocates and law-office staff and sets out verification, competence and confidentiality expectations on the founding principle that the advocate, never the AI system, provides the legal service.

body: Bundesrechtsanwaltskammer (German Federal Bar)
versions: [{"version":"Stand Dezember 2024","date":"2024-12-01","url":"https://www.brak.de/fileadmin/service/publikationen/Handlungshinweise/BRAK_Leitfaden_mit_Hinweisen_zum_KI-Einsatz_Stand_12_2024.pdf","changes":"First edition, announced by BRAK on 9 January 2025. Authored by Dr Frank Remmertz, chair of the BRAK's RDG committee. Month-only date: the source gives the month, so the 1st is recorded as the date."}]
summary: The German Federal Bar's orientation guide, dated December 2024 and announced on 9 January 2025, on using AI in a law firm consistently with professional law. Eight sections read §§ 43, 43a(2), 43e BRAO and § 5 BORA onto AI tools, set out the AI Act duties that fall on lawyers as deployers, and flag copyright, tax and professional-indemnity risks.
keyProvisions: § 43 BRAO and the principle of personal performance require independent review and final control of all AI output; AI may support but not replace legal work.; § 43a(2) BRAO confidentiality: prompts should be abstract and documents anonymised; under § 43e BRAO, transmitting client secrets to a public LLM is not 'necessary' and is therefore impermissible.; § 43e BRAO requires careful provider selection, a contract in at least text form with the statutory minimum content, immediate termination if safeguards lapse, and comparable secrecy protection for foreign providers.; Neither BRAO nor BORA currently obliges a lawyer to tell the client that AI was used, though transparency and a contractual clause are recommended.; Article 4 AI Act applies to law firms as 'Betreiber' from 2 February 2025; staff instructions and training are an essential part of responsible use.; Law-firm AI tools are normally not high-risk, because Annex III point 8(a) targets judicial authorities rather than the bar.

title: Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure Rule 4.06.1(2.1) and (2.2): Certification of authenticity of authorities (O. Reg. 384/24)
body: Ontario Civil Rules Committee
summary: An amendment to Ontario's Rules of Civil Procedure, in force 1 December 2024, requiring every factum to include a certification that the person signing it is satisfied as to the authenticity of every authority cited. Authorities drawn from CanLII or official court websites are presumed authentic. The rule targets fabricated citations without naming AI.
keyProvisions: Every factum must certify that the signer is satisfied of the authenticity of each cited authority.; Authorities from CanLII, official court sites or recognised reporters are presumed authentic.; Applies to lawyers and self-represented parties filing facta in Ontario civil courts.

title: Guidelines for New South Wales Judges in respect of use of Generative AI
body: Chief Justice of New South Wales
summary: Issued by the Chief Justice of New South Wales on 21 November 2024 alongside Practice Note SC Gen 23 and developed with the other heads of jurisdiction, these guidelines apply to all courts in New South Wales. They prohibit generative AI in the reasoning and drafting of judgments and list red flags for detecting undisclosed AI use.
keyProvisions: Judges must not use generative AI in formulating reasons for judgment or in assessing or analysing evidence preparatory to reasons.; Generative AI must not be used for editing or proofing draft judgments, and no part of a draft judgment may be submitted to a generative AI program.; Any generative AI research output must be closely scrutinised and verified, and must not substitute for personal research by traditional methods.; Associates, tipstaves and researchers must disclose generative AI use to the judge and separately verify any output.; Judges may require litigants and legal representatives to disclose AI use and to give an assurance about the verification process followed.; Lists red flags of AI-generated content, including non-existent citations, out-of-jurisdiction case law, non-specific repetitive language and foreign spelling.
sources: [{"label":"Supreme Court of NSW — Generative AI Practice Note and Judicial Guidelines (official PDF)","url":"https://supremecourt.nsw.gov.au/documents/Practice-and-Procedure/Practice-Notes/general/current/PN_Generative_AI_21112024.pdf"}]

title: Arizona Steering Committee on AI and the Courts: Generative AI — Ethical Best Practices for Lawyers and Judges
body: Arizona Steering Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts
summary: Supreme Court-sponsored, non-binding Arizona guidance on generative AI for lawyers and judges. It requires users to understand the technology, check all output for accuracy rather than deferring to AI judgment, avoid entering confidential information when in doubt, refrain from billing time saved by AI, and tell prospective clients when they are dealing with an AI intake program.
keyProvisions: A lawyer must understand the benefits and risks of using generative AI; A lawyer must check all work product for accuracy and must not defer to the judgment of generative AI; When in doubt, do not enter confidential or non-public information into a generative AI tool; A lawyer billing hourly may not bill clients for time saved by using AI; Where AI is used for client intake, prospective clients must be told they are communicating with an AI program; Client disclosure is required where the client would need to know about the AI use to make an informed decision

title: Mississippi Bar Ethics Opinion No. 267: lawyers' use of generative artificial intelligence
body: The Mississippi Bar, Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility
versions: [{"version":"Opinion No. 267","date":"2024-11-14","url":"https://www.msbar.org/ethics-discipline/ethics-opinions/formal-opinions/267/","changes":"Issued by the Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility"}]
summary: Mississippi's generative-AI ethics opinion is unusually specific about client disclosure. Routine AI use needs no disclosure, but three circumstances trigger mandatory disclosure and informed consent, and the opinion imposes an affirmative, risk-calibrated verification duty plus written agreement before AI costs are billed.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must maintain a reasonable understanding of the benefits and risks of the generative AI tools they use, or draw on others with that expertise (MRPC 1.1); Affirmative duty to verify the accuracy and sufficiency of AI work product, calibrated to risk; bulk contract review may be validated on a representative subset (MRPC 1.1, 3.3); Reasonable measures to protect confidential information; avoid inputting identifiable client information where possible; informed consent required where inadvertent disclosure remains a concern (MRPC 1.6); Three mandatory client disclosure and informed consent triggers (MRPC 1.4): confidential client information will be provided to a third-party AI provider; the AI tool's cost will be charged to the client; or disclosure is required by court rules; Billing must not duplicate charges or inflate hours; if AI cost is passed to the client, informed consent and a written billing arrangement are required before billing begins (MRPC 1.5); Supervisory attorneys must ensure subordinate lawyers and nonlawyer staff comply with confidentiality and verification duties, with training and written policies (MRPC 5.1, 5.3); Does not address affirmative disclosure to tribunals absent a court standing order
sources: [{"label":"Mississippi Bar Ethics Opinion 267 landing page","url":"https://www.msbar.org/ethics-discipline/ethics-opinions/formal-opinions/267/"}]

title: Recomendacao no 001/2024: Responsible Use of Generative AI in Legal Practice
body: Federal Council of the Brazilian Bar (Conselho Federal da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil)
summary: The Brazilian Bar's first national guidance on generative AI, approved 11 November 2024 and prepared by its Cybersecurity, AI and Data Protection Observatory. Four pillars: applicable law including the LGPD, Statute and Code of Ethics; confidentiality and privacy; ethical legal practice with human supervision and verification; and prior formal communication to clients about AI use.
keyProvisions: The lawyer must formalise to the client, before use, the intention to use AI in providing services.; Professional secrecy may not be compromised; no client data in AI systems without confidentiality and security guarantees.; AI output must be supervised and verified; responsibility stays with the lawyer.; Attention to algorithmic bias and to keeping up to date on AI implications.

title: 2024 Formal Ethics Opinion 1: Use of Artificial Intelligence in a Law Practice
body: North Carolina State Bar
summary: North Carolina State Bar 2024 Formal Ethics Opinion 1, adopted 1 November 2024, permits lawyers in North Carolina to use AI in their practice while applying the Rules of Professional Conduct. Lawyers must be competent in the tools, verify output, protect confidential information, supervise staff, and are encouraged to disclose substantive AI use to clients.
keyProvisions: Lawyers may use AI tools provided they understand the technology and its limitations.; Disclosure to clients is recommended where AI is used substantively in the representation.; All AI-generated research and drafting must be verified for accuracy.; Client confidentiality must be protected in the selection and use of tools.

title: L'intelligence artificielle générative: Guide pratique pour une utilisation responsable
body: Barreau du Québec
summary: Launched on 25 October 2024, the Barreau du Quebec's practical guide to responsible use of generative AI applies the Code of Professional Conduct of Lawyers to AI-assisted practice. It requires verification, confidentiality safeguards and competence, and directs members to comply with the AI notices issued by the Quebec and federal courts.
keyProvisions: Lawyers remain responsible for AI-assisted work under the Code of Professional Conduct of Lawyers.; Members must comply with the AI notices and directives issued by the Federal Court, Quebec Court of Appeal, Superior Court, Court of Québec and municipal courts.; Accompanied by member training first delivered on 25 October 2024 and repeated since.

summary: The Judicial Council of Georgia created an Ad Hoc Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts in 2024. The official orders charge the committee with assessing generative AI risks and benefits for courts, evidence, data security, lawyer competency, judicial conduct, education, and court administration.
keyProvisions: The Chief Justice established an ad hoc committee to assess risks and benefits of generative AI on the courts.; The committee was charged with recommendations to prevent AI use from eroding public trust and confidence.; The charge includes AI evidence authentication, deepfakes, court data security, lawyer competency, and judicial conduct.; The Supreme Court of Georgia appointed committee members in administrative minutes filed October 22, 2024.

title: Interim Policy on the Use of Generative AI by Judicial Officers and Court Personnel
body: Supreme Court of Delaware
summary: An interim policy adopted by the Supreme Court of Delaware on 21 October 2024 governing how judges and court personnel across the Delaware judiciary may use generative AI. Only approved tools may be used, users must complete training, decision-making cannot be delegated to AI, and users remain responsible for verifying and protecting the confidentiality of any output.
keyProvisions: Judicial officers and staff may use only generative AI tools approved by the judiciary.; Training is required before use of an approved tool.; AI may not be used to make decisions; the human user remains fully responsible.; Confidential and non-public information must not be entered into unapproved tools.

title: Standing Order Requiring Certification Re: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Filings
body: U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado — Judge Susan Prose
summary: Magistrate Judge Susan Prose’s District of Colorado standing order requires AI-use or non-use certifications for specified filings in consent cases and referred nondispositive opposed motions. The preparer must certify human review of AI-drafted language and that legal citations are actual authority, or the filing will be stricken.
keyProvisions: In consent cases, specified motions and opposed motions must contain a certification about use or non-use of generative AI.; In referral cases, the order applies to nondispositive opposed motions referred to the magistrate judge.; The preparer must certify no AI drafting or that AI-drafted language was personally reviewed by a human.; The certification must attest that legal citations are to actual cases or cited authority.; The court will strike filings that omit the certification.

body: Delaware Judiciary
summary: The Delaware Supreme Court’s October 21, 2024 order adopts an interim GenAI policy for judicial officers, employees, law clerks, interns, externs, and volunteers. Authorized users remain responsible for GenAI output, may not delegate decision-making to GenAI, and may not enter non-public information into non-approved GenAI tools.
keyProvisions: The policy applies to authorized users in official duties and on state technology resources.; Authorized users are responsible for GenAI output accuracy and must use caution.; Decision-making functions may not be delegated to approved GenAI.; Non-public information may not be input into non-approved GenAI, and non-approved GenAI may not be used on state resources.

title: SCC Guide to the use of artificial intelligence in cases administered under the SCC Rules
body: SCC Arbitration Institute (Stockholm Chamber of Commerce)
summary: Adopted by the SCC Board on 16 October 2024, this light-touch guide offers flexible, non-mandatory guidance to tribunals and participants in SCC cases. Citing the EU AI Act's high-risk classification of AI used by tribunals, it addresses confidentiality, quality through human review of outputs, integrity through disclosure of AI use, and non-delegation of arbitral decision-making.
keyProvisions: Confidentiality: participants, especially tribunals, should understand how input data is used by AI tools.; Quality: tribunals should apply an appropriate level of review and verification to AI outputs before use.; Integrity: tribunals are encouraged to disclose any use of AI in researching or interpreting facts and law.; Non-delegation: AI may support but cannot replace arbitral decision-making or its reasoning.

title: Formal Ethics Advisory Opinion 2024-004: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
body: State Bar of New Mexico Ethics Advisory Committee
summary: Formal Opinion 2024-004 answers yes, qualified, to whether New Mexico lawyers may use generative AI. It implicates Rules 16-101, 16-103, 16-104, 16-105, 16-106, 16-109, 16-303, 16-501, 16-503 and 16-804(C) NMRA, and requires competence, independent verification of output, confidentiality safeguards, conflicts checking and reasonable fees. The opinion is advisory and not binding on tribunals.
keyProvisions: Responsible generative AI use is consistent with the duties of competence, diligence and charging reasonable fees; Lawyers must not input confidential information into tools lacking adequate confidentiality and security protections, and should obtain informed client consent before doing so; Before filing, a lawyer must independently verify the accuracy and sufficiency of all AI-generated material (Rules 16-303, 16-804(C)); Lawyers must check court, agency and local rules on whether AI use is allowed and what disclosure is required; A lawyer may bill only for time actually spent when AI reduces the work, under Rule 16-105; Prior-client information retained by an AI tool can create Rule 16-109 conflicts that must be independently ruled out

keyProvisions: No pre-emptive declaration of AI use is required unless the court asks.; The user is responsible for all content filed, including verifying citations.; Generative AI must not be used to fabricate or alter evidence.; Personal costs orders may follow the citation of non-existent authorities.

title: ABA Formal Opinion 512: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools
body: American Bar Association Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility
summary: The American Bar Association's first formal ethics opinion on generative AI, issued 29 July 2024, applies the Model Rules to lawyers across the United States. It covers competence, confidentiality with informed client consent for self-learning tools, candor to tribunals, supervision of staff and vendors, and fees. It is permissive with cautions and has no successor opinion.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must understand the benefits and risks of the generative AI tools they use (Rule 1.1).; Informed client consent is required before entering confidential information into a self-learning tool (Rule 1.6).; Output must be verified before it is relied on or filed (Rules 1.1, 3.3).; Managerial and supervisory lawyers must establish policies for AI use by staff (Rules 5.1, 5.3).; Lawyers may not bill clients for time saved by AI or for learning to use a tool (Rule 1.5).

title: Gray County Court Standing Order Regarding Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: Gray County Court — Judge Chris Porter
summary: The Gray County Court standing order requires attorneys and self-represented litigants using AI for legal research or drafting to submit a certification before using AI-generated information in court. The certification requires traditional-source verification of AI-created language, quotations, sources, citations, arguments, and legal analysis.
keyProvisions: Applies to every pending and future Gray County Court case.; AI users must sign and submit a form before using AI-generated information in a submission or proceeding.; The form certifies human verification of AI-created legal content through traditional sources.

title: Practice Direction Number 14 of 2024: Expert evidence in criminal proceedings (other than sentences)
body: Supreme Court of Queensland
summary: Queensland's expert-evidence practice direction for criminal proceedings contains the most granular AI disclosure requirement in Australia: where an expert used generative AI to formulate or express an opinion, the report must name the program used and annex complete records of the prompts given and of the outputs delivered.
keyProvisions: Where generative AI assisted in formulating or expressing an opinion, the report must specify the name of the program used and how it was used.; The report must annex a complete record of the inputs (prompts), including source material, default values and variable sets.; The report must annex a complete record of the outputs delivered by the program.; Applies to all criminal proceedings commenced by indictment presented on or after 15 July 2024, other than sentences.

body: Hudspeth County Court — Judge Joanna E. MacKenzie

title: Haikala Chambers Initial Order: Use of AI to Create Court Submissions
body: United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama — Judge Madeline H. Haikala
summary: Judge Haikala of the Northern District of Alabama permits generative AI use in preparing court submissions but requires review and verification. The chambers initial order, dated by the court PDF as of July 8, 2024, cautions attorneys and pro se litigants about accuracy and Rule 11 obligations.

title: Guidelines on the Use of Generative AI for Judges, Judicial Officers and Support Staff
body: Hong Kong Judiciary
summary: Guidelines issued by the Hong Kong Judiciary in July 2024 for judges, judicial officers and support staff on generative AI. Using generative AI for legal analysis or reasoning is not recommended, administrative uses are permitted, confidential case information must not be entered into public tools, and any output must be verified. Sectoral guidelines for the legal profession are under consultation.
keyProvisions: Generative AI for legal analysis, research or reasoning in judicial work is not recommended.; Administrative and drafting assistance uses are permitted with human review.; Confidential or sensitive case material must not be entered into public tools.; Judicial officers remain responsible for all output used.

title: SAV-Wegleitung für den Umgang mit künstlicher Intelligenz
body: Schweizerischer Anwaltsverband / Fédération Suisse des Avocats (Swiss Bar Association)
versions: [{"version":"Approved by the SAV board","date":"2024-06-14","url":"https://www.sav-fsa.ch/documents/672183/2025869/SAV_KI+Guidelines+2024.pdf/68d5eab4-c2ad-50bd-506f-7ba6af15a839","changes":"Original guideline approved by the SAV Vorstand on 14 June 2024."},{"version":"Updated version","date":"2025-02-16","url":"https://digital.sav-fsa.ch/documents/1060627/0/SAV-Wegleitung_f%C3%BCr_den_Umgang_mit_k%C3%BCnstlicher_Intelligenz_16.2.25.pdf/0b498c8a-85aa-e089-32a2-18da59ee658c","changes":"Updated to reflect the Federal Council's 12 February 2025 decisions on AI regulation and the BAKOM Auslegeordnung."}]
summary: The Swiss Bar Association's guideline on AI, approved 14 June 2024 and updated 16 February 2025. It focuses on generative AI, sets a three-route test for putting client information into a tool, requires independent verification of output, addresses liability, copyright and notification duties, and explains the Swiss, EU and Council of Europe regulatory position.
keyProvisions: Before using any AI, clarify what happens to input data, who can access it and where it is stored, having regard to the Anwaltsgeheimnis, the DSG and the Standesregeln.; Only three routes permit confidential input: an on-premise install where no data leaves the firm network; compliance with the SAV's IT-outsourcing and cloud rules; or an informed consent-and-waiver from the client.; Output must be checked independently and critically; an AI cannot verify its own output. Failure sources named are hallucination, missing or dated training data, sycophancy and bias.; The lawyer is liable for defective performance and cannot plead that the AI made the mistake; a liability limitation should be agreed with the client where lawful.; A duty to disclose AI use may arise from the provider's terms, or where the client requires or legitimately expects personal performance.; Switzerland will not transpose the EU AI Act; the Federal Council decided on 12 February 2025 to adopt the Council of Europe AI Convention and legislate sector-specifically, with an EJPD consultation draft due by the end of 2026.

title: JAMS Rules Governing Disputes Involving Artificial Intelligence Systems
body: JAMS

summary: JAMS rules and model clause for arbitrating disputes about AI systems. They are procedural rules for AI subject-matter disputes rather than guidance on participants' use of AI: JAMS proposes panelists with technical expertise, and a default AI Disputes Protective Order limits inspection of AI systems, models and training data to experts in a secured environment.
keyProvisions: Rule 15(b): JAMS proposes only panelists approved for disputes involving technical subject matter.; Rule 16.1(a): default AI Disputes Protective Order applies unless the parties agree otherwise.; Rule 16.1(b): production of AI systems and related materials is limited to experts in a secured environment, with no removal of materials.

title: Shawnee County District Court Rule 3.125: Pleadings Using Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Third Judicial District of Kansas (Shawnee County District Court)
summary: Shawnee County District Court requires both verification and disclosure. Any filer who used generative AI for any portion of a pleading must check the output for accuracy against print reporters or traditional databases and must state on the first page, in writing, that the document contains AI-generated content, with a certification of the accuracy check. Sanctions may follow a violation.
keyProvisions: Applies where any portion of a pleading or other paper was drafted using generative AI, naming ChatGPT, Harvey.AI and Google Bard as examples; Filer must verify that any generated language, materials or content was checked for accuracy using print reporters, traditional legal databases or other reliable means; Filer must disclose to the court and opposing parties at the time of filing, in writing and clearly marked on the first page, that the document contains AI-generated content; The disclosure must include a certification that the content was checked for accuracy as required by the rule; AI systems may not be factually or legally trustworthy sources of information without human verification; Violation may subject attorneys and self-represented litigants to sanctions
sources: [{"label":"Shawnee County DCR 3.125","url":"https://www.shawneecourt.org/428/DCR-3125-Pleadings-Using-Generative-Arti"}]

title: Legal Ethics Opinion 24-01: Artificial Intelligence
body: West Virginia Lawyer Disciplinary Board
summary: LEI 24-01 holds that nothing in the West Virginia Rules of Professional Conduct per se prohibits AI use in law practice. It distinguishes non-generative from generative AI, maps the main legal use cases, and requires lawyers to exercise independent judgment, communicate with clients, maintain confidentiality, keep fees reasonable, comply with advertising rules and supervise AI-assisted work.
keyProvisions: Nothing in the Rules of Professional Conduct per se prohibits a lawyer from using AI as a tool in law practice; Lawyers must check jurisdiction-specific rules and standing orders on whether generative AI is prohibited, whether disclosure is required, and whether human verification must be certified; Lawyers must exercise independent judgment and not delegate it to an AI tool; Efficiency gains must not result in double billing or falsely inflated claims of time (Rules 1.5, 8.4(c), 8.4(d)); Client confidentiality must be maintained, with particular caution about generative AI intake chatbots; AI-assisted work must be supervised as with any other assistance

title: Artificial Intelligence: Model Personal Data Protection Framework
body: Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data, Hong Kong
summary: Published on 11 June 2024, the PCPD's Model Framework gives organisations that procure, implement and use AI, including generative AI, recommendations for complying with the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance. It builds on the PCPD's 2021 guidance on the ethical development and use of AI and is structured in four parts.
keyProvisions: Part I: establish AI strategy and governance, including governance considerations for procuring AI solutions, an AI governance committee, and employee training.; Part II: conduct risk assessment and set the level of human oversight using a risk-based approach.; Part III: prepare and manage data for customisation and use of AI systems, and test, validate and continuously monitor the systems.; Part IV: communicate and engage with stakeholders, including information provision, data subject rights and explainable AI.

title: Guidelines for Judges: The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Judicial Council of Ireland
summary: Guidelines from the Judicial Council of Ireland, dated June 2024 and published in November 2025 as a living document, on Irish judges' use of generative AI. Judges may use AI for routine and administrative tasks only, must verify any output, must not enter confidential case material into public tools, and must not use AI to decide cases or draft reasoning.
keyProvisions: Generative AI may be used for routine and administrative tasks only.; Judges must verify any AI output before relying on it.; Confidential or sensitive case information must not be entered into public tools.; AI must not be used to determine outcomes or draft judicial reasoning.

title: Proposed amendment to Fifth Circuit Rule 32.3 and Form 6 (generative AI certification)
body: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
summary: In late 2023 the Fifth Circuit proposed requiring every filer to certify either that no generative AI was used or that all AI-generated text had been reviewed by a human. After public comment the court announced in June 2024 that it would not adopt the rule, relying on existing Rule 11 and candor obligations. No AI-specific rule applies.
keyProvisions: Would have required a certificate in every brief about the use of generative AI.; Not adopted; the court concluded existing rules already govern accuracy and candor.; Parties remain bound by Rule 11 and professional conduct rules for any AI-assisted filing.

title: Guidance Statement No. 37: Artificial Intelligence in Legal Practice
body: Queensland Law Society
summary: Guidance Statement No. 37 from the Queensland Law Society, issued 31 May 2024, applies the Australian Solicitors Conduct Rules to solicitors' use of AI. It is permissive with cautions: solicitors must be competent in the tools they use, protect confidentiality, verify output before reliance, supervise staff use, and consider whether to inform clients about AI use.
keyProvisions: Solicitors must understand the AI tools they use and their limitations.; Confidential client information must be protected when using AI services.; AI-generated content must be verified before it is relied on or filed.; Principals must supervise AI use by employees and set firm policies.

title: Joint Formal Opinion 2024-200: Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence
body: Pennsylvania Bar Association Committee on Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility and Philadelphia Bar Association Professional Guidance Committee
summary: A joint opinion of the Pennsylvania and Philadelphia bar ethics committees concluding that, with appropriate safeguards, lawyers may use AI consistently with the Pennsylvania Rules of Professional Conduct. It sets out twelve best practices spanning truthfulness, citation verification, competence, confidentiality, conflicts, client communication, bias, misuse, billing, professional judgment and transparency.
keyProvisions: With appropriate safeguards, lawyers may use AI in accordance with the Pennsylvania Rules of Professional Conduct; Lawyers must be competent in the use of AI technologies and must verify that citations accurately reflect the content referenced; Lawyers must safeguard client information and ensure AI systems handling it adhere to strict confidentiality measures; Lawyers must communicate with clients about their AI use and, if necessary, obtain consent before using certain AI tools; AI-related expenses must be reasonable and appropriately disclosed to clients; Lawyers should be transparent with clients, colleagues and the courts about AI use, including its limitations and uncertainties; AI does not replace personal review of cases, statutes and other legislative materials

title: Ethics of Using Artificial Intelligence in Practice (NHBA Ethics Corner)
body: New Hampshire Bar Association Ethics Committee
versions: [{"version":"Ethics Corner article","date":"2024-05-15","url":"https://www.nhbar.org/using-artificial-intelligence-in-practice/","changes":"Initial publication; companion article on drafting documents with AI"}]
summary: A practical ethics article from the New Hampshire Bar Association Ethics Committee applying NH RPC 1.1, 1.6, 3.3, 3.4 and 4.1 to generative AI. It stresses technology competence, review of vendor privacy policies before entering client data, and verification of AI output, citing Mata v. Avianca. It is guidance rather than a formal opinion.
keyProvisions: NH RPC 1.1 requires understanding how an AI system is designed and operates before relying on output; NH RPC 1.6 requires reviewing vendor terms and privacy policies before inputting client information; Lawyers must verify the accuracy of AI results and be able to explain them to a court; Unverified AI content risks Rule 11 sanctions and violations of RPC 3.3, 3.4 and 4.1; Generative AI should generally not be used to draft pleadings because that usually discloses confidential client information to the tool

body: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania — Judge Kelley B. Hodge

body: Federal Court of Canada

summary: The Israel Bar's first ethics opinion on generative AI, adopted by the National Ethics Committee as decision At/60/24 in 2024. It permits AI use but requires individual verification of AI output against external authority, bars entering client, confidential, privileged or copyright-protected material into AI platforms, and requires written client consent before client personal data enters open systems.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must individually check the reliability of AI output and corroborate it with external sources; unverifiable material must be flagged to the court.; Client personal, confidential, privileged and copyright-protected information must not be entered into AI platforms.; Explicit written client consent is required before client personal information is used in open AI systems, specifying document types and security measures.; Closed, in-house AI systems are preferred for confidential work to limit unauthorised access.; The lawyer bears full civil and ethical responsibility for AI use; unverified reliance breaches the duties of loyalty and diligence, and sanctions can run to licence revocation.

summary: Guidance of 6 May 2024 from the conference of Germany's federal and state data protection authorities on using AI applications, in particular large language models, in compliance with data protection law. It is addressed primarily to controllers deploying AI and is the reference text the BRAK directs law firms to.
keyProvisions: Define the field of use and purpose, check its lawfulness, and prefer uses that need no personal data.; No automated final decision: a human must take the decision (reflecting Art. 22 GDPR).; Distinguish closed from open systems and be transparent about training use and prompt history, with a choice where possible.; Carry out a data protection impact assessment, set internal rules, define and bind responsibility, and involve the DPO and staff representatives.; Protect employees and set up business accounts rather than personal ones; apply privacy by design and by default.

summary: Non-binding OECD standard adopted in 2019 and revised on 3 May 2024, setting five values-based principles: inclusive growth; respect for the rule of law, human rights and democratic values including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; and accountability. Its AI-system definition is used by the EU AI Act.
keyProvisions: Principle 1.2: AI actors should respect the rule of law, human rights and democratic values throughout the AI lifecycle.; Principle 1.3: transparency and responsible disclosure so people can understand and challenge AI outcomes.; Principle 1.5: accountability of AI actors, including traceability and risk management.

title: The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence: Guidelines for Responsible Use by Non-Lawyers
body: Queensland Courts
summary: Guidelines published by Queensland Courts in May 2024 for self-represented litigants using generative AI. They caution that AI chatbots can produce inaccurate or fabricated legal content, that users must verify everything against official sources before relying on it in court, and that private or confidential information should not be entered into public tools.

title: Guidelines for Litigants: Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in Litigation
body: Supreme Court of Victoria
summary: Guidelines issued by the Supreme Court of Victoria in May 2024 for litigants and practitioners using AI in litigation. They asked parties to understand the tools they used, verify output, and disclose AI use where it was material to a document before the court. They were replaced on 14 May 2026 by Practice Note SC GEN 25.
keyProvisions: Parties should understand how any AI tool works before relying on it.; AI-assisted content must be checked for accuracy, including citations.; Where AI has been used in preparing material, that use should be disclosed where relevant.; Superseded by Practice Note SC GEN 25 on 14 May 2026.

title: SVAMC Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Arbitration (First Edition)
body: Silicon Valley Arbitration and Mediation Center
summary: Published 30 April 2024, the SVAMC Guidelines are seven best-practice guidelines for parties, counsel and arbitrators using AI in international arbitration, adoptable by agreement or procedural order. They cover understanding tools, confidentiality, case-by-case disclosure, counsel's duty of competence and to verify output, AI-generated evidence, and a ban on arbitrators delegating their mandate.
keyProvisions: Guideline 3: disclosure of AI use is not required as a general matter and is decided case by case.; Guideline 4: party representatives must observe competence and diligence rules and review AI output for accuracy.; Guideline 5: parties should identify AI-generated material and its limitations.; Guideline 6: an arbitrator shall not delegate any part of their personal mandate, especially decision-making, to an AI tool.; Model clause for incorporating the Guidelines into arbitration agreements.

title: Missouri Informal Opinion 2024-11: lawyer's use of generative artificial intelligence
body: Missouri Office of Legal Ethics Counsel
versions: [{"version":"Informal Opinion 2024-11","date":"2024-04-25","url":"https://mo-legal-ethics.org/informal-opinion/2024-11/","changes":"Adopted by the Office of Legal Ethics Counsel"}]
summary: Missouri's ethics counsel answered a firm asking how to build a generative-AI policy. The opinion walks through competence and training, platform assessment and confidentiality safeguards, obedience to court AI rules, professional independence, verification of AI output as nonlawyer work, supervision, fee reasonableness and candour toward the tribunal.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must obtain education and training to determine which generative AI is appropriate for firm use (Rule 4-1.1 and Comment [6]); Before use, assess the platform's terms and conditions, the security of information input, how that information is used, and what data sources produce responses (Rule 4-1.6); Make reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorised disclosure or access, including by supervised persons (Rule 4-1.6(c), Comments [15] and [16]); Rule 4-3.4(c) prohibits knowingly disobeying an obligation under a tribunal's rules, which reaches court AI orders; Lawyers must maintain professional independence and may not rely solely on AI-generated content (Rule 4-5.4); AI-assisted work must be verified for accuracy and content as with any nonlawyer assistance (Rule 4-5.3); Managers and supervisors must ensure conformity and provide appropriate training (Rule 4-5.1, 4-5.3); Consider how generative AI affects the reasonableness of fees (Rule 4-1.5(a)); Generative AI is not always accurate, so competence and supervision are needed to avoid false statements of material fact or law to a tribunal (Rule 4-3.3)

body: Supreme Court of Hawaii
summary: The Hawaii Supreme Court’s administrative order establishes a Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts, effective April 16, 2024. The committee is charged with studying AI capabilities and risks, possible court operations uses, guidance or policies, self-represented litigant needs, and potential rule recommendations.
keyProvisions: The order establishes a Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts.; The committee is directed to research AI capabilities, limitations, and risks to the judiciary.; The committee must determine approaches for incorporating AI into court operations.; The committee may provide guidance or policies regarding AI usage.; The committee may recommend rules for legal and ethical issues arising from AI in court operations and law practice.

title: Guidance on Use of Artificial Intelligence-Based Tools in Practice Before the United States Patent and Trademark Office
body: United States Patent and Trademark Office, including PTAB and TTAB — Judge Katherine K. Vidal
bodyShort: United States Patent and Trademark Office, including PTAB and TTAB (Judge Vidal)
summary: The USPTO guidance states that AI tools are not prohibited and generally need not be disclosed in USPTO practice, including PTAB and TTAB filings, but signed AI-assisted papers must be human reviewed, supported by reasonable inquiry, checked for factual and legal accuracy, and handled to protect confidentiality and USPTO systems.
keyProvisions: The guidance applies to practice before the USPTO, including filings submitted to the PTAB and TTAB.; There is no prohibition against using computer tools, including generative AI, to draft documents for USPTO submission.; There is not presently a general duty to inform the USPTO that an AI tool was used unless specifically requested.; Any paper submitted to the USPTO must be reviewed by the party or parties presenting it, who remain responsible for the contents.; Parties should confirm facts, citations, legal contentions, and confidentiality obligations when AI tools are used.; AI systems may not obtain USPTO.gov accounts or apply a person’s signature without that person personally entering it.

body: United States Patent and Trademark Office
summary: Guidance published by the United States Patent and Trademark Office on 11 April 2024 reminding practitioners that existing signature, candor and confidentiality duties apply when AI tools are used to prepare filings. Practitioners must review AI-assisted documents before submission, must not disclose client information to tools without safeguards, and remain responsible for accuracy.
keyProvisions: Signature requirements under 37 CFR 11.18 apply to AI-drafted submissions; the signer certifies reasonable inquiry.; Duty of candor and good faith extends to AI-assisted prior-art searches and responses.; Confidential client and export-controlled information must not be entered into tools that may disclose it.; No duty to disclose AI use unless specifically required or material to patentability.

title: White Paper: Licensee Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: Law Society of Ontario
summary: The Law Society of Ontario's April 2024 white paper on licensee use of generative AI applies the Rules of Professional Conduct and Paralegal Rules to lawyers and paralegals in Ontario. It is permissive with cautions: licensees must verify output, protect confidentiality and privilege, remain competent, and need not disclose AI use to clients solely because AI was used.

title: D.C. Bar Legal Ethics Opinion 388: Attorneys' Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Client Matters
body: D.C. Bar Legal Ethics Committee
versions: [{"version":"Opinion 388","date":"2024-04-01","url":"https://www.dcbar.org/for-lawyers/legal-ethics/ethics-opinions-210-present/ethics-opinion-388","changes":"Published April 2024; the source gives a month only (published April 2024), so the day is recorded as the 1st"}]
summary: The D.C. Bar's generative-AI opinion. Lawyers must understand that GAI generates rather than retrieves, must not rely blindly on output, must check whether a product retains inputs or feeds them to other users before entering client confidences, may bill only time actually spent, and must supervise AI use by others under Rules 5.1 and 5.3.
keyProvisions: Competence includes understanding enough about the technology to be reasonably confident it will advance the client's interests (Rule 1.1); Generative AI is not a search engine over a database; lawyers who rely blindly on GAI output do so at considerable peril; Before entering client confidences, determine whether the product saves the information and whether the interaction will affect answers given to future users outside the firm (Rule 1.6); Where a fee is based solely on time spent, a lawyer may bill only for time actually spent even if GAI reduces it (Rule 1.5); Absent prior agreement, a lawyer may not charge separately for the perceived value of GAI work but may pass through out-of-pocket GAI expenses the client agreed to pay; Lawyers must be attentive to candour and fairness duties, especially before tribunals that have adopted AI rules or orders (Rules 3.3, 3.4); Supervisory duties under Rules 5.1 and 5.3 extend to supervised lawyers' and nonlawyers' use of GAI

body: 30th District Court of Wichita County — Judge Jeff McKnight
bodyShort: 30th District Court of Wichita County (Judge McKnight)
summary: The 30th District Court of Wichita County standing order requires attorneys and self-represented litigants using AI for legal research or drafting to attach a certificate to each AI-generated pleading. It also prohibits AI in courtrooms or court offices for recording, listening to, or transcribing activities.
keyProvisions: AI users must attach the certification to each pleading generated using AI.; The certification requires traditional-source human verification of AI-created language, citations, and legal analysis.; AI recording, listening, or transcription in courtrooms and court offices is strictly prohibited.

title: KBA E-457: The Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
body: Kentucky Bar Association Ethics Committee
summary: Kentucky Bar Association Ethics Opinion E-457, issued 15 March 2024, addresses generative AI under the Kentucky Rules of Professional Conduct. Lawyers may use AI but must be competent in the technology, verify its output, protect client confidences, and supervise staff. There is no mandatory duty to disclose AI use to clients unless the client asks or the use is material.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must understand the AI tools they use and their risks.; No mandatory disclosure of AI use to clients absent a client request or material impact on the representation.; AI output must be verified before use in client work or court filings.; Confidential information requires safeguards before entry into third-party tools.; Supervisors are responsible for AI use by subordinate lawyers and nonlawyers.

keyProvisions: The PDPA applies to personal data used to design, train and deploy AI systems.; Sets out when the business improvement exception and the research exception permit use of personal data in AI development.; Addresses notification and consent for collection and use of personal data at deployment.; Addresses obligations of organisations that procure AI systems processing personal data.

title: Responsible AI Policy Framework v2.1
body: Connecticut Judicial Branch
summary: An internal governance framework adopted by the Connecticut Judicial Branch on 1 February 2024 for how the branch itself procures, deploys and monitors AI systems. It sets principles of accountability, transparency, fairness and security for court technology, requires risk assessment before deployment, and keeps human decision-makers responsible. It does not regulate filings by lawyers or litigants.
keyProvisions: AI systems used by the branch must be inventoried and risk-assessed before deployment.; Human oversight is required for any AI that affects court operations or the public.; Procurement must address data security, bias testing and vendor accountability.

title: Preliminary Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence by New Jersey Lawyers
body: Supreme Court of New Jersey (Notice to the Bar)
summary: Preliminary guidelines issued by the Supreme Court of New Jersey on 24 January 2024 by Notice to the Bar. Lawyers in New Jersey may use AI, and there is no blanket duty to disclose that use, but the existing Rules of Professional Conduct on competence, candor, confidentiality, supervision and communication apply in full and require verification of AI output.
keyProvisions: No general obligation to disclose AI use to clients or courts absent a specific rule.; Lawyers must verify the accuracy of AI-generated research and drafting.; Confidential client information must be protected when using AI tools.; Supervisory lawyers must ensure subordinate use of AI complies with the RPCs.
sources: [{"label":"New Jersey Courts — notices to the bar","url":"https://www.njcourts.gov/notices"}]

title: Notice to the Bar: Preliminary Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence by New Jersey Lawyers
body: Supreme Court of New Jersey — Judge Stuart Rabner
bodyShort: Supreme Court of New Jersey (Judge Rabner)
summary: The New Jersey Supreme Court’s January 24, 2024 Notice to the Bar provides preliminary AI guidelines for New Jersey lawyers. It states lawyers have an ethical duty to check and verify AI-generated information, remain responsible for pleadings, arguments, and evidence, and that the RPCs do not require court disclosure of AI use.
keyProvisions: Lawyers must check and verify all AI-generated information to ensure accuracy.; The RPCs do not require lawyers to disclose AI use to the court.; Lawyers remain responsible for pleadings, arguments, evidence, and client communications using AI.; Lawyers must ensure AI system security before entering non-public client information.

title: Louisiana Supreme Court letter to the Louisiana State Bar Association on the emergence of artificial intelligence
body: Supreme Court of Louisiana, Office of the General Counsel
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2024-01-22","url":"https://www.lsba.org/documents/News/LSBANews/LASCLetterAI.pdf","changes":"Letter from the Court's General Counsel on behalf of the Justices"}]
summary: The Louisiana Supreme Court chose not to make an AI rule. Its January 2024 letter to the State Bar states existing ethical and professional rules are broad enough for AI, lists the conduct rules and Code of Civil Procedure articles that apply, confirms judges' parallel responsibilities, and notes the Court's Technology Commission and Rules Committee will monitor developments.
keyProvisions: The ethical and professional rules governing the bench and the Bar are robust and broad enough to cover the landscape of issues presented by AI in its current forms; Attorneys remain ultimately responsible for their work product and pleadings regardless of AI use, and must maintain technology competence, protect confidential client information and avoid misrepresenting fact or law; Cites Rules of Professional Conduct 1.1, 1.3, 1.4, 1.6, 1.15, 3.1, 3.3 and 5.3 and Code of Civil Procedure articles 371 and 863; Judges remain ultimately responsible for their opinions and decisions and must maintain competence in technology (Canons 1, 2A, 2B, 3A(1), 3A(4), 3A(7), 3B(1)); The Court's Technology Commission and Rules Committee will monitor whether future rule changes are needed
sources: [{"label":"Louisiana Supreme Court letter (PDF)","url":"https://www.lsba.org/documents/News/LSBANews/LASCLetterAI.pdf"}]

title: Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 24-1: Lawyers' use of generative artificial intelligence
body: The Florida Bar
summary: Ethics Opinion 24-1, issued by the Florida Bar on 19 January 2024, permits Florida lawyers to use generative AI under the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar. Lawyers must obtain informed client consent before disclosing confidential information to a third-party AI tool, must verify output, must supervise the tool like nonlawyer staff, and may not charge for AI time savings.
keyProvisions: Informed client consent is required before confidential information is disclosed to a third-party generative AI.; Lawyers must review all AI-generated work product for accuracy and completeness.; AI tools must be supervised in the same way as nonlawyer assistants.; Fees must be reasonable; lawyers may not bill clients for time saved by AI.; AI use in advertising and intake chatbots must not be misleading.
sources: [{"label":"The Florida Bar — Ethics Opinion 24-1","url":"https://www.floridabar.org/etopinions/opinion-24-1/"}]

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Guidelines for Government
body: Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority

summary: Non-binding SDAIA guidance for Saudi government entities and employees on adopting and overseeing generative AI. It sets principles, risk classifications, data-handling rules and role definitions with a compliance checklist aligned to the Personal Data Protection Law, cybersecurity rules and the AI Ethics Principles. It reaches the Ministry of Justice and the courts as government bodies.
keyProvisions: Requires transparency, accountability, privacy protection, human oversight and risk management in government generative-AI use.; Sets risk classifications and role definitions for government users of generative AI.; Includes a compliance checklist aligned with the PDPL, national cybersecurity controls and the AI Ethics Principles.; Non-binding but treated as the authoritative baseline for Saudi public-sector AI adoption.
