body: Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority
versions: [{"version":"First issue","date":"2024-01-11","url":"https://sdaia.gov.sa/en/SDAIA/about/Files/GenerativeAIPublicEN.pdf","changes":"Issued January 2024; a 2025 edition is published at the same URL. The PDF was not read in full, so this record is unverified."}]
summary: Non-binding SDAIA guidance for individuals, organisations and developers using generative AI in Saudi Arabia. It identifies key harms — misinformation, deepfakes, privacy intrusion, biased output and cybersecurity risk — and recommends disclosure of synthetic content, provenance metadata, human-in-the-loop controls and data governance. It is not addressed to legal practice.
keyProvisions: Recommends disclosure of synthetic content and use of provenance metadata.; Recommends human-in-the-loop controls and verification of generative output.; Identifies misinformation, deepfakes, privacy intrusion, bias and cybersecurity as the principal risks.

title: B 05.1 Data Security Guideline [Tietoturvaohje]
body: Finnish Bar Association [Suomen Asianajajaliitto / Suomen Asianajajat]
versions: [{"version":"9.6.2023 amendment","date":"2024-01-01","url":"https://asianajajat.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/B-05.1-Tietoturvaohje-24.1.2019-muut.-16.1.2020-ja-9.6.2023-voimassa-1.1.2024-alkaen.pdf","changes":"Delegation amendments of 9 June 2023 in force 1 Jan 2024: added competence and documented-training duty, security policy and external audit for firms of 10+ staff, business-grade software requirement, device management and access control, encryption, backup and supplier-contract terms."},{"version":"16.1.2020 amendment","date":"2020-02-01","url":"https://asianajajat.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/B-05.1-Tietoturvaohje-24.1.2019-muut.-16.1.2020-ja-9.6.2023-voimassa-1.1.2024-alkaen.pdf","changes":"Added point 4 barring audits or information requests that would collect or disclose data on client relationships or engagements to outside parties."},{"version":"Original","date":"2019-06-01","url":"https://asianajajat.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/B-05.1-Tietoturvaohje-24.1.2019-muut.-16.1.2020-ja-9.6.2023-voimassa-1.1.2024-alkaen.pdf","changes":"Guideline adopted by the Bar's delegation on 24 January 2019, in force 1 June 2019."}]
summary: The Finnish Bar's binding information-security guideline, adopted by its delegation and in force in its current form since 1 January 2024. Eighteen numbered duties on advocates covering competence and documented training, security policy, external audits, business-grade software, device and access management, encryption, backups, supplier contracts and secure disposal.
keyProvisions: Point 6: software and services used in legal practice must be intended for business use; other services may be used only with the client's consent — the hook the Bar applies to AI applications.; Point 1: the advocate must ensure their own and staff information-security competence is sufficiently high, assured by planned training, with evidence produced on request as for continuing education (B 9).; Point 14: contracts with all external service providers must meet security requirements, in particular confidentiality terms, scoped access rights with periodic review, and agreed data destruction and portability.; Points 2 and 3: firms of 10 or more employees must have a board-approved security policy and commission periodic external security audits, logged, and after significant system changes.; Point 8: devices, tables, databases and cloud services holding client data must be encrypted; devices no longer receiving updates must be retired.

title: Practical Guidance Note No. 2 of 2023: large language models and generative AI in DIFC Courts proceedings
body: Dubai International Financial Centre Courts
summary: Guidance issued by the DIFC Courts on 21 December 2023 for parties and practitioners using large language models and generative AI in proceedings. It sets out four principles — transparency, accuracy and reliability, professional and legal obligations, and avoiding over-reliance — and requires parties to declare AI-generated content at the earliest possible opportunity.
keyProvisions: All parties and the Courts should be made aware of any AI-generated content used during the process.; Parties must declare at the earliest opportunity that they have used or intend to use AI-generated content; late disclosure risks adjournment and lost trial dates.; AI-generated material must be verified for accuracy and reliability against independent sources such as case law and statutes before submission.; Practitioners must comply with the DIFC Courts Mandatory Code of Conduct and applicable data-protection and intellectual-property law.; Technology must assist submissions, not replace the integral human decision-making required.; Witness statements must remain in the intended witness's own words under RDC 29.24.
sources: [{"label":"DIFC Courts — Practical Guidance Note No. 2 of 2023 (official)","url":"https://www.difccourts.ae/rules-decisions/practice-directions/practical-guidance-note-no-2-2023-guidelines-use-large-language-models-and-generative-ai-proceedings-difc-courts"}]

title: Royal Decree-Law 6/2023: automated, proactive and assisted actions in the Administration of Justice
body: Government of Spain (Gobierno de Espana)
summary: Digital-efficiency measures for the Spanish justice system. It distinguishes automated actions of simple processing, proactive actions such as alerts, and assisted actions in which systems including AI generate full or partial drafts to support judges, prosecutors and court lawyers; a draft cannot become a resolution without the operator's intervention and validation.
keyProvisions: Arts 56-57: definitions of automated, proactive and assisted actions in the administration of justice.; Assisted drafts serve only as support and require human validation before becoming resolutions.; Art. 35: data-oriented justice enables quality draft generation.
sources: [{"label":"BOE consolidated text","url":"https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2023-25758"}]

title: Circular Letter No. 9 of 2023 on Artificial Intelligence Ethics [SE Menkominfo No. 9/2023 Etika Kecerdasan Artifisial]
body: Ministry of Communication and Digital [Kementerian Komunikasi dan Digital, Komdigi]
summary: Indonesia's only in-force AI instrument as at September 2026: a ministerial circular of 19 December 2023 setting nine ethical values for artificial intelligence, addressed to AI businesses and to public and private electronic system operators. It makes no mention of courts, judges or legal services.
keyProvisions: Sets nine ethical values: inclusivity, humanity, security, accessibility, transparency, credibility and accountability, personal data protection, sustainability, and intellectual property.; Addressed to AI businesses and public and private electronic system operators.; Contains no provisions on courts, judges or legal services.

title: Part Rules: Artificial Intelligence
body: New York State Supreme Court, Westchester County — Judge Helen M. Blackwood
bodyShort: New York State Supreme Court, Westchester County (Judge Blackwood)
summary: Justice Helen M. Blackwood’s part rules, amended December 13, 2023, require counsel and self-represented parties to disclose to the court if any portion of a written submission was generated by any form of artificial intelligence and, if so, to identify what portion used that technology.
keyProvisions: Counsel must disclose when a portion of a written submission was generated by AI.; Self-represented parties are subject to the same disclosure requirement.; The disclosure must state what portion of the submission used AI technology.

title: Notice of Proposed Amendments to Local Rules
body: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan
summary: The Eastern District of Michigan notice dated December 8, 2023, proposed a Local Rule 5.1 amendment requiring filers to disclose use of generative AI to compose or draft any paper presented for filing. It would require an attestation that citations were human-verified with traditional sources and that the paper was checked for accuracy.
keyProvisions: The notice published proposed amendments to Local Rule 5.1 for comment after approval for publication by district judges.; The proposed rule defines artificial intelligence and generative artificial intelligence.; If generative AI is used to compose or draft a paper presented for filing, the filer must disclose the use.; The filer must attest that citations of authority were verified by a human using print volumes or traditional legal databases.; The filer must also attest that the language in the paper was checked for accuracy.

title: Guidelines for use of generative artificial intelligence in Courts and Tribunals
body: Courts of New Zealand (Chief Justice)
summary: Three sets of guidelines issued by the Chief Justice of New Zealand on 7 December 2023 for judges, lawyers and non-lawyers using generative AI in courts and tribunals. Existing duties continue to apply, users must verify all AI output and protect confidential information, and there is no mandatory disclosure of AI use. The guidelines remain unchanged as of September 2026.
keyProvisions: Separate guidelines for judicial officers, lawyers and non-lawyers.; AI output must be checked for accuracy; fabricated citations are the user's responsibility.; Confidential, suppressed or private information must not be entered into public tools.; No requirement to disclose AI use in court documents.

title: CCJE Opinion No. 26 (2023): Moving forward - the use of assistive technology in the judiciary
body: Consultative Council of European Judges, Council of Europe
summary: Opinion of the Council of Europe's judges' advisory body, adopted at its 24th plenary in December 2023, on technology including AI in courts. It holds that technology must assist and not replace judicial decision-making, that judges should be involved in decisions to adopt tools, and that they should be kept up to date on technological innovation through training.
keyProvisions: Assistive technology, including AI, must support rather than replace the judge's decision-making.; Judges should be consulted and, where necessary, concur in the adoption of new technology in courts.; Judicial training must keep judges up to date with technological innovation.

title: People v. Zachariah C. Crabill, 23PDJ067 (Colo. O.P.D.J. 22 Nov 2023)
body: Colorado Office of the Presiding Disciplinary Judge
versions: [{"version":"Stipulation to discipline","date":"2023-11-22","url":"https://www.coloradolegalregulation.com/wp-content/uploads/PDJ/Decisions/Crabill,%20Stipulation%20to%20Discipline,%2023PDJ067,%2011-22-23.pdf","changes":"Approved by the Presiding Disciplinary Judge"}]
summary: Colorado's Presiding Disciplinary Judge suspended Zachariah Crabill for one year and one day, with ninety days served, after he filed ChatGPT-generated citations without reading them, failed to correct the record and blamed a legal intern. Violations found of Colo. RPC 1.1, 1.3, 3.3(a)(1) and 8.4(c).
keyProvisions: Not reading or verifying AI-generated citations before filing violated Colo. RPC 1.1 and 1.3; Failing to alert the court or withdraw the motion after discovering the citations were fictitious violated Colo. RPC 3.3(a)(1); Falsely attributing the errors to a legal intern violated Colo. RPC 8.4(c); Sanction: suspension of one year and one day, ninety days active, remainder stayed on two years' probation

title: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
body: State Bar of California (Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct)
summary: Practical guidance approved by the State Bar of California on 16 November 2023, the first state bar guidance on generative AI in the United States. California lawyers must not enter confidential client information into tools without adequate protections, must review and verify all output, should consider disclosing AI use to clients, and may not bill for time not spent.
keyProvisions: Confidential information may not be input into a tool lacking adequate confidentiality and security protections.; Lawyers must critically review AI output for accuracy and bias before use.; Disclosure to clients of generative AI use is recommended where material to the engagement.; Fees must reflect time actually spent; AI efficiency savings cannot be billed as hours.; Supervising lawyers must set policies for AI use by subordinate lawyers and staff.
sources: [{"label":"State Bar of California — AI ethics resources page","url":"https://www.calbar.ca.gov/legal-professionals/ethics-compliance-practice-resources/ethics/ethics-technology-resources/artificial-intelligence"}]

title: General Order 23-1: In Re Use of Unverified Sources
body: U.S. District Court for the District of Hawaii
summary: District of Hawaii General Order 23-1 addresses filings generated by AI platforms and other unverified sources. Counsel and pro se parties submitting such material must file a concurrent declaration identifying reliance on unverified sources and verifying that the material is not fictitious.
keyProvisions: AI platforms such as ChatGPT or Bard are included within unverified sources.; Counsel or pro se parties submitting material generated by an unverified source must file a concurrent declaration.; The declaration must be captioned Reliance on Unverified Source.; The declaration must advise the court of reliance and verify that material is not fictitious.; No declaration is required if all sources can be located on Westlaw, Lexis, Bloomberg, or similar basic research tools.

title: Guidance on Professional Responsibility and Generative AI
body: Law Society of British Columbia
summary: Guidance from the Law Society of British Columbia, issued November 2023, on how the Code of Professional Conduct applies when BC lawyers use generative AI. It is permissive with cautions, stressing that lawyers must verify output, keep client information confidential, remain competent in the technology, and understand that AI does not change their professional obligations.
keyProvisions: Lawyers remain responsible for the accuracy of AI-assisted work, including citations.; Confidential client information should not be entered into public generative AI tools.; Competence includes understanding the limits and risks of the tools used.; Lawyers should consider whether to inform clients of AI use in their matter.

title: Risk Outlook report: The use of artificial intelligence in the legal market
body: Solicitors Regulation Authority
summary: The SRA's November 2023 Risk Outlook report analyses how solicitors in England and Wales are adopting AI and the risks that follow. It is a risk analysis rather than a rule, taking a permissive stance while warning about hallucinated authorities, confidentiality of client data in public tools, and the need for firm-level controls.
keyProvisions: Identifies inaccurate or fabricated output as a principal risk of generative AI in legal work.; Warns that entering client information into public AI tools may breach confidentiality duties.; Encourages firms to understand the tools they use and to set internal policies before adoption.; Frames AI as an opportunity for access to justice provided existing professional standards are met.
sources: [{"label":"SRA — Risk Outlook report on AI in the legal market","url":"https://www.sra.org.uk/sra/research-publications/risk-outlook-report-use-ai-legal-market/"}]

body: Nova Scotia Provincial Court

It requires parties to disclose the use of AI in preparing court submissions and to protect the integrity of those submissions by verifying AI-derived material before filing.

title: State Bar of Michigan Judicial Ethics Opinion JI-155: judicial use of artificial intelligence
body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Judicial Ethics
summary: One of the earliest US judicial ethics opinions on AI. JI-155 treats technology competence as an ethical duty, requires judges to assess algorithmic bias before relying on AI, to document AI use in their reasoning on the record, and to keep decision-making human, with due-process concerns where AI is opaque.
keyProvisions: Technology competence is an ethical responsibility for all attorneys in Michigan; Judges must assess potential algorithmic bias before relying on AI tools; Judges must document their reasoning when using AI on the record; Judges must distinguish between AI informing a decision and AI deciding a matter; Judges must recognise due-process obligations where AI tools lack transparency
sources: [{"label":"SBM Judicial Ethics Opinion JI-155","url":"https://www.michbar.org/opinions/ethics/numbered_opinions/JI-155"}]

title: JIC Advisory Opinion 2023-22 (judicial use of artificial intelligence)
body: West Virginia Judicial Investigation Commission
summary: Answering an inquiry about judges' use of AI, the West Virginia Judicial Investigation Commission applied Code of Judicial Conduct Rules 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, 2.4(B), 2.5(A) and 2.7 and concluded that a judge may use AI for research but not to decide a case's outcome, and that drafting opinions or orders with AI demands extreme caution.
keyProvisions: A judge may use AI for research purposes but may not use it to decide the outcome of a case; The use of AI in drafting opinions or orders should be done with extreme caution because of built-in or perceived bias; AI is analogous to a law clerk: the judge must decide the ruling, direct the tool accordingly, and review the final draft for current law and accuracy; Responsibility for the finished product rests solely with the judge — 'AI made me do it' is no defence; Judges must research an AI product's data handling and refrain from inputting information that may be retained or disclosed, especially in juvenile and abuse-and-neglect matters; Plagiarism and attribution are additional concerns when drafting with AI
sources: [{"label":"WV JIC Advisory Opinion 2023-22 (official PDF)","url":"https://www.courtswv.gov/sites/default/pubfilesmnt/2023-11/JIC%20Advisory%20Opinion%202023-22_Redacted.pdf"}]

title: Notice to the Profession and General Public: Ensuring the Integrity of Court Submissions when Using Large Language Models
body: Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2023-10-12","url":"https://www.court.nl.ca/supreme/files/2023-10-12-Notice-to-Profession-and-General-Public-AI-Submissions.pdf","changes":"Recorded from the court's notice listing; the PDF was not read in full, so this record is unverified."}]
summary: A notice issued on 12 October 2023 by the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador to the profession and the general public, requiring anyone preparing court submissions with large language models to verify all authorities and analysis against authoritative sources before those submissions are filed with the court.
keyProvisions: Authorities generated with large language models must be verified against authoritative sources before filing.; Applies to counsel and members of the public alike.
sources: [{"label":"Courts of Newfoundland and Labrador — notice (PDF)","url":"https://www.court.nl.ca/supreme/files/2023-10-12-Notice-to-Profession-and-General-Public-AI-Submissions.pdf"}]

title: Notice to the Profession and Public: Ensuring the Integrity of Court Submissions When Using Large Language Models
body: Court of Appeal of Alberta, Court of King's Bench of Alberta and Alberta Court of Justice
summary: A joint notice issued on 6 October 2023 by all three Alberta courts. It urges caution when referencing legal authorities or analysis derived from large language models, requires reliance exclusively on authoritative sources such as official court sites, established commercial publishers or CanLII, and requires meaningful human control over AI-assisted submissions.
keyProvisions: Exercise caution when referencing legal authorities or analysis derived from large language models.; Rely exclusively on authoritative sources: official court and legislative websites, recognised commercial publishers, or CanLII.; AI-assisted submissions require meaningful human control and cross-checking against reliable legal databases before filing.
sources: [{"label":"Alberta Courts — tri-court notice (official PDF)","url":"https://albertacourts.ca/docs/default-source/qb/npp/tri-court-notice-to-profession-and-public---large-language-models.pdf?sfvrsn=713d5a82_7"},{"label":"Court of King's Bench of Alberta — announcement page","url":"https://albertacourts.ca/kb/resources/announcements/notice-to-the-profession-public---use-of-ai-in-citations-submissions"}]

body: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma — Judge Jason A. Robertson
summary: Magistrate Judge Robertson’s standing order requires parties using generative AI in preparing documents for filing to disclose that use in the document, identify the specific tool, and certify that AI-drafted portions have been checked for accuracy, including citations and legal authority.
keyProvisions: Any party using generative AI in document preparation must disclose use in the document.; The document must identify the specific AI tool used.; The filer must certify accuracy of AI-drafted portions, including citations and legal authority.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Information Privacy Principles
body: Office of the Privacy Commissioner | Te Mana Matapono Matatapu
summary: The New Zealand Privacy Commissioner's expectations for agencies using generative AI under the Privacy Act 2020, published 21 September 2023 with a companion page on generative AI. The Office approves or endorses no AI technology or provider and expects a privacy assessment before an agency uses an AI tool on personal information.
keyProvisions: The Information Privacy Principles apply to personal information put into, and produced by, AI tools.; Agencies should complete a privacy assessment before using AI tools on personal information.; The Office does not approve or endorse any AI technology or AI technology provider.
sources: [{"label":"OPC — Artificial Intelligence and the Information Privacy Principles","url":"https://www.privacy.org.nz/resources-and-learning/a-z-topics/ai/"},{"label":"OPC — Generative Artificial Intelligence","url":"https://www.privacy.org.nz/resources-and-learning/a-z-topics/ai/generative-artificial-intelligence/"}]

title: Stanovisko k užívání umělé inteligence (AI) při poskytování právních služeb
body: Czech Bar Association [Česká advokátní komora, ČAK]
versions: [{"version":"1.0","date":"2023-09-20","url":"https://www.cak.cz/cs/download/priloha_4_2023_09_-ai_stanovisko.pdf","changes":"Initial opinion, six points; issued as annex 4 to the September 2023 ČAK materials, authored by Martin Maisner."}]
summary: A six-point non-binding opinion of the Czech Bar Association. Lawyers may use any technology, including AI, provided they meet all statutory and professional duties. AI cannot itself provide legal services; entering client data into AI tools will normally breach confidentiality unless the client gives specific prior informed consent.
keyProvisions: Point 1: the Bar does not and will not restrict lawyers' use of technology, provided confidentiality, data-protection and ethics duties are met.; Point 2: AI in any form cannot be a provider of legal services within the meaning of § 1 of the Act on Advocacy (Act No. 85/1996 Coll.).; Point 4: answers addressing a concrete legal problem are legal advice reserved to authorised persons; website AI that leads a potential client to believe they are receiving lawyer's advice is 'highly inappropriate'. Using AI does not affect the lawyer's own liability.; Point 5: AI acts autonomously and unpredictably and is potentially risky as to accuracy; entering client information — even solely to train the tool — will most likely breach the statutory duty of confidentiality, for which the lawyer is always responsible.; Point 6: prior client consent must expressly state that the client knows AI may behave unpredictably and expressly permit sharing the information, even anonymised, with unspecified similar systems.
sources: [{"label":"ČAK — Stanovisko k užívání umělé inteligence (AI) při poskytování právních služeb (PDF)","url":"https://www.cak.cz/cs/download/priloha_4_2023_09_-ai_stanovisko.pdf"}]

title: DIFC Data Protection Regulations, Regulation 10 — Processing Personal Data through Autonomous and Semi-autonomous Systems
body: Dubai International Financial Centre Authority / Commissioner of Data Protection
versions: [{"version":"Enacted","date":"2023-09-01","url":"https://www.difc.com/business/registrars-and-commissioners/commissioner-of-data-protection/regulation-10","changes":"Added to the DIFC Data Protection Regulations, in force 1 September 2023."}]
summary: Regulation 10 of the DIFC Data Protection Regulations, in force 1 September 2023, is the first instrument in the Middle East, Africa and South Asia to govern personal data processed through autonomous and semi-autonomous systems, including generative AI. It sets behavioural boundaries for entities that deploy or operate such systems rather than regulating algorithms directly.
keyProvisions: Applies to entities that deploy or operate autonomous and semi-autonomous systems, including AI and generative machine-learning tools, to process personal data in the DIFC.; Requires clear notices, transparency and accountability in AI design and deployment.; Requires systems to process data for human-defined purposes, with audit and certification obligations.; Supplements, and is enforced alongside, the DIFC Data Protection Law.

summary: SDAIA's national AI ethics framework, first issued in September 2023, sets non-binding principles for AI across all Saudi sectors and applies a risk-based classification to AI systems. It is the Kingdom's principal horizontal AI instrument; Saudi Arabia has no AI statute. Nothing in it addresses legal practice or courts specifically.
keyProvisions: Non-binding ethical principles applying across public and private sectors.; Risk-based classification of AI systems.; Emphasis on transparency, secure data practices, human oversight, fairness and accountability.

title: Judicial Yuan statement on generative-AI judgment drafting for criminal cases
body: Judicial Yuan, Information Department
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2023-08-27","url":"https://www.judicial.gov.tw/tw/cp-1887-929494-8a9fb-1.html","changes":"Press release announcing the on-premises drafting system and the intention to adopt AI guidelines."}]
summary: Judicial Yuan press release of 27 August 2023 describing its generative-AI system that drafts judgment text for dangerous-driving and fraud-accessory cases, with drug offences piloted from December 2023. Fact-finding, application of law and sentencing remain entirely with the judge; the model is fine-tuned and hosted on-premises to protect privacy and official secrets.
keyProvisions: Judges alone determine facts, law and sentence; the system provides draft text only.; On-premises deployment; case data is not sent to external services.; Limited to specified offence types.
sources: [{"label":"Judicial Yuan press release (official)","url":"https://www.judicial.gov.tw/tw/cp-1887-929494-8a9fb-1.html"}]

title: Relationship between AI-based contract-drafting, review and management support services and Article 72 of the Attorney Act
body: Ministry of Justice, Judicial System Department
summary: Ministry of Justice guideline of August 2023 explaining when AI-assisted contract drafting, review and management services fall outside the Attorney Act Article 72 prohibition on unauthorised legal practice. A service breaches Article 72 only if provided for remuneration, concerning a legal case, and constituting legal affairs; generative-AI services are assessed on the same framework.
keyProvisions: Three cumulative elements: purpose of remuneration, a 'legal case', and 'legal affairs'; absence of any one takes the service outside Art. 72.; Remuneration includes indirect consideration such as subscriptions or paid upsells.; Generative-AI-based services are judged on the same framework.
sources: [{"label":"Ministry of Justice guideline (official PDF)","url":"https://www.moj.go.jp/content/001400675.pdf"}]

title: General Order 23-01: Pleadings Using Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Western District of Oklahoma
summary: The Western District of Oklahoma Bankruptcy Court requires an attestation for any filed document drafted with generative AI. The attestation must identify the tool and specific text portions, certify that the document was checked by reliable means, and certify that no confidential information was disclosed to unauthorized parties.
keyProvisions: AI-drafted documents must be accompanied by an attestation.; The attestation must identify the program and the specific AI-generated portions.; The attestation must certify accuracy checking and no unauthorized confidential disclosure.

title: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
body: Cyberspace Administration of China with the NDRC, MoE, MoST, MIIT, MPS and NRTA
summary: Horizontal regulation on public-facing generative-AI services in force since 15 August 2023. Providers must use lawfully sourced training data, obtain consent for personal data, label generated content, undergo security assessment and algorithm filing where services have public-opinion attributes, protect user inputs, and handle access, correction and deletion requests. Not specific to legal services.
keyProvisions: Security assessment and algorithm filing for services with public-opinion attributes.; Lawful training data, respect for intellectual property, and consent for personal information.; Labelling of generated images and video per the deep-synthesis rules.; Protection of user input records, with user rights and complaint channels.
sources: [{"label":"CAC text (official)","url":"https://www.cac.gov.cn/2023-07/13/c_1690898327029107.htm"}]

title: Practice Direction GENERAL-29: Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools
body: Supreme Court of Yukon
summary: Practice Direction GENERAL-29, issued by the Supreme Court of Yukon on 26 June 2023, requires any party relying on artificial intelligence for legal research or submissions to advise the court of the tool used and how it was used. It followed the Manitoba direction by three days and applies to lawyers and self-represented litigants.
keyProvisions: Parties must advise the court when AI was used for legal research or submissions.; The disclosure must identify the tool and describe its use.; Applies in all matters before the Supreme Court of Yukon.
sources: [{"label":"Yukon Courts — GENERAL-29 (PDF)","url":"https://www.yukoncourts.ca/sites/default/files/2023-06/GENERAL-29%20Use%20of%20AI.pdf"}]

title: Practice Direction: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Submissions
body: Court of King's Bench of Manitoba
summary: A practice direction issued 23 June 2023 by the Court of King's Bench of Manitoba, one of the first court rules on AI anywhere. When artificial intelligence has been used in the preparation of materials filed with the court, the materials must indicate how AI was used. The direction applies to lawyers and self-represented parties alike.
keyProvisions: Materials filed with the court must indicate how AI was used in their preparation.; Applies to all submissions by counsel and self-represented litigants.; Issued in response to concerns about reliability of AI-generated legal content.
sources: [{"label":"Manitoba Courts — practice direction (PDF)","url":"https://www.manitobacourts.mb.ca/site/assets/files/2045/practice_direction_-_use_of_artificial_intelligence_in_court_submissions.pdf"}]

title: General Order 2023-03: Pleadings Using Generative Artificial Intelligence
body: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Northern District of Texas
summary: The Northern District of Texas Bankruptcy Court’s General Order 2023-03 addresses pleadings or other papers drafted with generative AI. It requires filers to verify that AI-generated language was checked for accuracy by reliable non-AI means and warns that noncompliance may lead to Bankruptcy Rule 9011 sanctions.
keyProvisions: Any AI-drafted pleading or paper must be verified for accuracy.; Verification must use print reporters, traditional legal databases, or other reliable means.; Failure may lead to Rule 9011 sanctions.

body: United States Court of International Trade — Judge Stephen Alexander Vaden
bodyShort: United States Court of International Trade (Judge Vaden)
summary: Judge Stephen Alexander Vaden of the Court of International Trade requires any party filing AI-drafted text in his cases to provide a notice identifying the generative AI program and the specific drafted portions, and to certify that no confidential or business proprietary information was disclosed to an unauthorized party.
keyProvisions: Applies to submissions in cases assigned to Judge Vaden containing text drafted with generative AI based on natural language prompts.; Names ChatGPT and Google Bard as examples of covered generative AI programs.; Requires a disclosure notice identifying the program used and the specific portions of text drafted with it.; Requires certification that use of the program did not disclose confidential or business proprietary information to unauthorized parties.; Allows any party to seek relief under statute or USCIT rules after the notice is filed.

title: Standing Order Re: Artificial Intelligence in Cases Assigned to Judge Baylson
body: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, Judge Michael M. Baylson
summary: A standing order issued 6 June 2023 by Judge Michael Baylson of the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. Any attorney or self-represented party who used generative AI in preparing a filing must disclose that use in a clear statement and certify that every citation to law or the record has been verified as accurate. It applies to all his cases.
keyProvisions: Filers must disclose in a clear and plain statement that AI was used to prepare any part of a filing.; Filers must certify that each citation to law or the record has been verified as accurate.; Applies to attorneys and pro se litigants alike.

title: Alert on the use of generative AI services
body: Personal Information Protection Commission
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2023-06-02","url":"https://www.ppc.go.jp/news/press/2023/230602kouhou/","changes":"Original alert and administrative notice to OpenAI."}]
summary: Personal Information Protection Commission alert of 2 June 2023 cautioning businesses and public bodies on entering personal data into generative-AI prompts: use only within the stated purpose, and do not input data that may be used for model training without a legal basis. It also issued a notice to OpenAI on collection of sensitive data.
keyProvisions: Personal data entered into generative AI must stay within the notified purpose of use.; Businesses should confirm whether inputs are used for training and avoid inputting sensitive data.; Administrative notice issued to OpenAI regarding sensitive personal information.

title: Standing Order for Civil Cases (generative AI provision), Magistrate Judge Gabriel A. Fuentes
body: United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, Magistrate Judge Gabriel A. Fuentes
summary: A standing order for civil cases before Magistrate Judge Gabriel Fuentes of the Northern District of Illinois, revised 31 May 2023 to address generative AI. Any party using a generative AI tool to prepare or draft a filing must disclose that use and identify the tool, and Rule 11 verification obligations apply in full to the resulting content.
keyProvisions: Parties must disclose in the filing that generative AI was used and name the tool.; Rule 11 applies to AI-assisted filings; counsel must verify all legal authorities.; Use of AI for legal research must itself be disclosed if it informed the filing.

title: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr)
body: United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, Judge Brantley Starr
summary: The first judge-specific generative AI order in the United States federal courts, issued by Judge Brantley Starr of the Northern District of Texas on 30 May 2023. Every attorney and self-represented litigant must certify either that no generative AI was used or that any AI-generated content was checked for accuracy by a human using print reporters or traditional databases.
keyProvisions: Certificate required on the docket for every filer appearing before the judge.; Filers must attest that no portion of a filing was drafted by generative AI, or that all AI output was human-verified.; Verification must use print reporters or traditional legal databases.; Filings without the certificate may be struck; false certification exposes the filer to sanctions.
sources: [{"label":"N.D. Tex. — Judge Brantley Starr judge-specific requirements","url":"https://www.txnd.uscourts.gov/judges/brantley-starr"}]

title: Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI, 2023 v1.0
body: National Council for Artificial Intelligence, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
versions: [{"version":"1.0","date":"2023-04-19","url":"https://ai.gov.eg/SynchedFiles/en/Resources/Egyptian%20Charter%20For%20Responsible%20AI.pdf","changes":"First edition, adopted by the National Council for Artificial Intelligence."}]
summary: Egypt's first responsible-AI instrument, adopted by the National Council for Artificial Intelligence in April 2023. It is voluntary and sets principles of human-centred design, transparency, justice, accountability and security for AI development and deployment. It contains no provision addressed to courts, judges, lawyers or legal services.
keyProvisions: Voluntary principles-based charter: human-centred design, transparency, justice, accountability and security.; States that accountability must always lie with natural or legal persons and that AI systems should not be given legal personality.; Positions Egypt as an early adherent to the OECD AI Principles and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, adapting them to local context.; No sector-specific provisions for the administration of justice or the legal profession.

title: Opinions on Regulating and Strengthening the Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Judicial Field
body: Supreme People's Court of China
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2022-12-08","url":"https://english.court.gov.cn/2022-12/12/c_838810.htm","changes":"Issued 8 December 2022; the official Chinese page on court.gov.cn returned 404 on 4 September 2026."}]
summary: Supreme People's Court normative opinion of 8 December 2022 governing AI across Chinese courts. AI output may only be an auxiliary reference: it shall never substitute for the judge's decision in any case, users may decline AI assistance, and accountability remains with the decision-maker. Systems must be lawful, secure, fair and transparent.
keyProvisions: Auxiliary-adjudication principle: AI shall not substitute for judges; results are supplementary references only and users may opt out.; Security and legality: no harm to state secrets, network security, data or privacy.; Transparency and credibility: systems examined by authoritative entities, with capabilities and limits disclosed.; Fairness: prevent discrimination and remain accessible to diverse users.; Targets of integrated AI support across judicial work by 2025 and a full framework by 2030.

It is the conceptual base on which the PCPD's 2024 Model Personal Data Protection Framework is built, and it remains the office's general statement of ethical expectations for organisations developing or deploying AI.

title: Resolucao CNJ no 332/2020: Ethics, Transparency and Governance in the Production and Use of AI in the Judiciary
body: National Council of Justice (Conselho Nacional de Justica)
versions: [{"version":"Original","date":"2020-08-21","url":"https://atos.cnj.jus.br/atos/detalhar/3429","changes":"First CNJ framework for AI in courts; revoked by Resolucao 615/2025, in force 14 July 2025."}]
summary: Brazil's first judicial AI framework, issued 21 August 2020, set principles of transparency, non-discrimination, human supervision and accountability for AI models developed or used by courts, required registration on the Sinapses platform, and barred AI-based criminal sentencing recommendations. It was replaced by Resolution 615/2025, which took effect on 14 July 2025.
keyProvisions: Principles: benefit to users, non-discrimination, publicity, transparency, user control, security and governance.; AI models to be registered and shared through the CNJ Sinapses platform.; Human supervision of AI-supported decisions; no AI in criminal sentencing recommendations.; Revoked by Resolucao CNJ 615/2025.
sources: [{"label":"CNJ — Resolucao 332/2020","url":"https://atos.cnj.jus.br/atos/detalhar/3429"}]

title: European Ethical Charter on the use of artificial intelligence in judicial systems and their environment
body: European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice, Council of Europe
summary: Adopted by CEPEJ on 3-4 December 2018, the Charter sets five principles for AI in judicial systems: respect for fundamental rights, non-discrimination, quality and security, transparency, impartiality and fairness, and use under user control. It is addressed to policy makers, legislators and justice professionals and underpins CEPEJ's later assessment tool and generative-AI guidelines.
keyProvisions: Respect for fundamental rights: AI design and use must be compatible with the ECHR and data-protection law.; Non-discrimination: prevent development or intensification of discrimination between individuals or groups.; Quality and security: certified sources, multidisciplinary models, secure technological environment.; Transparency, impartiality and fairness: processing methods must be accessible and understandable, with external audits authorised.; Under user control: users must be informed actors in control of their choices; a judge may depart from AI output at any time.
sources: [{"label":"CEPEJ — European Ethical Charter (PDF)","url":"https://rm.coe.int/ethical-charter-en-for-publication-4-december-2018/16808f699c"},{"label":"CEPEJ — AI in justice systems","url":"https://www.coe.int/en/web/cepej/artificial-intelligence-in-justice-systems"}]
